```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Overlay-repo submission tree (Doze-off/vendor_hardware_overlay)
# =============================================================================
# Writes what Doze-off/vendor_hardware_overlay expects, from the same resources
# this project compiles into a module. TrebleDroid/vendor_hardware_overlay is
# the upstream it continues; the tree is identical, so a PR there works too.
#
#   <brand>/<model>/AndroidManifest.xml
#   <brand>/<model>/Android.mk
#   <brand>/<model>/res/values/*, res/values-land/*, res/xml/*
#   <brand>/<model>-SystemUI/…            (when src/systemui has resources)
#   _submission/HOW-TO-SUBMIT.md          (steps, checklist, what changed)
#   _submission/overlay.mk.lines          (the PRODUCT_PACKAGES lines to add)
#
# That tree is packed into out/<overlay>-hardware-overlay.zip by build.sh; a
# maintainer merges it into the repo, the GSI builds it, and the device gets the
# values without installing a module.
#
# Differences from the module build, on purpose:
#
#   * The match condition targets a property that exists on a stock device.
#     A module is matched by persist.sys.overlay.<codename>, which this project
#     sets itself at boot — a preinstalled overlay never sees it. So the
#     submission gates on ro.product.vendor.device (exact) by default.
#
#   * Resource names on the repo's blacklist (tests/blacklist) are dropped.
#     Those are user-preference resources the repo refuses to let an overlay
#     force; keeping them fails the repo's own test script.
#
#   * android:requiredSystemPropertyValue is compared with plain string
#     equality (AOSP FrameworkParsingPackageUtils#checkRequiredSystemProperties),
#     so no "*" or "+" globs: the value must be what the device reports.
#
# Sourced by build.sh (common.sh loaded, config.env sourced, identity derived).
# Standalone, with an optional config file (default: ./config.env):
#
#   ./stuff/scripts/hardware-overlay.sh plan [config.env]  what would be written
#   ./stuff/scripts/hardware-overlay.sh write <dir> [config.env] write the tree
# =============================================================================
# Sourced by build.sh, or run directly for the standalone commands below.
if [ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" != "$0" ] && [ -z "${ROOT:-}" ]; then
    echo "This is an internal build module — run ./build.sh instead." >&2
    return 1 2>/dev/null || exit 1
=== stuff/scripts/validate.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# config.env preflight
# =============================================================================
# Catches the mistakes that build fine and only show up on the phone:
# placeholders left in place, a padding value with no corner to match it,
# brightness arrays whose lengths do not line up, a half-filled UDFPS triple,
# a key that no script reads (a typo), and so on.
#
# Everything here is a warning, because a value that looks odd can still be
# deliberate. Resources that cannot compile at all (a radius of "abc") are
# already an error in stuff/scripts/resources.sh.
#
# Sourced by build.sh right after config.env is loaded. Standalone:
#
#   ./stuff/scripts/validate.sh      read ./config.env and report
#   ./stuff/scripts/validate.sh --strict   exit 1 when anything is reported
# =============================================================================
if [ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" != "$0" ] && [ -z "${ROOT:-}" ]; then
    echo "This is an internal build script — run ./build.sh check instead." >&2
    return 1 2>/dev/null || exit 1
fi
VALIDATE_WARNINGS=0
VALIDATE_NOTES=0
_v_warn() {
    VALIDATE_WARNINGS=$((VALIDATE_WARNINGS + 1))
    if command -v warn >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        warn "$*"
    else
        echo "  ! $*" >&2
    fi
}
_v_note() {
    VALIDATE_NOTES=$((VALIDATE_NOTES + 1))
    if command -v info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        info "$*"
    else
        echo "  - $*"
    fi
}
```

```
#!/system/bin/sh
# =============================================================================
# Treble Overlay — module addons
# =============================================================================
# An addon is a tweak the *module* makes on the phone. It is not a config.env
# key, and it is chosen in the app's Addons tab (or the page's Addons card),
# not in the overlay resource files.
#
# There are two kinds, and the catalog says which is which:
#
#   setting  a Settings value the module writes. One `settings put` changes it
#            on a running phone — no APK, no reboot — and service.sh re-applies
#            it at every boot. The overlay APK alone cannot do one.
#   overlay  a resource the build bakes into an overlay APK — framework (the
#            navigation bar height, the 180° rotation flag) or SystemUI (the
#            status bar background). It only changes after a rebuild and a
#            flash, because a resource is read when its process starts.
#
# The live addons survive an overlay rebuild; the overlay ones *are* the rebuild.
#
# One catalog lives in this file and every front-end reads it:
#
#   the desktop app   runs this script in the clone (Addons tab)
#   the module page   runs it in webroot/ on the phone (Addons card)
#   service.sh        runs it at every boot so saved choices stick
#
#   sh addons.sh list                 catalog + saved + live values, as JSON
#   sh addons.sh set ID=VALUE ...     save choices; apply the live ones now
#   sh addons.sh apply [ID ...]       apply what is saved (all ids, or those)
#   sh addons.sh reset                back to the defaults, forget the choices
#   sh addons.sh status               what the device resolves now, as key=value
#   sh addons.sh restore-conf         customize.sh: bring the saved file back
#
# The saved file is addons.conf at the module root (src/module/addons.conf in
# the clone). Only the addons that differ from the default are written into it:
# a value nobody changed is not enforced on every boot, so an untouched phone
# keeps behaving like the ROM shipped it.
#
# ADDONS_CONF, ADDONS_DIR and ADDONS_SETTINGS exist so this can be exercised
# off-device (stuff/tests/addons-sh.test.js) and by the desktop app, which has
# no installed module but does have the clone.
# =============================================================================

# The module directory is one level above this script (webroot/), except when
# the script is run by its bare name from the module root ('sh addons.sh'), in
# which case '..' would be the folder above the module.
SELF="$0"
case "$SELF" in
    */*) SELF_DIR=${SELF%/*}
         MODDIR=$(cd "$SELF_DIR/.." 2>/dev/null && pwd) ;;
    *)   SELF_DIR=.
         MODDIR=$(pwd) ;;
esac
MODDIR=${ADDONS_DIR:-$MODDIR}
[ -n "$MODDIR" ] || MODDIR=$SELF_DIR
# In the clone the module files are kept in src/module/, so the script in
# src/webui/ has one directory in between; an installed module keeps the same
# files at its root.
[ -d "$MODDIR/module" ] && MODDIR="$MODDIR/module"
```

```
func (a *App) handleAddons(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
  doc, err := a.addonsDoc()
  if err != nil {
    writeError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err.Error())
    return
  }
  writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, doc)
}

// handleAddonsSave stores the choices, which is also what applies them: the
// script's `set` writes the file and makes the values true on the phone when
// there is one. A phone is not required — the file is what the build packs.
func (a *App) handleAddonsSave(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
  var body struct {
    Values map[string]string `json:"values"`
    Reset  bool              `json:"reset"`
  }
  if !decode(w, r, &body) {
    return
  }

  if body.Reset {
    if _, err := a.runAddons("reset"); err != nil {
      writeError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err.Error())
      return
    }
  } else {
    pairs := make([]string, 0, len(body.Values))
    for id, value := range body.Values {
      if !addonID.MatchString(id) {
        writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "not an addon id: "+id)
        return
      }
      if !addonChoice.MatchString(value) {
        writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "not an addon value: "+value)
        return
      }
      pairs = append(pairs, id+"="+value)
    }
    sort.Strings(pairs)
    if len(pairs) > 0 {
      if _, err := a.runAddons(append([]string{"set"}, pairs...)...); err != nil {
        writeError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err.Error())
        return
      }
    }
  }

  doc, err := a.addonsDoc()
  if err != nil {
    writeError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err.Error())
    return
  }
  writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, doc)
}
```

```
- path: gui/matchprop.go
  content: |
      package main
      
      // ============================================================================
      // Which property should the submitted overlay match on?
      // ============================================================================
      // A static RRO for the overlay repo matches with android:requiredSystemProperty
      // Name/Value, compared with plain string equality. Getting it wrong is silent:
      // the overlay installs, `cmd overlay list` shows it enabled, and nothing changes.
      //
      // Two things decide whether a candidate works, and both are readable from the
      // phone without root:
      //
      //   * zygote has to be able to read the property. A zygote overlay is matched
      //     while zygote preloads the framework, so a property in a SELinux area
      //     zygote is denied reads as empty and the condition never holds. `getprop -Z`
      //     prints the area (build_prop and build_vendor_prop are the safe ones,
      //     build_odm_prop and build_bootimage_prop are the usual traps).
      //   * the value has to name this device and survive what is installed. The
      //     vendor, odm and bootimage partitions keep the OEM value under a GSI;
      //     /system, /product and /system_ext are replaced, so ro.product.device on a
      //     GSI holds the GSI's own name (phh_treble, mivendor, …).
      //
      // Neither rule alone is enough — on a GSI the surviving property is often the
      // one zygote cannot read, and the readable one has been renamed — so this ranks
      // every candidate, says what each one is gambling on, and refuses to call a
      // winner when no property actually carries the codename. The values below are
      // what the reference phones report: Samsung SM-A908N (everything is r3q) and
      // Xiaomi 26012RN62A (ro.product.device is zephyr, but its vendor property is the
      // shared mivendor and build.product is missi).
      
      import (
        "regexp"
        "sort"
        "strings"
      )
      
      // What a codename looks like: lower case, no separators bash would eat, short
      // enough to be a name rather than a build string.
      var codenameShape = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,23}$`)
      
      // MatchCandidate is one property the submission could be matched on.
      type MatchCandidate struct {
        Prop  string `json:"prop"`
        Value string `json:"value"`
        Score int    `json:"score"`
        Zone  string `json:"zone"`
        Label string `json:"label"`
        Trust string `json:"trust"` // high, medium, low
        // Perfect means this is a pick nothing has to be argued about: the value
        // is the codename, zygote can read the property, and a GSI leaves it alone.
        // Only a perfect pick is offered as the answer; anything less and the card
        // tells the user to keep the match they already have.
        Perfect bool   `json:"perfect"`
        Why     string `json:"why"`
        Risk    string `json:"risk,omitempty"`
      }
      
      // MatchRejection is a property with a device-ish name that was ruled out, and
      // why. The reasons are the answers to the question users ask most often, so
      // they are part of the answer rather than something to work out again.
      type MatchRejection struct {
        Prop   string `json:"prop"`
        Value  string `json:"value"`
        Reason string `json:"reason"`
      }
      
      // MatchReport is what the Config tab shows: the codename it settled on, the
      // ranked candidates, the properties it refused, and how sure it is.
      type MatchReport struct {
        Serial     string           `json:"serial"`
        Model      string           `json:"model"`
        Codename   string           `json:"codename"`
        Confidence string           `json:"confidence"` // high, medium, low
        ModuleProp string           `json:"moduleProp"`
        Candidates []MatchCandidate `json:"candidates"`
        Rejected   []MatchRejection `json:"rejected"`
      }
      
      // matchProp is one entry of the fixed candidate list. zone says which partition
      // the value comes from (that is what decides GSI survival) and kind says what
      // the property holds.
      type matchProp struct {
        name string
        zone string
        kind string
      }
      
      var matchPropCandidates = []matchProp{
        {"ro.product.vendor.device", "vendor", "device"},
        {"ro.product.odm.device", "odm", "device"},
        {"ro.product.bootimage.device", "bootimage", "device"},
        {"ro.product.device", "system", "device"},
        {"ro.product.product.device", "product", "device"},
        {"ro.product.system.device", "system", "device"},
        {"ro.product.system_ext.device", "system_ext", "device"},
        {"ro.build.product", "build", "device"},
        {"ro.product.vendor.name", "vendor", "name"},
        {"ro.product.odm.name", "odm", "name"},
        {"ro.product.bootimage.name", "bootimage", "name"},
        {"ro.product.name", "product", "name"},
        {"ro.product.vendor.model", "vendor", "model"},
        {"ro.product.model", "product", "model"},
      }
      
      // zoneScore: vendor/odm/bootimage keep the OEM value when a GSI replaces
      // /system; a `ro.product.*` value is whatever is installed now.
      var zoneScore = map[string]int{
        "vendor": 40, "odm": 35, "bootimage": 35,
        "product": 25, "system": 22, "system_ext": 18, "build": 10,
      }
      
      var kindScore = map[string]int{"device": 25, "name": 12, "model": 15}
      
      // labelScore: what the SELinux area means for zygote reading it. The negative
      // numbers are the documented traps, not guesses — build_bootimage_prop and
      // build_odm_prop are refused to zygote on most GSI builds.
      var labelScore = map[string]int{
        "build_prop":           30,
        "build_vendor_prop":    30,
        "vendor_default_prop":  25,
        "default_prop":         15,
        "build_system_prop":    -20,
        "build_odm_prop":       -35,
        "build_bootimage_prop": -35,
        "bootloader_prop":      -20,
      }
      
      // Values that name a build rather than a device. They are the reason a "looks
      // like a codename" filter is not enough: mivendor is a Xiaomi vendor tree shared
      // by a whole family, generic is the GSI itself, qcom is a SoC vendor.
      var genericMatchValues = map[string]string{
        "generic":        "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_x86":    "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_arm64":  "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_x86_64": "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "aosp":           "an AOSP build name, not a device",
        "aosp_arm64":     "an AOSP build name, not a device",
        "mainline":       "the mainline/module build name, not a device",
        "treble":         "the Treble build name, not a device",
        "phh_treble":     "the GSI's own name — present on every device running that GSI",
        "mivendor":       "Xiaomi's vendor build name — shared by many Xiaomi devices, not a codename",
        "emulator":       "an emulator, not a phone",
        "unknown":        "no value",
        "qcom":           "a SoC vendor, shared by every Qualcomm device",
        "mediatek":       "a SoC vendor, shared by every MediaTek device",
        "mtk":            "a SoC vendor, shared by every MediaTek device",
        "exynos":         "a SoC vendor, shared by every Exynos device",
        "android":        "not a device name",
      }
      
      // rankMatchProps turns a phone's `getprop` and `getprop -Z` output into ranked
      // candidates. Both maps are keyed by property name; a missing value or label is
      // simply an empty string, because adb output loses lines on some ROMs.
      func rankMatchProps(values, labels map[string]string) MatchReport {
        report := MatchReport{
          Candidates: []MatchCandidate{},
          Rejected:   []MatchRejection{},
        }
      
        brand := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.brand"]))
        manufacturer := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.manufacturer"]))
        report.Model = strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.model"])
      
        // Phase 1: what is this phone called? Partition order is the rule, not a sum:
        // vendor, odm and bootimage are the OEM's own naming and are what a GSI leaves
        // alone, while /system, /product and /system_ext hold the ROM's name (on a
        // GSI that is the GSI itself: generic, phh_treble, mivendor). A value the OEM
        // partitions agree on is the codename; the later props are only consulted
        // when those are empty or generic.
        codenameOrder := []string{
          "ro.product.vendor.device",
          "ro.product.odm.device",
          "ro.product.bootimage.device",
          "ro.product.device",
          "ro.product.system.device",
          "ro.product.product.device",
          "ro.product.system_ext.device",
          "ro.build.product",
        }
        codename := ""
        codenameProp := ""
        for _, name := range codenameOrder {
          value := strings.TrimSpace(values[name])
          if value == "" || genericMatchValues[strings.ToLower(value)] != "" {
            continue
          }
          if !codenameShape.MatchString(value) {
            continue
          }
          if value == brand || value == manufacturer {
            continue
          }
          codename, codenameProp = value, name
          break
        }
        report.Codename = codename
      
        // Phase 2: rank every property against that answer.
        for _, p := range matchPropCandidates {
          value := strings.TrimSpace(values[p.name])
          if value == "" {
            continue
          }
          label := shortPropertyLabel(labels[p.name])
          if reason := genericMatchValues[strings.ToLower(value)]; reason != "" {
            report.Rejected = append(report.Rejected, MatchRejection{
              Prop: p.name, Value: value, Reason: reason,
            })
            continue
          }
          if brand != "" && strings.EqualFold(value, brand) {
            report.Rejected = append(report.Rejected, MatchRejection{
              Prop: p.name, Value: value,
              Reason: "the brand, not the device — it would match every phone of this make",
            })
            continue
          }
      
          c := MatchCandidate{
            Prop:  p.name,
            Value: value,
            Zone:  p.zone,
            Label: label,
          }
          c.Score = zoneScore[p.zone] + kindScore[p.kind] + labelScore[label]
      
          var why, risk []string
          switch p.zone {
          case "vendor", "odm", "bootimage":
            why = append(why, "lives on /"+p.zone+", which a GSI leaves alone")
          default:
            why = append(why, "read from the installed /"+p.zone+" partition")
            risk = append(risk, "a GSI replaces /"+p.zone+", so the value changes and the match stops")
          }
          switch label {
          case "build_prop", "build_vendor_prop", "vendor_default_prop", "default_prop":
            why = append(why, "zygote can read "+label)
          case "":
            risk = append(risk, "this ROM did not report its SELinux area, so readability is unchecked")
          default:
            risk = append(risk, label+" is often denied to zygote — the overlay can show as enabled and do nothing")
          }
          if codename != "" && value == codename {
            c.Score += 30
            why = append(why, "holds the codename")
            if p.name == codenameProp {
              c.Score += 10
            }
          } else if codename != "" && strings.Contains(value, codename) {
            c.Score += 10
            why = append(why, "contains the codename")
          } else {
            // The missi case: a property that names this build, not this phone.
            // Matching on it would claim a different device, so every such row
            // ranks below the ones that carry the codename.
            c.Score -= 20
            if p.kind == "device" {
              risk = append(risk, "holds a different name ("+value+") than this phone's codename ("+codename+")")
            } else {
              risk = append(risk, "does not hold the codename, so it names this variant rather than the device")
            }
          }
          if codenameShape.MatchString(value) {
            c.Score += 10
          } else {
            c.Score -= 5
            if strings.ContainsRune(value, ' ') {
              risk = append(risk, "contains a space — exact matching works, but it is easy to break while editing")
            }
          }
          if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(value), "global") {
            c.Score -= 10
            risk = append(risk, "has a region suffix, so another region's build would not match")
          }
          if p.zone == "system" && strings.HasSuffix(p.name, ".device") && value == codename && label == "build_prop" {
            // This is the normal, good answer on a stock ROM: say so instead of
            // making the user read the /system risk as a deal-breaker.
            risk = []string{"if a GSI is installed later this property becomes the GSI's name"}
          }
      
          c.Why = strings.Join(why, " · ")
          c.Risk = strings.Join(risk, " · ")
          c.Perfect = codename != "" && value == codename && p.kind == "device" &&
            readableByZygote(label) && survivesGSI(p.zone)
          switch {
          case c.Perfect:
            c.Trust = "high"
          case value == codename:
            c.Trust = "medium"
          default:
            c.Trust = "low"
          }
          report.Candidates = append(report.Candidates, c)
        }
      
        sort.SliceStable(report.Candidates, func(i, j int) bool {
          a, b := report.Candidates[i], report.Candidates[j]
          if a.Score != b.Score {
            return a.Score > b.Score
          }
          // Same score: the one that actually carries the codename is the more
          // useful row, and after that the order only has to be stable.
          if (a.Value == codename) != (b.Value == codename) {
            return a.Value == codename
          }
          return a.Prop < b.Prop
        })
      
        // Confidence is about the answer, not the ranking. "high" is reserved for a
        // property that satisfies every rule at once (readable by zygote, carries the
        // codename, survives a GSI); anything less and the honest advice is to keep
        // the match that already works, because a submitted condition that does not
        // hold is invisible.
        report.Confidence = "low"
        if len(report.Candidates) > 0 {
          top := report.Candidates[0]
          switch {
          case top.Perfect:
            report.Confidence = "high"
          case top.Value == codename && codename != "":
            report.Confidence = "medium"
          }
        }
        if codename != "" {
          report.ModuleProp = "persist.sys.overlay." + strings.ToLower(codename)
        }
        return report
      }
      
      // survivesGSI: a property in these areas keeps the OEM value after a GSI flash.
      func survivesGSI(zone string) bool {
        switch zone {
        case "vendor", "odm", "bootimage":
          return true
        }
        return false
      }
      
      func readableByZygote(label string) bool {
        switch label {
        case "build_prop", "build_vendor_prop", "vendor_default_prop", "default_prop":
          return true
        }
        return false
      }
      
      // shortPropertyLabel turns "u:object_r:build_vendor_prop:s0" into
      // "build_vendor_prop", which is the part that means something here.
      func shortPropertyLabel(label string) string {
        parts := strings.Split(strings.TrimSpace(label), ":")
        if len(parts) >= 3 {
          return parts[2]
        }
        return ""
      }
      
      // parseGetprop reads `getprop` output: one `[key]: [value]` per line. Lines that
      // do not fit are skipped — some ROMs print warnings into the same stream.
      func parseGetprop(out string) map[string]string {
        props := map[string]string{}
        for _, line := range strings.Split(out, "\n") {
          line = strings.TrimRight(line, "\r")
          key, rest, ok := strings.Cut(line, "]: [")
          if !ok || !strings.HasPrefix(key, "[") || !strings.HasSuffix(rest, "]") {
            continue
          }
          props[strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(key, "["))] = strings.TrimSuffix(rest, "]")
        }
        return props
      }
      
      // parseGetpropLabels reads `getprop -Z`: `[key]: [u:object_r:xyz_prop:s0]`.
      func parseGetpropLabels(out string) map[string]string {
        return parseGetprop(out)
      }
      
```

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Everything that can be checked without Android tools
# =============================================================================
# CI runs this on every push (see .github/workflows/check.yml), and it is worth
# running before a release:
#
#   bash stuff/tests/run.sh
#
# 1. shell syntax of every shipped script (bash -n / sh -n, no execution)
# 2. the WebUI resource-table writer against stuff/tests/fixtures/*.apk
# 3. the WebUI manifest and the overlay-repo submission tree (Doze-off
#    vendor_hardware_overlay), built from
#    resource XML that stuff/tests/gen-res.sh generates into a temp directory (so
#    a fresh clone needs no build first)
# 4. every relative link and #anchor in the docs
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.."

status=0
step() { printf '\n== %s ==\n' "$*"; }

step "shell syntax"
for f in build.sh treble-rro-creator.sh gui/build.sh stuff/scripts/*.sh stuff/tests/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if bash -n "$f"; then :; else echo "bash -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
done
# apply.sh, addons.sh and the module scripts run under Android's mksh
# (/system/bin/sh).
for f in src/webui/apply.sh src/webui/addons.sh src/module/*.sh stuff/templates/*.sh stuff/templates/recoveries/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if command -v sh >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        if sh -n "$f"; then :; else echo "sh -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
    fi
done
[ "$status" -eq 0 ] && echo "all scripts parse"

# The bug this guards: `clean --all` copied config.env from a frozen file, so a
# full clean handed back a version from an older commit. The copies below are
# now only the no-.git fallback, so they must equal the committed blob — not the
# working file, because local edits to config.env are normal.
step "template fallbacks match the release"
if command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 && git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    copy_status=0
    check_copy() {
        local rel="$1" copy="$2"
        if [ ! -f "$copy" ]; then
            echo "missing fallback: $copy"
            copy_status=1
        elif ! git show "HEAD:$rel" | diff -q - "$copy" >/dev/null; then
            echo "$copy differs from HEAD:$rel — run: git show HEAD:$rel > $copy"
            copy_status=1
        fi
    }
    check_copy config.env stuff/templates/recoveries/config.env
    check_copy src/module/sepolicy.rule stuff/templates/recoveries/sepolicy.rule
    if [ "$copy_status" -eq 0 ]; then echo "fallbacks match"; else status=1; fi
else
---
```

```
- path: stuff/scripts/common.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # Treble Overlay — shared helpers
      # =============================================================================
      # Sourced by build.sh and by the modules in stuff/scripts/. Never run directly.
      #
      # The entry point sets ROOT (the project directory) and then sources this file,
      # so every helper below can assume it exists and that the current directory is
      # the project root.
      # =============================================================================
      
      : "${ROOT:?stuff/scripts/common.sh must be sourced by build.sh (ROOT is not set)}"
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Paths
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Absolute paths are used for file tests and for zip destinations. Arguments
      # handed to native tools (aapt2/zipalign) must stay RELATIVE: MSYS on Windows
      # does not reliably convert a /c/... path for a native .exe.
      # Everything that is not the thing you build lives under stuff/, so the root
      # only holds the two entry points, config.env and the folders you open.
      STUFF_DIR="$ROOT/stuff"
      TOOLS_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/tools"
      BUILD_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/build"
      OUT_DIR="$ROOT/out"
      KEYS_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/keys"
      BACKUP_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/backups"
      TEMPLATES_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/templates"
      # Not "the old version of your files": the no-git fallback for
      # restore_from_release(). Kept identical to the committed files by stuff/tests/run.sh.
      RECOVERIES_DIR="$TEMPLATES_DIR/recoveries"
      
      SRC_DIR="$ROOT/src"
      FRAMEWORK_DIR="$SRC_DIR/framework"
      FRAMEWORK_RES="$FRAMEWORK_DIR/res"
      SYSTEMUI_DIR="$SRC_DIR/systemui"
      SYSTEMUI_RES="$SYSTEMUI_DIR/res"
      MODULE_DIR="$SRC_DIR/module"
      VENDOR_DIR="$SRC_DIR/vendor"
      
      CONFIG_FILE="$ROOT/config.env"
      CONFIG_EXAMPLE="$ROOT/config.env.example"
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Restoring a tracked file to what this release ships
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # "Start over" must never hand back a copy that froze at some old commit. The
      # committed blob IS the template for a tracked file, so ask git for it; the
      # copy in stuff/templates/recoveries/ is only the fallback for a checkout with no .git
      # (a fork downloaded as a zip). stuff/tests/run.sh fails if the two ever drift.
      #
      #   restore_from_release <path relative to ROOT> [fallback copy]
      #
      # Returns 0 when the file on disk now holds the release version.
      restore_from_release() {
          local rel="$1" fallback="${2:-}"
      
          if [ -d "$ROOT/.git" ] && command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 \
             && git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --verify --quiet "HEAD:${rel}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              if git -C "$ROOT" checkout HEAD -- "$rel" 2>/dev/null; then
                  return 0
              fi
          fi
      
          if [ -n "$fallback" ] && [ -f "$fallback" ]; then
              mkdir -p "$(dirname "$ROOT/$rel")"
              cp "$fallback" "$ROOT/$rel" && return 0
          fi
          return 1
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Platform
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      IS_WINDOWS=false
      case "$(uname -s 2>/dev/null)" in
          MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) IS_WINDOWS=true ;;
      esac
      
      # WSL reports Linux but lives inside Windows. The build is allowed there only
      # when the checkout is on the Linux filesystem (see wsl_guard).
      IS_WSL=false
      if ! $IS_WINDOWS && [ -r /proc/version ] && grep -qi microsoft /proc/version 2>/dev/null; then
          IS_WSL=true
      fi
      
      IS_TERMUX=false
      if [ -d /data/data/com.termux ] && [ -n "${PREFIX:-}" ]; then
          IS_TERMUX=true
      fi
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Output
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      RED='\033[0;31m'; GREEN='\033[0;32m'; YELLOW='\033[1;33m'
      CYAN='\033[0;36m'; BOLD='\033[1m'; NC='\033[0m'
      
      ok()   { echo -e "  ${GREEN}✓${NC} $*"; }
      info() { echo -e "  ${YELLOW}→${NC} $*"; }
      warn() { echo -e "  ${YELLOW}⚠${NC} $*"; }
      err()  { echo -e "  ${RED}✗${NC} $*" >&2; }
      step() { echo -e "\n${BOLD}━━━ $* ━━━${NC}"; }
      
      banner() {
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}$*${NC}"
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────${NC}"
          echo ""
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Prompts
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # ask <question> <default>   -> answer in $REPLY
      #
      # `read` returns 1 at EOF (stdin redirected, CI, IDE task, no console). Under
      # `set -e` that used to kill the scripts silently right after a menu had been
      # printed. Falling back to a stated default keeps everything runnable
      # unattended, and pressing Enter also takes the default.
      ask() {
          local question="$1" default="${2:-}" answer=""
          printf '%s' "$question"
          if ! read -r answer; then
              echo ""
              info "No terminal input available — using '${default}'."
              answer="$default"
          fi
          [ -z "$answer" ] && answer="$default"
          REPLY="$answer"
      }
      
      # confirm <question> <y|n>   -> returns 0 for yes
      confirm() {
          local question="$1" default="${2:-n}" answer
          ask "$question" "$default"
          answer="$REPLY"
          case "$answer" in
              [Yy]|[Yy][Ee][Ss]) return 0 ;;
              *) return 1 ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # WSL safety
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # A checkout on a Windows drive that is built from inside WSL would put Linux
      # binaries into the same stuff/tools/ folder the Windows build reads, and would hand
      # Windows a build tree it cannot use. Refuse with instructions instead of
      # producing a half-broken toolchain. (This is the "VS Code opened the folder
      # with WSL" case.)
      wsl_guard() {
          $IS_WSL || return 0
          case "$ROOT" in
              /mnt/[a-z]/*) ;;
              *) return 0 ;;
          esac
      
          echo ""
          err "This project is on a Windows drive, but you are running inside WSL."
          echo ""
          echo "    Project:  $ROOT"
          echo "    Shell:    WSL (Linux)"
          echo ""
          echo "  The Linux toolchain would be installed into the same stuff/tools/ folder the"
          echo "  Windows build uses, so both platforms would then see the wrong binaries."
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Use one of these instead:${NC}"
          echo "    • Windows (cmd, PowerShell, VS Code):   build.cmd"
          echo "    • Linux / Termux:                       clone the project inside Linux"
          echo "                                            (e.g. ~/treble-rro-creator)"
          echo "                                            and run ./build.sh there"
          echo ""
          echo "  In VS Code, check the bottom-left corner: if it says \"WSL: ...\","
          echo "  close the remote window (or open a Windows terminal) and run build.cmd."
          echo ""
          exit 1
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Legacy layout
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Older versions of this project kept res/, systemui_overlay/, customize.sh,
      # service.sh, sepolicy.rule and system/vendor/ at the top level. Users who
      # upgrade by pulling can still have personal (untracked) copies there. Move
      # them into src/ instead of silently ignoring them.
      migrate_layout() {
          local moved=false f
      
          # res/ -> src/framework/res
          if [ -d "$ROOT/res" ]; then
              if [ ! -d "$FRAMEWORK_RES" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$FRAMEWORK_DIR"
                  cp -R "$ROOT/res" "$FRAMEWORK_DIR/res"
                  rm -rf "$ROOT/res"
                  info "Moved legacy ./res → src/framework/res"
                  moved=true
              else
                  warn "Legacy ./res exists but is no longer used — the build reads src/framework/res"
              fi
          fi
      
          # systemui_overlay/ -> src/systemui/res
          if [ -d "$ROOT/systemui_overlay/res" ]; then
              if [ ! -d "$SYSTEMUI_RES" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$SYSTEMUI_DIR"
                  cp -R "$ROOT/systemui_overlay/res" "$SYSTEMUI_DIR/res"
                  rm -rf "$ROOT/systemui_overlay"
                  info "Moved legacy ./systemui_overlay → src/systemui"
                  moved=true
              else
                  warn "Legacy ./systemui_overlay exists but is no longer used — the build reads src/systemui/res"
              fi
          fi
      
          # system/vendor -> src/vendor
          if [ -d "$ROOT/system/vendor" ]; then
              mkdir -p "$VENDOR_DIR"
              cp -R "$ROOT/system/vendor/." "$VENDOR_DIR/" 2>/dev/null || true
              rm -rf "$ROOT/system"
              info "Moved legacy ./system/vendor → src/vendor"
              moved=true
          fi
      
          # Root module scripts -> src/module
          mkdir -p "$MODULE_DIR"
          for f in customize.sh service.sh sepolicy.rule; do
              [ -f "$ROOT/$f" ] || continue
              if [ -f "$MODULE_DIR/$f" ] && cmp -s "$ROOT/$f" "$MODULE_DIR/$f"; then
                  rm -f "$ROOT/$f"
              else
                  mv -f "$ROOT/$f" "$MODULE_DIR/$f"
                  info "Moved legacy ./$f → src/module/$f (now the copy that gets built)"
              fi
              moved=true
          done
      
          # YOUR BACKUPS -> stuff/backups
          if [ -d "$ROOT/YOUR BACKUPS" ] && [ ! -d "$BACKUP_DIR" ]; then
              mv "$ROOT/YOUR BACKUPS" "$BACKUP_DIR"
              info "Moved legacy ./YOUR BACKUPS → stuff/backups"
              moved=true
          fi
      
          # Everything that is not src/, docs/ or an entry point now lives in stuff/.
          # A git pull moves these itself; this covers an upgrade from a zip, which
          # would otherwise leave a second copy in the way at the root.
          mkdir -p "$STUFF_DIR"
          for f in keys templates windows tests scripts tools build backups; do
              [ -d "$ROOT/$f" ] || continue
              if [ -d "$STUFF_DIR/$f" ]; then
                  warn "Legacy ./$f exists but stuff/$f is the one in use — remove the old copy"
                  continue
              fi
              mv "$ROOT/$f" "$STUFF_DIR/$f"
              info "Moved legacy ./$f → stuff/$f"
              moved=true
          done
      
          $moved && info "Layout upgraded — internals live in stuff/, the entry points stay at the root"
          return 0
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Binary inspection
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Windows cannot execute Linux binaries. If this checkout is also opened from
      # WSL/Kali (a copy on the same drive), a Linux `aapt2` can land in the same
      # stuff/tools/ folder the Windows build puts on PATH, shadow `aapt2.exe`, and fail
      # much later with "Exec format error". Classify by magic bytes so it is caught
      # up front.
      classify_binary() {
          local f="$1"
          if [ ! -e "$f" ]; then echo "missing"; return 0; fi
          if [ -d "$f" ]; then echo "directory"; return 0; fi
          local magic
          magic=$(head -c 4 "$f" 2>/dev/null | od -An -tx1 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' \n')
          case "$magic" in
              4d5a*)     echo "windows-pe" ;;   # MZ  -> .exe
              7f454c46)  echo "linux-elf" ;;    # \x7fELF -> WSL/Linux build
              2321*)     echo "script" ;;       # #!
              504b0304)  echo "zip" ;;          # PK.. -> apk / jar
              "")        echo "unreadable" ;;
              *)         echo "unknown" ;;
          esac
      }
      
      kind_label() {
          case "$1" in
              windows-pe) echo "Windows executable" ;;
              linux-elf)  echo "Linux binary (ELF)" ;;
              script)     echo "shell script" ;;
              zip)        echo "archive" ;;
              missing)    echo "missing" ;;
              *)          echo "$1" ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # A native binary built for the OTHER platform. This is the real contamination
      # signal: scripts, jars and apks are fine to share between Windows and WSL.
      kind_foreign() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS; then
              [ "$1" = "linux-elf" ]
          else
              [ "$1" = "windows-pe" ]
          fi
      }
      
      # Can a binary of this kind run on the machine we are on right now?
      kind_usable() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS; then
              case "$1" in
                  windows-pe|script|zip) return 0 ;;
                  *) return 1 ;;
              esac
          fi
          case "$1" in
              linux-elf|script|zip) return 0 ;;
              *) return 1 ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # Every path a tool could be picked up from, in the order build.sh resolves it.
      tool_candidates() {
          local name="$1" c
          for c in "$(command -v "$name" 2>/dev/null)" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}.exe" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}.bat"; do
              [ -n "$c" ] && [ -f "$c" ] && printf '%s\n' "$c"
          done
          return 0
      }
      
      # Is this tool usable HERE (PATH, stuff/tools/, .exe/.bat on Windows)?
      tool_ready() {
          local name="$1" cand
          while IFS= read -r cand; do
              [ -n "$cand" ] || continue
              kind_usable "$(classify_binary "$cand")" && return 0
          done <<< "$(tool_candidates "$name")"
          return 1
      }
      
      # First usable copy of a tool (prints the path, returns 1 when there is none).
      tool_path() {
          local name="$1" cand
          while IFS= read -r cand; do
              [ -n "$cand" ] || continue
              if kind_usable "$(classify_binary "$cand")"; then
                  printf '%s\n' "$cand"
                  return 0
              fi
          done <<< "$(tool_candidates "$name")"
          return 1
      }
      
      # Where the aapt2 resource dictionary lives, if it is installed.
      framework_res_path() {
          local c
          for c in "$TOOLS_DIR/framework-res.apk" \
                   "/usr/share/android-framework-res/framework-res.apk"; do
              [ -f "$c" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$c"; return 0; }
          done
          # Optional local Android SDK (Arch Linux layout)
          if [ -d "/opt/android-sdk/platforms" ]; then
              c=$(find /opt/android-sdk/platforms -name "framework-res.apk" 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)
              [ -n "$c" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$c"; return 0; }
          fi
          return 1
      }
      
      # Everything the build needs, as a space-separated list (empty = ready).
      # zipalign is not in the Termux package repository (pkg cannot install it) and
      # an unaligned RRO still loads, so it is optional there instead of blocking the
      # build forever. Everything else still requires it.
      zipalign_optional() {
          $IS_TERMUX && ! tool_ready zipalign
      }
      
      # align_apk <unsigned> <aligned> — zipalign when available, plain copy if not.
      # An unaligned APK is valid and installs; it just cannot be mmap'ed as
      # efficiently, so this is a warning, not a failure.
      ALIGN_WARNED=false
      align_apk() {
          if tool_ready zipalign; then
              zipalign -f 4 "$1" "$2"
              return $?
          fi
          if ! $ALIGN_WARNED; then
              warn "zipalign not available — APKs stay unaligned (valid, slightly slower to map)"
              $IS_TERMUX && warn "  Termux: pkg install aapt  (that package ships zipalign)"
              ALIGN_WARNED=true
          fi
          cp -f "$1" "$2"
      }
      
      toolchain_missing() {
          local missing="" t
          for t in aapt2 zipalign apksigner; do
              [ "$t" = "zipalign" ] && zipalign_optional && continue
              tool_ready "$t" || missing="$missing $t"
          done
          command -v java >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing="$missing java"
          framework_res_path >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing="$missing framework-res.apk"
          printf '%s' "${missing# }"
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Device identity
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Turns the raw DEVICE_* values from config.env into the module id, the overlay
      # package names and the match condition. Called by build.sh right after
      # config.env is sourced, and by the standalone scripts (manifest.sh,
      # hardware-overlay.sh) so they agree with the build.
      #
      # Users only need to set DEVICE_CODENAME and DEVICE_MANUFACTURER; everything
      # else is derived. A value containing "<" is a template placeholder.
      derive_overlay_identity() {
          [ -z "${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER:-}" ] || [[ "$DEVICE_MANUFACTURER" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_MANUFACTURER="generic"
          [ -z "${DEVICE_CODENAME:-}" ]     || [[ "$DEVICE_CODENAME" == *"<"* ]]     && DEVICE_CODENAME="generic"
      
          # Clean manufacturer for Java package names (lowercase alphanumeric only)
          SAFE_MANUFACTURER=$(printf '%s' "${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]//g')
      
          # Clean codename for package name: replace non-alphanumeric with dots
          # e.g. "Infinix-X6852" → "infinix.x6852" (dots are valid Java package separators)
          PACKAGE_SEGMENT=$(printf '%s' "${DEVICE_CODENAME}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]/./g' | sed 's/\.\.*/./g' | sed 's/^\.//;s/\.$//')
      
          # Module ids are shared by Magisk, KernelSU and APatch: they must match
          # ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$ (no spaces or slashes). Use the already-cleaned
          # manufacturer/codename pieces for the generated default; an explicit
          # OVERLAY_NAME in config.env is kept as-is.
          DEFAULT_MANUFACTURER="${SAFE_MANUFACTURER:-generic}"
          DEFAULT_CODENAME="${PACKAGE_SEGMENT:-generic}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_NAME:-}" ]        || [[ "$OVERLAY_NAME" == *"<"* ]]        && OVERLAY_NAME="treble-overlay-${DEFAULT_MANUFACTURER}-${DEFAULT_CODENAME}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_PACKAGE:-}" ]     || [[ "$OVERLAY_PACKAGE" == *"<"* ]]     && OVERLAY_PACKAGE="me.phh.treble.overlay.${SAFE_MANUFACTURER}.${PACKAGE_SEGMENT}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI:-}" ] || [[ "$OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI="${OVERLAY_PACKAGE}.systemui"
          [[ "${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_PROP_VALUE="${DEVICE_CODENAME}"
          # Only placeholders are replaced. An EMPTY DEVICE_PROP_NAME is meaningful: it
          # builds an overlay with no match condition (always active), which is the safe
          # default for framework overlays — see the Overlay Activation section of
          # config.env for why ro.product.* conditions fail on GSI setups.
          [[ "${DEVICE_PROP_NAME:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_PROP_NAME="ro.product.device"
      
          if [ -n "${DEVICE_PROP_NAME:-}" ]; then
              OVERLAY_CONDITION="        android:requiredSystemPropertyName=\"${DEVICE_PROP_NAME}\"
              android:requiredSystemPropertyValue=\"${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE}\" />"
              CONDITION_DESC="${DEVICE_PROP_NAME} == \"${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE}\""
          else
              OVERLAY_CONDITION="        />"
              CONDITION_DESC="none (always active)"
          fi
      
          [ -z "${ANDROID_VERSION:-}" ]     && ANDROID_VERSION="14"
          [ -z "${COMPILE_SDK_VERSION:-}" ] && COMPILE_SDK_VERSION="34"
          [ -z "${MIN_SDK_VERSION:-}" ]     && MIN_SDK_VERSION="34"
          [ -z "${TARGET_SDK_VERSION:-}" ]  && TARGET_SDK_VERSION="34"
      
          # Module metadata: module.prop, both manifests and the hardware overlay
          # read these. Empty or still a <placeholder> falls back to the release
          # values, so a config.env written before these keys existed still builds.
          [[ -z "${OVERLAY_VERSION:-}" || "${OVERLAY_VERSION}" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_VERSION="1.0"
          [[ -z "${OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE:-}" || "${OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE}" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE="1"
          # Author is free text; only an empty or placeholder one is replaced.
          [[ -z "${MODULE_AUTHOR:-}" || "${MODULE_AUTHOR}" == *"<"* ]] && MODULE_AUTHOR="${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER}"
      
          [[ "${LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE="android.sensor.light"
          [[ "${DEVICE_MODEL:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_MODEL="Generic Device"
          # Status bar landscape height: only set fallback if explicitly a placeholder
          # (otherwise leave empty so the status bar section skips it)
          [[ "${STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT_LANDSCAPE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT_LANDSCAPE=24
      
          return 0
      }
      
      # Does this power_profile.xml contain actual data, or is it the empty template?
      power_profile_is_placeholder() {
          local f="$1"
          [ -f "$f" ] || return 0
          ! grep -qE '<item[[:space:]>]' "$f"
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Portable helpers
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Convert an MSYS path to a native Windows path (no-op elsewhere).
      to_win_path() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS && command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              cygpath -w "$1"
          else
              printf '%s' "$1"
          fi
      }
      
      # Create <dest> from the contents of <src>, using whichever zip tool exists:
      # Info-ZIP (Linux/Termux), 7-Zip, or PowerShell's ZipArchive API (Windows).
      create_zip() {
          local src="$1" dest="$2"
          rm -f "$dest"
          if command -v zip >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              ( cd "$src" && zip -r "$dest" . >/dev/null ) || return 1
          elif command -v 7z >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              ( cd "$src" && 7z a -tzip "$dest" . >/dev/null ) || return 1
          elif command -v powershell >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ -f "$STUFF_DIR/windows/zipdir.ps1" ]; then
              powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass \
                  -File "$(to_win_path "$STUFF_DIR/windows/zipdir.ps1")" \
                  -Source "$(to_win_path "$(cd "$src" && pwd)")" \
                  -Dest "$(to_win_path "$dest")" >/dev/null || return 1
          else
              err "No zip tool available (install zip, 7-Zip, or re-run the build on Windows)"
              return 1
          fi
      }
      
      # Make the local toolchain visible. Windows tools are .exe files in stuff/tools/;
      # on Linux the build-tools zipalign needs the bundled libc++ from lib64/.
      tools_on_path() {
          case ":$PATH:" in
              *":$TOOLS_DIR:"*) ;;
              *) export PATH="$TOOLS_DIR:$PATH" ;;
          esac
      
          [ -d "$TOOLS_DIR" ] || return 0
          if ! $IS_WINDOWS; then
              local lib
              for lib in "$TOOLS_DIR"/android-sdk/build-tools/*/lib64; do
                  [ -d "$lib" ] && [ -f "$lib/libc++.so" ] || continue
                  export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$lib${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
                  break
              done
          fi
          return 0
      }
```

```
- path: gui/matchprop.go
  content: |
      package main
      
      // ============================================================================
      // Which property should the submitted overlay match on?
      // ============================================================================
      // A static RRO for the overlay repo matches with android:requiredSystemProperty
      // Name/Value, compared with plain string equality. Getting it wrong is silent:
      // the overlay installs, `cmd overlay list` shows it enabled, and nothing changes.
      //
      // Two things decide whether a candidate works, and both are readable from the
      // phone without root:
      //
      //   * zygote has to be able to read the property. A zygote overlay is matched
      //     while zygote preloads the framework, so a property in a SELinux area
      //     zygote is denied reads as empty and the condition never holds. `getprop -Z`
      //     prints the area (build_prop and build_vendor_prop are the safe ones,
      //     build_odm_prop and build_bootimage_prop are the usual traps).
      //   * the value has to name this device and survive what is installed. The
      //     vendor, odm and bootimage partitions keep the OEM value under a GSI;
      //     /system, /product and /system_ext are replaced, so ro.product.device on a
      //     GSI holds the GSI's own name (phh_treble, mivendor, …).
      //
      // Neither rule alone is enough — on a GSI the surviving property is often the
      // one zygote cannot read, and the readable one has been renamed — so this ranks
      // every candidate, says what each one is gambling on, and refuses to call a
      // winner when no property actually carries the codename. The values below are
      // what the reference phones report: Samsung SM-A908N (everything is r3q) and
      // Xiaomi 26012RN62A (ro.product.device is zephyr, but its vendor property is the
      // shared mivendor and build.product is missi).
      
      import (
        "regexp"
        "sort"
        "strings"
      )
      
      // What a codename looks like: lower case, no separators bash would eat, short
      // enough to be a name rather than a build string.
      var codenameShape = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,23}$`)
      
      // MatchCandidate is one property the submission could be matched on.
      type MatchCandidate struct {
        Prop  string `json:"prop"`
        Value string `json:"value"`
        Score int    `json:"score"`
        Zone  string `json:"zone"`
        Label string `json:"label"`
        Trust string `json:"trust"` // high, medium, low
        // Perfect means this is a pick nothing has to be argued about: the value
        // is the codename, zygote can read the property, and a GSI leaves it alone.
        // Only a perfect pick is offered as the answer; anything less and the card
        // tells the user to keep the match they already have.
        Perfect bool   `json:"perfect"`
        Why     string `json:"why"`
        Risk    string `json:"risk,omitempty"`
      }
      
      // MatchRejection is a property with a device-ish name that was ruled out, and
      // why. The reasons are the answers to the question users ask most often, so
      // they are part of the answer rather than something to work out again.
      type MatchRejection struct {
        Prop   string `json:"prop"`
        Value  string `json:"value"`
        Reason string `json:"reason"`
      }
      
      // MatchReport is what the Config tab shows: the codename it settled on, the
      // ranked candidates, the properties it refused, and how sure it is.
      type MatchReport struct {
        Serial     string           `json:"serial"`
        Model      string           `json:"model"`
        Codename   string           `json:"codename"`
        Confidence string           `json:"confidence"` // high, medium, low
        ModuleProp string           `json:"moduleProp"`
        Candidates []MatchCandidate `json:"candidates"`
        Rejected   []MatchRejection `json:"rejected"`
      }
      
      // matchProp is one entry of the fixed candidate list. zone says which partition
      // the value comes from (that is what decides GSI survival) and kind says what
      // the property holds.
      type matchProp struct {
        name string
        zone string
        kind string
      }
      
      var matchPropCandidates = []matchProp{
        {"ro.product.vendor.device", "vendor", "device"},
        {"ro.product.odm.device", "odm", "device"},
        {"ro.product.bootimage.device", "bootimage", "device"},
        {"ro.product.device", "system", "device"},
        {"ro.product.product.device", "product", "device"},
        {"ro.product.system.device", "system", "device"},
        {"ro.product.system_ext.device", "system_ext", "device"},
        {"ro.build.product", "build", "device"},
        {"ro.product.vendor.name", "vendor", "name"},
        {"ro.product.odm.name", "odm", "name"},
        {"ro.product.bootimage.name", "bootimage", "name"},
        {"ro.product.name", "product", "name"},
        {"ro.product.vendor.model", "vendor", "model"},
        {"ro.product.model", "product", "model"},
      }
      
      // zoneScore: vendor/odm/bootimage keep the OEM value when a GSI replaces
      // /system; a `ro.product.*` value is whatever is installed now.
      var zoneScore = map[string]int{
        "vendor": 40, "odm": 35, "bootimage": 35,
        "product": 25, "system": 22, "system_ext": 18, "build": 10,
      }
      
      var kindScore = map[string]int{"device": 25, "name": 12, "model": 15}
      
      // labelScore: what the SELinux area means for zygote reading it. The negative
      // numbers are the documented traps, not guesses — build_bootimage_prop and
      // build_odm_prop are refused to zygote on most GSI builds.
      var labelScore = map[string]int{
        "build_prop":           30,
        "build_vendor_prop":    30,
        "vendor_default_prop":  25,
        "default_prop":         15,
        "build_system_prop":    -20,
        "build_odm_prop":       -35,
        "build_bootimage_prop": -35,
        "bootloader_prop":      -20,
      }
      
      // Values that name a build rather than a device. They are the reason a "looks
      // like a codename" filter is not enough: mivendor is a Xiaomi vendor tree shared
      // by a whole family, generic is the GSI itself, qcom is a SoC vendor.
      var genericMatchValues = map[string]string{
        "generic":        "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_x86":    "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_arm64":  "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "generic_x86_64": "the AOSP/GSI build name, shared by every generic image",
        "aosp":           "an AOSP build name, not a device",
        "aosp_arm64":     "an AOSP build name, not a device",
        "mainline":       "the mainline/module build name, not a device",
        "treble":         "the Treble build name, not a device",
        "phh_treble":     "the GSI's own name — present on every device running that GSI",
        "mivendor":       "Xiaomi's vendor build name — shared by many Xiaomi devices, not a codename",
        "emulator":       "an emulator, not a phone",
        "unknown":        "no value",
        "qcom":           "a SoC vendor, shared by every Qualcomm device",
        "mediatek":       "a SoC vendor, shared by every MediaTek device",
        "mtk":            "a SoC vendor, shared by every MediaTek device",
        "exynos":         "a SoC vendor, shared by every Exynos device",
        "android":        "not a device name",
      }
      
      // rankMatchProps turns a phone's `getprop` and `getprop -Z` output into ranked
      // candidates. Both maps are keyed by property name; a missing value or label is
      // simply an empty string, because adb output loses lines on some ROMs.
      func rankMatchProps(values, labels map[string]string) MatchReport {
        report := MatchReport{
          Candidates: []MatchCandidate{},
          Rejected:   []MatchRejection{},
        }
      
        brand := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.brand"]))
        manufacturer := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.manufacturer"]))
        report.Model = strings.TrimSpace(values["ro.product.model"])
      
        // Phase 1: what is this phone called? Partition order is the rule, not a sum:
        // vendor, odm and bootimage are the OEM's own naming and are what a GSI leaves
        // alone, while /system, /product and /system_ext hold the ROM's name (on a
        // GSI that is the GSI itself: generic, phh_treble, mivendor). A value the OEM
        // partitions agree on is the codename; the later props are only consulted
        // when those are empty or generic.
        codenameOrder := []string{
          "ro.product.vendor.device",
          "ro.product.odm.device",
          "ro.product.bootimage.device",
          "ro.product.device",
          "ro.product.system.device",
          "ro.product.product.device",
          "ro.product.system_ext.device",
          "ro.build.product",
        }
        codename := ""
        codenameProp := ""
        for _, name := range codenameOrder {
          value := strings.TrimSpace(values[name])
          if value == "" || genericMatchValues[strings.ToLower(value)] != "" {
            continue
          }
          if !codenameShape.MatchString(value) {
            continue
          }
          if value == brand || value == manufacturer {
            continue
          }
          codename, codenameProp = value, name
          break
        }
        report.Codename = codename
      
        // Phase 2: rank every property against that answer.
        for _, p := range matchPropCandidates {
          value := strings.TrimSpace(values[p.name])
          if value == "" {
            continue
          }
          label := shortPropertyLabel(labels[p.name])
          if reason := genericMatchValues[strings.ToLower(value)]; reason != "" {
            report.Rejected = append(report.Rejected, MatchRejection{
              Prop: p.name, Value: value, Reason: reason,
            })
            continue
          }
          if brand != "" && strings.EqualFold(value, brand) {
            report.Rejected = append(report.Rejected, MatchRejection{
              Prop: p.name, Value: value,
              Reason: "the brand, not the device — it would match every phone of this make",
            })
            continue
          }
      
          c := MatchCandidate{
            Prop:  p.name,
            Value: value,
            Zone:  p.zone,
            Label: label,
          }
          c.Score = zoneScore[p.zone] + kindScore[p.kind] + labelScore[label]
      
          var why, risk []string
          switch p.zone {
          case "vendor", "odm", "bootimage":
            why = append(why, "lives on /"+p.zone+", which a GSI leaves alone")
          default:
            why = append(why, "read from the installed /"+p.zone+" partition")
            risk = append(risk, "a GSI replaces /"+p.zone+", so the value changes and the match stops")
          }
          switch label {
          case "build_prop", "build_vendor_prop", "vendor_default_prop", "default_prop":
            why = append(why, "zygote can read "+label)
          case "":
            risk = append(risk, "this ROM did not report its SELinux area, so readability is unchecked")
          default:
            risk = append(risk, label+" is often denied to zygote — the overlay can show as enabled and do nothing")
          }
          if codename != "" && value == codename {
            c.Score += 30
            why = append(why, "holds the codename")
            if p.name == codenameProp {
              c.Score += 10
            }
          } else if codename != "" && strings.Contains(value, codename) {
            c.Score += 10
            why = append(why, "contains the codename")
          } else {
            // The missi case: a property that names this build, not this phone.
            // Matching on it would claim a different device, so every such row
            // ranks below the ones that carry the codename.
            c.Score -= 20
            if p.kind == "device" {
              risk = append(risk, "holds a different name ("+value+") than this phone's codename ("+codename+")")
            } else {
              risk = append(risk, "does not hold the codename, so it names this variant rather than the device")
            }
          }
          if codenameShape.MatchString(value) {
            c.Score += 10
          } else {
            c.Score -= 5
            if strings.ContainsRune(value, ' ') {
              risk = append(risk, "contains a space — exact matching works, but it is easy to break while editing")
            }
          }
          if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(value), "global") {
            c.Score -= 10
            risk = append(risk, "has a region suffix, so another region's build would not match")
          }
          if p.zone == "system" && strings.HasSuffix(p.name, ".device") && value == codename && label == "build_prop" {
            // This is the normal, good answer on a stock ROM: say so instead of
            // making the user read the /system risk as a deal-breaker.
            risk = []string{"if a GSI is installed later this property becomes the GSI's name"}
          }
      
          c.Why = strings.Join(why, " · ")
          c.Risk = strings.Join(risk, " · ")
          c.Perfect = codename != "" && value == codename && p.kind == "device" &&
            readableByZygote(label) && survivesGSI(p.zone)
          switch {
          case c.Perfect:
            c.Trust = "high"
          case value == codename:
            c.Trust = "medium"
          default:
            c.Trust = "low"
          }
          report.Candidates = append(report.Candidates, c)
        }
      
        sort.SliceStable(report.Candidates, func(i, j int) bool {
          a, b := report.Candidates[i], report.Candidates[j]
          if a.Score != b.Score {
            return a.Score > b.Score
          }
          // Same score: the one that actually carries the codename is the more
          // useful row, and after that the order only has to be stable.
          if (a.Value == codename) != (b.Value == codename) {
            return a.Value == codename
          }
          return a.Prop < b.Prop
        })
      
        // Confidence is about the answer, not the ranking. "high" is reserved for a
        // property that satisfies every rule at once (readable by zygote, carries the
        // codename, survives a GSI); anything less and the honest advice is to keep
        // the match that already works, because a submitted condition that does not
        // hold is invisible.
        report.Confidence = "low"
        if len(report.Candidates) > 0 {
          top := report.Candidates[0]
          switch {
          case top.Perfect:
            report.Confidence = "high"
          case top.Value == codename && codename != "":
            report.Confidence = "medium"
          }
        }
        if codename != "" {
          report.ModuleProp = "persist.sys.overlay." + strings.ToLower(codename)
        }
        return report
      }
      
      // survivesGSI: a property in these areas keeps the OEM value after a GSI flash.
      func survivesGSI(zone string) bool {
        switch zone {
        case "vendor", "odm", "bootimage":
          return true
        }
        return false
      }
      
      func readableByZygote(label string) bool {
        switch label {
        case "build_prop", "build_vendor_prop", "vendor_default_prop", "default_prop":
          return true
        }
        return false
      }
      
      // shortPropertyLabel turns "u:object_r:build_vendor_prop:s0" into
      // "build_vendor_prop", which is the part that means something here.
      func shortPropertyLabel(label string) string {
        parts := strings.Split(strings.TrimSpace(label), ":")
        if len(parts) >= 3 {
          return parts[2]
        }
        return ""
      }
      
      // parseGetprop reads `getprop` output: one `[key]: [value]` per line. Lines that
      // do not fit are skipped — some ROMs print warnings into the same stream.
      func parseGetprop(out string) map[string]string {
        props := map[string]string{}
        for _, line := range strings.Split(out, "\n") {
          line = strings.TrimRight(line, "\r")
          key, rest, ok := strings.Cut(line, "]: [")
          if !ok || !strings.HasPrefix(key, "[") || !strings.HasSuffix(rest, "]") {
            continue
          }
          props[strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(key, "["))] = strings.TrimSuffix(rest, "]")
        }
        return props
      }
      
      // parseGetpropLabels reads `getprop -Z`: `[key]: [u:object_r:xyz_prop:s0]`.
      func parseGetpropLabels(out string) map[string]string {
        return parseGetprop(out)
      }
```

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# device-probe.sh — read the display settings an overlay has to match
# =============================================================================
# The overlay writes a handful of numbers that are properties of the panel, not
# style choices: the cutout path, the corner radius, the status bar height, the
# refresh rates. Guessing them puts content under a camera or leaves the clock
# off the edge, so this asks the phone (or an unpacked ROM) and keeps every
# answer with the source it came from.
#
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh                 # connected device
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --firmware DIR  # extracted ROM dump
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --json          # for the desktop app
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --write         # put the winners in config.env
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --power-profile # print res/xml/power_profile.xml
#
# --power-profile prints the compiled XML tree of the power profile (the
# desktop app turns it back into a file); everything else about the run goes to
# stderr.
#
# What answers, and how far to trust it:
#
#   runtime   dumpsys display / dumpsys window — what the panel driver and the
#             running framework report. Survives a GSI for anything the display
#             hardware tells Android (corners, refresh rates), but says nothing
#             about the OEM ROM once the OEM system partition is gone.
#   resource  cmd overlay lookup android:... — the value the framework is
#             serving right now. On a GSI that can be the GSI's own default, so
#             it is evidence of "what Android uses", not of "what the OEM chose".
#   firmware  aapt2 over framework-res.apk and the overlay APKs of an unpacked
#             ROM. The only source that still has the OEM's cutout path when a
#             GSI has replaced the system partition.
#
# Nothing here is root-only.
# =============================================================================

set -uo pipefail

# adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
# are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1

winpath() {
    if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then cygpath -w "$1"; else printf '%s' "$1"; fi
}

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"

mode="device"
serial=""
want_json=0
want_write=0
power_mode=0
check_profile=0
adb="${ADB:-}"
aapt2="${AAPT2:-}"
fwdir=""

usage() {
    sed -n '3,39p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
}

die() { printf 'device-probe: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }

# Multi-device selection lives next to this script and is shared with the UDFPS
# probe, so both ask the same question and accept the same --device value.
ADB_DEVICE_LIB="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/adb-device.sh"
[ -f "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB" ] || die "stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh is missing — the checkout is incomplete"
. "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB"

---
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# adb-device.sh — which connected phone a probe talks to
# =============================================================================
# Sourced by device-probe.sh and udfps-probe.sh. Both used to carry the same
# rule ("exactly one device, or stop"), which stops being useful the moment a
# second phone is on the desk.
#
#   adb_pick_device ADB SERIAL PROGRAM
#
# ADB is the adb binary to run, SERIAL is what --device said ("" for automatic),
# PROGRAM names the script in the messages. On success DEVICE_SERIAL holds the
# serial to pass to `adb -s`; on failure the reason has already been printed.
#
# The state matters. adb can see a phone it cannot talk to (unauthorized,
# offline, no permissions), and each of those has its own fix — telling the user
# to plug the phone in is wrong advice for all three.
#
# Detection is the fragile part, so it is hardened against what adb actually
# does rather than what its manual says:
#
#   * `adb devices` is a stream, not a table. A daemon start, a version
#     mismatch, or a "no permissions" line shares it with the devices, so only
#     lines whose second column is a real state are read as devices.
#   * the listing can lie. It is a snapshot, so the chosen serial is confirmed
#     with `get-state` before anything is run against it.
#   * a wedged server hangs instead of failing. Every adb call here is bounded,
#     and a timeout says "adb kill-server" instead of hanging the probe.
#   * the first call after the server restarts can come back with no header at
#     all. That is retried; a genuinely empty list is not.
#   * a phone that is still "connecting" (wireless adb, or just plugged in)
#     becomes ready in a second or two, so it is waited for briefly.
#   * a serial can be listed twice, and wireless transports look like
#     `192.168.1.5:5555`; duplicates are dropped and the transport is labelled.
# =============================================================================

# The states adb puts in the second column of `devices`, space-padded so a
# value can be tested with `index(states, " " $2 " ")`.
ADB_DEVICE_STATES=" device offline unauthorized bootloader recovery sideload rescue host connecting no "

# The model and product from one `adb devices -l` line, for a menu a human can
# read. Both are optional in adb's output, so this never assumes either. A
# TCP/mDNS serial is called out: with USB and wireless adb on, the same phone
# can be listed twice and the two entries are otherwise identical.
adb_device_label() {
    local line="$1" model product serial suffix=""
    model="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* model:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
    product="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* product:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
    [ -n "$model" ] || model="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* device:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
    serial="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | awk '{print $1}')"
```
