```
- path: build.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # Treble Overlay Creator
      # =============================================================================
      # One command for everything. The first run installs whatever is missing,
      # then builds; later runs go straight to the build.
      #
      #   ./build.sh                 build (auto-installs the toolchain if needed)
      #   ./build.sh setup           install / repair the toolchain only
      #   ./build.sh doctor          check the toolchain (read-only)
      #   ./build.sh check           validate config.env without building
      #   ./build.sh --dry-run       print the resources config.env emits, build nothing
      #   ./build.sh clean           remove build output
      #   ./build.sh clean --all     start over for a different device
      #
      #   -y, --yes                  no questions (also: --with-vendor-hals)
      #   -h, --help                 this help
      #
      # On Windows use build.cmd (cmd, PowerShell or a double-click). It finds Git
      # Bash and passes the same arguments here. WSL is not supported on a Windows
      # drive — see docs/windows.md.
      # =============================================================================
      
      set -e
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Project root
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
      # Launched from cmd.exe, PWD can be "C:/..." instead of "/c/..."; MSYS does
      # not recognise that form, so convert it before anything else uses it.
      if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then
          ROOT=$(cygpath -u "$ROOT")
      fi
      export ROOT
      cd "$ROOT"
      
      source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/common.sh"
      source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/toolchain.sh"
      
      # Put stuff/tools/ on PATH (and its lib64 on LD_LIBRARY_PATH on Linux).
      tools_on_path
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Options
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      MODE="build"
      CHECK_MODE=false
      DRY_RUN=false
      ASSUME_YES=false
      FORCE_VENDOR_HALS=false
      CLEAN_ALL=false
      FORCE_RES=""
      ALLOW_UNKNOWN_RESOURCES=false
      
      usage() {
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Usage:${NC} ./build.sh [command] [options]"
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Commands${NC}"
          echo "    (none)             Build the overlay module (installs tools if needed)"
          echo "    setup              Install or repair the build tools"
          echo "    doctor             Check the toolchain, install nothing"
          echo "    check              Validate config.env, build nothing"
          echo "    clean              Remove build output"
          echo "    --dry-run          Print the resources config.env emits, build nothing"
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Options${NC}"
          echo "    -y, --yes              Accept defaults, skip prompts"
          echo "    --with-vendor-hals     With --yes: include src/vendor/ in the module"
          echo "    --all                  With clean: also remove config and device files"
          echo "    --force                With setup: re-pick the resource dictionary"
          echo "    --allow-unknown-resources  Build even if a resource is missing from the target"
          echo "    -h, --help             Show this help"
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Windows:${NC} build.cmd [command] [options]"
          echo ""
      }
      
      for arg in "$@"; do
          case "$arg" in
              build)          MODE="build" ;;
              setup|--setup)  MODE="setup" ;;
              doctor|--doctor) MODE="doctor" ;;
              check|--check)  MODE="check" ;;
              clean|--clean)  MODE="clean" ;;
              dry-run|--dry-run) MODE="dryrun" ;;
              -y|--yes)       ASSUME_YES=true ;;
              --with-vendor-hals) FORCE_VENDOR_HALS=true ;;
              --all)          CLEAN_ALL=true ;;
              --force)        FORCE_RES="force" ;;
              --allow-unknown-resources) ALLOW_UNKNOWN_RESOURCES=true ;;
              -h|--help)      usage; exit 0 ;;
              *)
                  err "            Unknown option: ${arg}"
      
                  usage
                  exit 2
                  ;;
          esac
      done
      
      # A checkout on a Windows drive cannot be built from WSL (shared stuff/tools/).
      wsl_guard
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Dispatch
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      case "$MODE" in
          doctor)
              if run_doctor; then exit 0; else exit 1; fi
              ;;
      
          setup)
              banner "Setup — build tools"
              migrate_layout
              # -y means "no questions": the desktop app has no terminal, so the
              # interactive menu would fall back to its default instead of using the
              # packages this machine already has. Auto is the installer a plain
              # build runs; it still asks for a sudo password when it needs one —
              # in a terminal sudo prompts, and the app has its own dialog for it.
              if $ASSUME_YES; then
                  ensure_toolchain auto "$FORCE_RES"
              else
                  ensure_toolchain interactive "$FORCE_RES"
              fi
              exit $?
              ;;
      
          check)
              # Config validation only: no tools, no output.
              CHECK_MODE=true
              source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/build.sh"
              ;;
      
          clean)
              migrate_layout
              source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/clean.sh"
              ;;
      
          dryrun)
              # Needs config.env and the resource generators, no toolchain: the point
              # is to see the plan in seconds.
              DRY_RUN=true
              source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/build.sh"
              ;;
      
          build)
              # Move any files left in the old top-level layout into src/.
              migrate_layout
              if $IS_WINDOWS; then
                  banner "Treble Overlay Builder — Windows"
              elif $IS_TERMUX; then
                  banner "Treble Overlay Builder — Termux"
              else
                  banner "Treble Overlay Builder — Linux"
              fi
              # Installs only what is missing; prints a summary and returns non-zero
              # when the machine still cannot build.
              ensure_toolchain auto
              # The installer may just have created stuff/tools/, so refresh PATH.
              tools_on_path
              source "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/build.sh"
              ;;
      esac
      
- path: treble-rro-creator.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # Treble RRO Creator — desktop app
      # =============================================================================
      # One command, from anywhere:
      #
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh                  build if needed, then open the window
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh --rebuild        rebuild first (after a git pull, say)
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh --release        no console window (Windows; the default)
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh --detach         accepted for scripts; hand-off is automatic
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh --browser        no window; use the default browser
      #   ./treble-rro-creator.sh -clone ~/other   start on a different clone
      #
      # The first launch builds the app, downloading Go and (on Windows) a MinGW-w64
      # gcc into stuff/tools/ when the machine has none; a checkout that already has
      # gui/bin/ filled in runs without a toolchain at all, and the app finds its
      # clone by walking up from where it lives, so no path has to be typed.
      #
      # Windows: double-click treble-rro-creator.cmd; it finds Git Bash and calls this.
      # =============================================================================
      set -euo pipefail
      
      here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
      exe="$here/gui/bin/treble-rro-creator-gui"
      case "$(uname -s)" in
          MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) exe="$exe.exe" ;;
      esac
      
      rebuild=false
      release=false
      detach=false
      browser=false
      app_args=()
      for arg in "$@"; do
          case "$arg" in
              -h|--help)
                  # The launcher's own flags, which the app knows nothing about: the
                  # block between the second and third rule in the header above.
                  printf '%s\n\n' "Treble RRO Creator — desktop app"
                  awk '/^# =====/ { n++; next } n == 2 { sub(/^# ?/, ""); print }' "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}"
                  exit 0
                  ;;
              --rebuild) rebuild=true ;;
              --release) release=true ;;
              # Accepted for the launchers and for people used to typing it: on
              # Windows the hand-off happens anyway.
              --detach) detach=true ;;
              --browser|-browser) browser=true ; app_args+=("$arg") ;;
              *) app_args+=("$arg") ;;
          esac
      done
      
      # On Windows the app is always the window-only build. The window is the whole
      # UI, so a binary linked against a console only drags one along behind it —
      # and dies when that console is closed. --browser is the exception: that run
      # keeps its console, because that is where the server is watched and stopped.
      case "$(uname -s)" in
          MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*)
              if [ "$browser" = "false" ]; then
                  release=true
              fi
              ;;
      esac
      build_flags=()
      if [ "$release" = "true" ]; then
          build_flags+=("--release")
      fi
      
      # Whether Windows gives a program a console window is decided by one field in
      # the executable itself: the PE subsystem, 3 for a console build (the default)
      # and 2 for one linked with -H windowsgui. Reading it means the launcher knows
      # what the binary on disk really is — including one unpacked from a release
      # archive — instead of trusting a side file that can go stale.
      pe_subsystem() {
          local off
          off=$(od -An -tu4 -j60 -N4 "$1" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' \r')
          if [ -z "$off" ]; then
              return 2
          fi
          # 0x5c into the PE header
          od -An -tu2 -j$((off + 92)) -N2 "$1" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' \r'
      }
      
      # Is the binary older than anything that goes into it? The UI is embedded, so a
      # changed app.js or app.css means the window would still show the old page.
      sources_newer() {
          [ -f "$exe" ] || return 0
          [ -n "$(find "$here/gui" -name '*.go' -newer "$exe" -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ] && return 0
          [ -n "$(find "$here/gui/ui" -type f -newer "$exe" -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ] && return 0
          [ -n "$(find "$here/go.mod" "$here/go.sum" -newer "$exe" -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ] && return 0
          return 1
      }
      
      # Rebuild when the binary is missing or older than the Go sources and the UI.
      # --rebuild wins regardless, which is the dependable option after a pull that
      # only touched go.sum.
      stale() {
          sources_newer && return 0
          # Asked for a window-only build but the exe on disk has a console (or the
          # other way round): the mode is linked in, so that needs a rebuild.
          case "$(uname -s)" in
              MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*)
                  local want=3
                  if [ "$release" = "true" ]; then
                      want=2
                  fi
                  if [ "$(pe_subsystem "$exe")" != "$want" ]; then
                      return 0
                  fi
                  ;;
          esac
          return 1
      }
      
      if [ "$rebuild" = "true" ] || stale; then
          echo "building the app…"
          if ! bash "$here/gui/build.sh" ${build_flags[@]+"${build_flags[@]}"}; then
              if [ -f "$exe" ]; then
                  # The build is what would make the window new; failing it is no
                  # reason to refuse to open the one that is already there.
                  echo "the build failed — starting the app that is already built." >&2
                  if sources_newer; then
                      echo "  That binary is older than gui/, so the window shows the OLD page:" >&2
                      echo "  the UI is embedded in it, not read from disk." >&2
                      echo "  Fix what the build reported, then: ./treble-rro-creator.sh --rebuild" >&2
                  fi
              else
                  exit 1
              fi
          fi
      fi
      
      # Windows: hand the window to the background and return, however the launcher
      # was started — double-clicked, or typed into a cmd window. The window owns no
      # console of its own, so it outlives the cmd.exe that started it, and that
      # cmd.exe finishing is what closes the console instead of leaving one sitting
      # behind the app. Its output goes nowhere: with the console gone there is
      # nothing to read it on, and keeping the handles is what would hold the console
      # open. Failures land in gui.log next to the executable.
      #
      # A console build is the one thing left in the console, and only when there is
      # no go to relink with: it would take the console down with it, so it says why.
      if [ "$browser" = "false" ]; then
          case "$(uname -s)" in
              MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*)
                  if [ "$(pe_subsystem "$exe")" = "2" ]; then
                      "$exe" ${app_args[@]+"${app_args[@]}"} >/dev/null 2>&1 &
                      exit 0
                  fi
                  echo "note: this is a console build, so the console stays while the window is open." >&2
                  echo "      the relink needs a C compiler; run ./treble-rro-creator.sh --rebuild once it is installed." >&2
                  ;;
          esac
      fi
      
      exec "$exe" ${app_args[@]+"${app_args[@]}"}
      
- path: build.cmd
  content: |
      @echo off
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      rem build.cmd - Windows entry point
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      rem Finds Git for Windows (never WSL) and runs build.sh, which does everything:
      rem
      rem   build.cmd                  build (downloads the toolchain on first run)
      rem   build.cmd setup            install / repair the build tools
      rem   build.cmd doctor           check the toolchain
      rem   build.cmd check            validate config.env
      rem   build.cmd clean            remove build output
      rem   build.cmd clean --all      start over for a different device
      rem
      rem Requirements: Git for Windows + JDK 17+ on PATH.
      rem Tip: run this from cmd or PowerShell (.\\build.cmd), not from WSL.
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      setlocal EnableExtensions
      call "%~dp0stuff\windows\run-bash.cmd" build.sh %*
      set "RC=%ERRORLEVEL%"
      
      rem Keep the window open only when double-clicked from Explorer. Explorer runs
      rem   cmd.exe /c ""C:\path\build.cmd" "
      rem and a terminal -- cmd, PowerShell, VS Code -- starts cmd.exe with no /c. The
      rem /c is the difference, and matching on it is the only test that works:
      rem Windows leaves a space after the trailing quotes, so a last-three-characters
      rem test never matches.
      set "DOUBLE="
      echo %cmdcmdline% | "%SystemRoot%\System32\findstr.exe" /i /c:" /c " >nul && set "DOUBLE=1"
      if defined DOUBLE pause
      
      exit /b %RC%
      
- path: treble-rro-creator.cmd
  content: |
      @echo off
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      rem treble-rro-creator.cmd - launch the desktop app
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      rem Builds it on first run, then opens the window. The cmd companion to
      rem treble-rro-creator.sh, for people who would rather double-click.
      rem
      rem   treble-rro-creator.cmd               build if needed, then open the window
      rem   treble-rro-creator.cmd --rebuild     rebuild first
      rem   treble-rro-creator.cmd --release     no console window (the default here)
      rem   treble-rro-creator.cmd --browser     use the default browser instead
      rem   treble-rro-creator.cmd -h            this message
      rem
      rem Requirements: Git for Windows (already needed by build.cmd); Go and a
      rem MinGW-w64 gcc are downloaded on the first run. See docs/gui.md.
      rem ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      setlocal EnableExtensions
      
      if "%~1"=="-h" goto usage
      if "%~1"=="--help" goto usage
      
      rem The launcher closes its console either way (treble-rro-creator.sh always
      rem starts the window in the background), so all that is left to decide here is
      rem whether a failure should hold the window open. Explorer starts this file as
      rem   cmd.exe /c ""C:\path\treble-rro-creator.cmd" "
      rem and a terminal starts cmd.exe interactively, with no /c. The /c is the
      rem difference: nobody is watching a double-click, and a terminal is.
      rem
      rem (The command line is not matched on its trailing quotes: Windows leaves a
      rem space after them, so `" "` arrives as `" " ` and a last-three-characters
      rem test never matches.)
      set "DOUBLE="
      echo %cmdcmdline% | "%SystemRoot%\System32\findstr.exe" /i /c:" /c " >nul && set "DOUBLE=1"
      
      call "%~dp0stuff\windows\run-bash.cmd" treble-rro-creator.sh %*
      set "RC=%ERRORLEVEL%"
      
      rem Only hold the console open when something failed and this was started by
      rem double-clicking; a successful launch has already closed the console.
      if "%RC%"=="0" goto done
      if defined DOUBLE pause
      
      :done
      exit /b %RC%
      
      :usage
      echo Treble RRO Creator - desktop app
      echo.
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd               build if needed, then open the window
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd --rebuild     rebuild first (after a git pull, say)
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd --release     no console window (the default here)
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd --detach      accepted for scripts; the console closes anyway
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd --browser     no window; use the default browser
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd -clone PATH   start on a different clone
      echo   treble-rro-creator.cmd -h            this message
      echo.
      echo Builds on the first run (Go and MinGW-w64 gcc are downloaded);
      echo later launches open straight away. Full guide: docs\gui.md
      exit /b 0
```

> _Reasoning_
> Now the key decision: implement the interactive CLI in bash (stuff/scripts/*.sh) so it works everywhere bash does (Termux, Linux, Windows Git Bash) — no Go needed. The logic exists in bash already for: device probe (device-probe.sh), udfps (udfps-probe.sh), addons on-device (src/webui/addons.sh), toolchain, build. What's missing in bash: the match-prop ranking (matchprop.go), adb install/platform-tools (adb.go), update check (git.go). Those are feasible in bash but significant.
> 
> Scope decision: The user asks to "completely revamp build.sh so users get full web app features right from build.sh/cmd with interactive menus, options". Full parity with GUI is enormous. A careful approach: build a TUI menu system in bash that covers the GUI's main tabs:
> 
> 1. Build (verb picker: build/dry-run/check/doctor/setup/clean, with flags)
> 2. Config (edit config.env: list settings grouped by section, edit value, detect prop name/value, match prop via phone probe)
> 3. Addons (list catalog from src/webui/addons.sh, toggle/set, reset, save into src/module/addons.conf)
> 4. Device (adb devices, detect codename, install module zip)
> 5. UDFPS (probe location, set values)
> 6. Extras: docs, update check, open output.
> 
> That's basically a full CLI. This is big but doable in bash. However, risk: writing 2000+ lines bash with no way to fully test (no device, but can test menus with piped input). Also must not break existing non-interactive behavior (GUI calls `build.sh -y`, sets config, etc.).

```
- path: stuff/scripts/common.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # Treble Overlay — shared helpers
      # =============================================================================
      # Sourced by build.sh and by the modules in stuff/scripts/. Never run directly.
      #
      # The entry point sets ROOT (the project directory) and then sources this file,
      # so every helper below can assume it exists and that the current directory is
      # the project root.
      # =============================================================================
      
      : "${ROOT:?stuff/scripts/common.sh must be sourced by build.sh (ROOT is not set)}"
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Paths
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Absolute paths are used for file tests and for zip destinations. Arguments
      # handed to native tools (aapt2/zipalign) must stay RELATIVE: MSYS on Windows
      # does not reliably convert a /c/... path for a native .exe.
      # Everything that is not the thing you build lives under stuff/, so the root
      # only holds the two entry points, config.env and the folders you open.
      STUFF_DIR="$ROOT/stuff"
      TOOLS_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/tools"
      BUILD_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/build"
      OUT_DIR="$ROOT/out"
      KEYS_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/keys"
      BACKUP_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/backups"
      TEMPLATES_DIR="$STUFF_DIR/templates"
      # Not "the old version of your files": the no-git fallback for
      # restore_from_release(). Kept identical to the committed files by stuff/tests/run.sh.
      RECOVERIES_DIR="$TEMPLATES_DIR/recoveries"
      
      SRC_DIR="$ROOT/src"
      FRAMEWORK_DIR="$SRC_DIR/framework"
      FRAMEWORK_RES="$FRAMEWORK_DIR/res"
      SYSTEMUI_DIR="$SRC_DIR/systemui"
      SYSTEMUI_RES="$SYSTEMUI_DIR/res"
      MODULE_DIR="$SRC_DIR/module"
      VENDOR_DIR="$SRC_DIR/vendor"
      
      CONFIG_FILE="$ROOT/config.env"
      CONFIG_EXAMPLE="$ROOT/config.env.example"
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Restoring a tracked file to what this release ships
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # "Start over" must never hand back a copy that froze at some old commit. The
      # committed blob IS the template for a tracked file, so ask git for it; the
      # copy in stuff/templates/recoveries/ is only the fallback for a checkout with no .git
      # (a fork downloaded as a zip). stuff/tests/run.sh fails if the two ever drift.
      #
      #   restore_from_release <path relative to ROOT> [fallback copy]
      #
      # Returns 0 when the file on disk now holds the release version.
      restore_from_release() {
          local rel="$1" fallback="${2:-}"
      
          if [ -d "$ROOT/.git" ] && command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 \
             && git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --verify --quiet "HEAD:${rel}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              if git -C "$ROOT" checkout HEAD -- "$rel" 2>/dev/null; then
                  return 0
              fi
          fi
      
          if [ -n "$fallback" ] && [ -f "$fallback" ]; then
              mkdir -p "$(dirname "$ROOT/$rel")"
              cp "$fallback" "$ROOT/$rel" && return 0
          fi
          return 1
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Platform
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      IS_WINDOWS=false
      case "$(uname -s 2>/dev/null)" in
          MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) IS_WINDOWS=true ;;
      esac
      
      # WSL reports Linux but lives inside Windows. The build is allowed there only
      # when the checkout is on the Linux filesystem (see wsl_guard).
      IS_WSL=false
      if ! $IS_WINDOWS && [ -r /proc/version ] && grep -qi microsoft /proc/version 2>/dev/null; then
          IS_WSL=true
      fi
      
      IS_TERMUX=false
      if [ -d /data/data/com.termux ] && [ -n "${PREFIX:-}" ]; then
          IS_TERMUX=true
      fi
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Output
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      RED='\033[0;31m'; GREEN='\033[0;32m'; YELLOW='\033[1;33m'
      CYAN='\033[0;36m'; BOLD='\033[1m'; NC='\033[0m'
      
      ok()   { echo -e "  ${GREEN}✓${NC} $*"; }
      info() { echo -e "  ${YELLOW}→${NC} $*"; }
      warn() { echo -e "  ${YELLOW}⚠${NC} $*"; }
      err()  { echo -e "  ${RED}✗${NC} $*" >&2; }
      step() { echo -e "\n${BOLD}━━━ $* ━━━${NC}"; }
      
      banner() {
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}$*${NC}"
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────${NC}"
          echo ""
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Prompts
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # ask <question> <default>   -> answer in $REPLY
      #
      # `read` returns 1 at EOF (stdin redirected, CI, IDE task, no console). Under
      # `set -e` that used to kill the scripts silently right after a menu had been
      # printed. Falling back to a stated default keeps everything runnable
      # unattended, and pressing Enter also takes the default.
      ask() {
          local question="$1" default="${2:-}" answer=""
          printf '%s' "$question"
          if ! read -r answer; then
              echo ""
              info "No terminal input available — using '${default}'."
              answer="$default"
          fi
          [ -z "$answer" ] && answer="$default"
          REPLY="$answer"
      }
      
      # confirm <question> <y|n>   -> returns 0 for yes
      confirm() {
          local question="$1" default="${2:-n}" answer
          ask "$question" "$default"
          answer="$REPLY"
          case "$answer" in
              [Yy]|[Yy][Ee][Ss]) return 0 ;;
              *) return 1 ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # WSL safety
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # A checkout on a Windows drive that is built from inside WSL would put Linux
      # binaries into the same stuff/tools/ folder the Windows build reads, and would hand
      # Windows a build tree it cannot use. Refuse with instructions instead of
      # producing a half-broken toolchain. (This is the "VS Code opened the folder
      # with WSL" case.)
      wsl_guard() {
          $IS_WSL || return 0
          case "$ROOT" in
              /mnt/[a-z]/*) ;;
              *) return 0 ;;
          esac
      
          echo ""
          err "This project is on a Windows drive, but you are running inside WSL."
          echo ""
          echo "    Project:  $ROOT"
          echo "    Shell:    WSL (Linux)"
          echo ""
          echo "  The Linux toolchain would be installed into the same stuff/tools/ folder the"
          echo "  Windows build uses, so both platforms would then see the wrong binaries."
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Use one of these instead:${NC}"
          echo "    • Windows (cmd, PowerShell, VS Code):   build.cmd"
          echo "    • Linux / Termux:                       clone the project inside Linux"
          echo "                                            (e.g. ~/treble-rro-creator)"
          echo "                                            and run ./build.sh there"
          echo ""
          echo "  In VS Code, check the bottom-left corner: if it says \"WSL: ...\","
          echo "  close the remote window (or open a Windows terminal) and run build.cmd."
          echo ""
          exit 1
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Legacy layout
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Older versions of this project kept res/, systemui_overlay/, customize.sh,
      # service.sh, sepolicy.rule and system/vendor/ at the top level. Users who
      # upgrade by pulling can still have personal (untracked) copies there. Move
      # them into src/ instead of silently ignoring them.
      migrate_layout() {
          local moved=false f
      
          # res/ -> src/framework/res
          if [ -d "$ROOT/res" ]; then
              if [ ! -d "$FRAMEWORK_RES" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$FRAMEWORK_DIR"
                  cp -R "$ROOT/res" "$FRAMEWORK_DIR/res"
                  rm -rf "$ROOT/res"
                  info "Moved legacy ./res → src/framework/res"
                  moved=true
              else
                  warn "Legacy ./res exists but is no longer used — the build reads src/framework/res"
              fi
          fi
      
          # systemui_overlay/ -> src/systemui/res
          if [ -d "$ROOT/systemui_overlay/res" ]; then
              if [ ! -d "$SYSTEMUI_RES" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$SYSTEMUI_DIR"
                  cp -R "$ROOT/systemui_overlay/res" "$SYSTEMUI_DIR/res"
                  rm -rf "$ROOT/systemui_overlay"
                  info "Moved legacy ./systemui_overlay → src/systemui"
                  moved=true
              else
                  warn "Legacy ./systemui_overlay exists but is no longer used — the build reads src/systemui/res"
              fi
          fi
      
          # system/vendor -> src/vendor
          if [ -d "$ROOT/system/vendor" ]; then
              mkdir -p "$VENDOR_DIR"
              cp -R "$ROOT/system/vendor/." "$VENDOR_DIR/" 2>/dev/null || true
              rm -rf "$ROOT/system"
              info "Moved legacy ./system/vendor → src/vendor"
              moved=true
          fi
      
          # Root module scripts -> src/module
          mkdir -p "$MODULE_DIR"
          for f in customize.sh service.sh sepolicy.rule; do
              [ -f "$ROOT/$f" ] || continue
              if [ -f "$MODULE_DIR/$f" ] && cmp -s "$ROOT/$f" "$MODULE_DIR/$f"; then
                  rm -f "$ROOT/$f"
              else
                  mv -f "$ROOT/$f" "$MODULE_DIR/$f"
                  info "Moved legacy ./$f → src/module/$f (now the copy that gets built)"
              fi
              moved=true
          done
      
          # YOUR BACKUPS -> stuff/backups
          if [ -d "$ROOT/YOUR BACKUPS" ] && [ ! -d "$BACKUP_DIR" ]; then
              mv "$ROOT/YOUR BACKUPS" "$BACKUP_DIR"
              info "Moved legacy ./YOUR BACKUPS → stuff/backups"
              moved=true
          fi
      
          # Everything that is not src/, docs/ or an entry point now lives in stuff/.
          # A git pull moves these itself; this covers an upgrade from a zip, which
          # would otherwise leave a second copy in the way at the root.
          mkdir -p "$STUFF_DIR"
          for f in keys templates windows tests scripts tools build backups; do
              [ -d "$ROOT/$f" ] || continue
              if [ -d "$STUFF_DIR/$f" ]; then
                  warn "Legacy ./$f exists but stuff/$f is the one in use — remove the old copy"
                  continue
              fi
              mv "$ROOT/$f" "$STUFF_DIR/$f"
              info "Moved legacy ./$f → stuff/$f"
              moved=true
          done
      
          $moved && info "Layout upgraded — internals live in stuff/, the entry points stay at the root"
          return 0
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Binary inspection
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Windows cannot execute Linux binaries. If this checkout is also opened from
      # WSL/Kali (a copy on the same drive), a Linux `aapt2` can land in the same
      # stuff/tools/ folder the Windows build puts on PATH, shadow `aapt2.exe`, and fail
      # much later with "Exec format error". Classify by magic bytes so it is caught
      # up front.
      classify_binary() {
          local f="$1"
          if [ ! -e "$f" ]; then echo "missing"; return 0; fi
          if [ -d "$f" ]; then echo "directory"; return 0; fi
          local magic
          magic=$(head -c 4 "$f" 2>/dev/null | od -An -tx1 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' \n')
          case "$magic" in
              4d5a*)     echo "windows-pe" ;;   # MZ  -> .exe
              7f454c46)  echo "linux-elf" ;;    # \x7fELF -> WSL/Linux build
              2321*)     echo "script" ;;       # #!
              504b0304)  echo "zip" ;;          # PK.. -> apk / jar
              "")        echo "unreadable" ;;
              *)         echo "unknown" ;;
          esac
      }
      
      kind_label() {
          case "$1" in
              windows-pe) echo "Windows executable" ;;
              linux-elf)  echo "Linux binary (ELF)" ;;
              script)     echo "shell script" ;;
              zip)        echo "archive" ;;
              missing)    echo "missing" ;;
              *)          echo "$1" ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # A native binary built for the OTHER platform. This is the real contamination
      # signal: scripts, jars and apks are fine to share between Windows and WSL.
      kind_foreign() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS; then
              [ "$1" = "linux-elf" ]
          else
              [ "$1" = "windows-pe" ]
          fi
      }
      
      # Can a binary of this kind run on the machine we are on right now?
      kind_usable() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS; then
              case "$1" in
                  windows-pe|script|zip) return 0 ;;
                  *) return 1 ;;
              esac
          fi
          case "$1" in
              linux-elf|script|zip) return 0 ;;
              *) return 1 ;;
          esac
      }
      
      # Every path a tool could be picked up from, in the order build.sh resolves it.
      tool_candidates() {
          local name="$1" c
          for c in "$(command -v "$name" 2>/dev/null)" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}.exe" \
                   "${TOOLS_DIR}/${name}.bat"; do
              [ -n "$c" ] && [ -f "$c" ] && printf '%s\n' "$c"
          done
          return 0
      }
      
      # Is this tool usable HERE (PATH, stuff/tools/, .exe/.bat on Windows)?
      tool_ready() {
          local name="$1" cand
          while IFS= read -r cand; do
              [ -n "$cand" ] || continue
              kind_usable "$(classify_binary "$cand")" && return 0
          done <<< "$(tool_candidates "$name")"
          return 1
      }
      
      # First usable copy of a tool (prints the path, returns 1 when there is none).
      tool_path() {
          local name="$1" cand
          while IFS= read -r cand; do
              [ -n "$cand" ] || continue
              if kind_usable "$(classify_binary "$cand")"; then
                  printf '%s\n' "$cand"
                  return 0
              fi
          done <<< "$(tool_candidates "$name")"
          return 1
      }
      
      # Where the aapt2 resource dictionary lives, if it is installed.
      framework_res_path() {
          local c
          for c in "$TOOLS_DIR/framework-res.apk" \
                   "/usr/share/android-framework-res/framework-res.apk"; do
              [ -f "$c" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$c"; return 0; }
          done
          # Optional local Android SDK (Arch Linux layout)
          if [ -d "/opt/android-sdk/platforms" ]; then
              c=$(find /opt/android-sdk/platforms -name "framework-res.apk" 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)
              [ -n "$c" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$c"; return 0; }
          fi
          return 1
      }
      
      # Everything the build needs, as a space-separated list (empty = ready).
      # zipalign is not in the Termux package repository (pkg cannot install it) and
      # an unaligned RRO still loads, so it is optional there instead of blocking the
      # build forever. Everything else still requires it.
      zipalign_optional() {
          $IS_TERMUX && ! tool_ready zipalign
      }
      
      # align_apk <unsigned> <aligned> — zipalign when available, plain copy if not.
      # An unaligned APK is valid and installs; it just cannot be mmap'ed as
      # efficiently, so this is a warning, not a failure.
      ALIGN_WARNED=false
      align_apk() {
          if tool_ready zipalign; then
              zipalign -f 4 "$1" "$2"
              return $?
          fi
          if ! $ALIGN_WARNED; then
              warn "zipalign not available — APKs stay unaligned (valid, slightly slower to map)"
              $IS_TERMUX && warn "  Termux: pkg install aapt  (that package ships zipalign)"
              ALIGN_WARNED=true
          fi
          cp -f "$1" "$2"
      }
      
      toolchain_missing() {
          local missing="" t
          for t in aapt2 zipalign apksigner; do
              [ "$t" = "zipalign" ] && zipalign_optional && continue
              tool_ready "$t" || missing="$missing $t"
          done
          command -v java >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing="$missing java"
          framework_res_path >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing="$missing framework-res.apk"
          printf '%s' "${missing# }"
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Device identity
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Turns the raw DEVICE_* values from config.env into the module id, the overlay
      # package names and the match condition. Called by build.sh right after
      # config.env is sourced, and by the standalone scripts (manifest.sh,
      # hardware-overlay.sh) so they agree with the build.
      #
      # Users only need to set DEVICE_CODENAME and DEVICE_MANUFACTURER; everything
      # else is derived. A value containing "<" is a template placeholder.
      derive_overlay_identity() {
          [ -z "${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER:-}" ] || [[ "$DEVICE_MANUFACTURER" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_MANUFACTURER="generic"
          [ -z "${DEVICE_CODENAME:-}" ]     || [[ "$DEVICE_CODENAME" == *"<"* ]]     && DEVICE_CODENAME="generic"
      
          # Clean manufacturer for Java package names (lowercase alphanumeric only)
          SAFE_MANUFACTURER=$(printf '%s' "${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]//g')
      
          # Clean codename for package name: replace non-alphanumeric with dots
          # e.g. "Infinix-X6852" → "infinix.x6852" (dots are valid Java package separators)
          PACKAGE_SEGMENT=$(printf '%s' "${DEVICE_CODENAME}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]/./g' | sed 's/\.\.*/./g' | sed 's/^\.//;s/\.$//')
      
          # Module ids are shared by Magisk, KernelSU and APatch: they must match
          # ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$ (no spaces or slashes). Use the already-cleaned
          # manufacturer/codename pieces for the generated default; an explicit
          # OVERLAY_NAME in config.env is kept as-is.
          DEFAULT_MANUFACTURER="${SAFE_MANUFACTURER:-generic}"
          DEFAULT_CODENAME="${PACKAGE_SEGMENT:-generic}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_NAME:-}" ]        || [[ "$OVERLAY_NAME" == *"<"* ]]        && OVERLAY_NAME="treble-overlay-${DEFAULT_MANUFACTURER}-${DEFAULT_CODENAME}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_PACKAGE:-}" ]     || [[ "$OVERLAY_PACKAGE" == *"<"* ]]     && OVERLAY_PACKAGE="me.phh.treble.overlay.${SAFE_MANUFACTURER}.${PACKAGE_SEGMENT}"
          [ -z "${OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI:-}" ] || [[ "$OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_PACKAGE_SYSTEMUI="${OVERLAY_PACKAGE}.systemui"
          [[ "${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_PROP_VALUE="${DEVICE_CODENAME}"
          # Only placeholders are replaced. An EMPTY DEVICE_PROP_NAME is meaningful: it
          # builds an overlay with no match condition (always active), which is the safe
          # default for framework overlays — see the Overlay Activation section of
          # config.env for why ro.product.* conditions fail on GSI setups.
          [[ "${DEVICE_PROP_NAME:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_PROP_NAME="ro.product.device"
      
          if [ -n "${DEVICE_PROP_NAME:-}" ]; then
              OVERLAY_CONDITION="        android:requiredSystemPropertyName=\"${DEVICE_PROP_NAME}\"
              android:requiredSystemPropertyValue=\"${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE}\" />"
              CONDITION_DESC="${DEVICE_PROP_NAME} == \"${DEVICE_PROP_VALUE}\""
          else
              OVERLAY_CONDITION="        />"
              CONDITION_DESC="none (always active)"
          fi
      
          [ -z "${ANDROID_VERSION:-}" ]     && ANDROID_VERSION="14"
          [ -z "${COMPILE_SDK_VERSION:-}" ] && COMPILE_SDK_VERSION="34"
          [ -z "${MIN_SDK_VERSION:-}" ]     && MIN_SDK_VERSION="34"
          [ -z "${TARGET_SDK_VERSION:-}" ]  && TARGET_SDK_VERSION="34"
      
          # Module metadata: module.prop, both manifests and the hardware overlay
          # read these. Empty or still a <placeholder> falls back to the release
          # values, so a config.env written before these keys existed still builds.
          [[ -z "${OVERLAY_VERSION:-}" || "${OVERLAY_VERSION}" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_VERSION="1.0"
          [[ -z "${OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE:-}" || "${OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE}" == *"<"* ]] && OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE="1"
          # Author is free text; only an empty or placeholder one is replaced.
          [[ -z "${MODULE_AUTHOR:-}" || "${MODULE_AUTHOR}" == *"<"* ]] && MODULE_AUTHOR="${DEVICE_MANUFACTURER}"
      
          [[ "${LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE="android.sensor.light"
          [[ "${DEVICE_MODEL:-}" == *"<"* ]] && DEVICE_MODEL="Generic Device"
          # Status bar landscape height: only set fallback if explicitly a placeholder
          # (otherwise leave empty so the status bar section skips it)
          [[ "${STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT_LANDSCAPE:-}" == *"<"* ]] && STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT_LANDSCAPE=24
      
          return 0
      }
      
      # Does this power_profile.xml contain actual data, or is it the empty template?
      power_profile_is_placeholder() {
          local f="$1"
          [ -f "$f" ] || return 0
          ! grep -qE '<item[[:space:]>]' "$f"
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Portable helpers
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Convert an MSYS path to a native Windows path (no-op elsewhere).
      to_win_path() {
          if $IS_WINDOWS && command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              cygpath -w "$1"
          else
              printf '%s' "$1"
          fi
      }
      
      # Create <dest> from the contents of <src>, using whichever zip tool exists:
      # Info-ZIP (Linux/Termux), 7-Zip, or PowerShell's ZipArchive API (Windows).
      create_zip() {
          local src="$1" dest="$2"
          rm -f "$dest"
          if command -v zip >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              ( cd "$src" && zip -r "$dest" . >/dev/null ) || return 1
          elif command -v 7z >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              ( cd "$src" && 7z a -tzip "$dest" . >/dev/null ) || return 1
          elif command -v powershell >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ -f "$STUFF_DIR/windows/zipdir.ps1" ]; then
              powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass \
                  -File "$(to_win_path "$STUFF_DIR/windows/zipdir.ps1")" \
                  -Source "$(to_win_path "$(cd "$src" && pwd)")" \
                  -Dest "$(to_win_path "$dest")" >/dev/null || return 1
          else
              err "No zip tool available (install zip, 7-Zip, or re-run the build on Windows)"
              return 1
          fi
      }
      
      # Make the local toolchain visible. Windows tools are .exe files in stuff/tools/;
      # on Linux the build-tools zipalign needs the bundled libc++ from lib64/.
      tools_on_path() {
          case ":$PATH:" in
              *":$TOOLS_DIR:"*) ;;
              *) export PATH="$TOOLS_DIR:$PATH" ;;
          esac
      
          [ -d "$TOOLS_DIR" ] || return 0
          if ! $IS_WINDOWS; then
              local lib
              for lib in "$TOOLS_DIR"/android-sdk/build-tools/*/lib64; do
                  [ -d "$lib" ] && [ -f "$lib/libc++.so" ] || continue
                  export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$lib${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
                  break
              done
          fi
          return 0
      }
```

```
2:# =============================================================================
3:# device-probe.sh — read the display settings an overlay has to match
4:# =============================================================================
5:# The overlay writes a handful of numbers that are properties of the panel, not
6:# style choices: the cutout path, the corner radius, the status bar height, the
7:# refresh rates. Guessing them puts content under a camera or leaves the clock
8:# off the edge, so this asks the phone (or an unpacked ROM) and keeps every
9:# answer with the source it came from.
11:#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh                 # connected device
12:#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --firmware DIR  # extracted ROM dump
13:#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --json          # for the desktop app
14:#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --write         # put the winners in config.env
15:#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --power-profile # print res/xml/power_profile.xml
17:# --power-profile prints the compiled XML tree of the power profile (the
18:# desktop app turns it back into a file); everything else about the run goes to
19:# stderr.
21:# What answers, and how far to trust it:
23:#   runtime   dumpsys display / dumpsys window — what the panel driver and the
24:#             running framework report. Survives a GSI for anything the display
25:#             hardware tells Android (corners, refresh rates), but says nothing
26:#             about the OEM ROM once the OEM system partition is gone.
27:#   resource  cmd overlay lookup android:... — the value the framework is
28:#             serving right now. On a GSI that can be the GSI's own default, so
29:#             it is evidence of "what Android uses", not of "what the OEM chose".
30:#   firmware  aapt2 over framework-res.apk and the overlay APKs of an unpacked
31:#             ROM. The only source that still has the OEM's cutout path when a
32:#             GSI has replaced the system partition.
34:# Nothing here is root-only.
35:# =============================================================================
39:# adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
40:# are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
59:usage() {
65:# Multi-device selection lives next to this script and is shared with the UDFPS
66:# probe, so both ask the same question and accept the same --device value.
106:# Facts, kept parallel: one row per (setting, value) pair. Two sources that
107:# disagree both stay, because the disagreement is the useful part.
113:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
114:# Bookkeeping
115:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
121:# add_fact key label unit value source confidence kind detail
123:# The same value from a second source is not a second answer, so it is dropped;
124:# a different value is kept and the page shows both.
144:# demote key value note — when this module's own overlay turns out to hold a
145:# value that a framework lookup already reported, that answer stops being
146:# independent evidence. The row stays (it is still what Android uses), but its
147:# confidence drops and the detail says why.
161:# first_fact key — the highest-priority answer recorded for a key. Facts are
162:# added best-source-first, so the first one is the winner.
171:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
172:# Tools
173:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
196:# apk_string_res APK RESNAME — the default-config value of a string resource.
210:# apk_dimen_res APK RESNAME WANT_CONFIG — "unit value" as aapt2 prints it, e.g.
211:# "px 113.0". WANT_CONFIG is "land" for the landscape qualifier, "" otherwise.
228:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
229:# Device mode
230:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
231:# </dev/null matters: adb inherits stdin, and a call made inside a `while read`
232:# loop would otherwise eat the rest of the loop's input after the first pass.
235:# Overlay state needs root on some ROMs (HyperOS is one): the plain call returns
236:# an error, which read as "no overlays" and silently fell back to the GSI's own
237:# values. Every overlay query goes through these two.
251:# pull that also works for a root-only file (/vendor/overlay is one): adb pull
252:# runs as the shell user, `su 0 cat` does not.
262:# cmd overlay lookup needs the shell permission; fall back to su when a build
263:# only allows root. An error string is a miss, not a value.
276:# 113.0px / 24.0dp — the module wants px. dp is converted with the panel density
277:# when it is known, and left alone (with a note) when it is not.
820:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
821:# Firmware mode
822:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
899:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
900:# Power profile
901:# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
902:# aapt2 prints a compiled XML file as an indented tree, and that is what the
903:# desktop app converts back to <device>...</device>. Nothing here tries to write
904:# XML: the tree is faithful, and a converter that is tested can be changed.
909:# A device profile has numbers only a device would: CPU frequencies in the
910:# hundreds of MHz to GHz, screen currents in mA, a battery in thousands of mAh.
911:# AOSP's fallback — and the copy many ROMs leave in framework-res — is 0.1 for
===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# device-probe.sh — read the display settings an overlay has to match
# =============================================================================
# The overlay writes a handful of numbers that are properties of the panel, not
# style choices: the cutout path, the corner radius, the status bar height, the
# refresh rates. Guessing them puts content under a camera or leaves the clock
# off the edge, so this asks the phone (or an unpacked ROM) and keeps every
# answer with the source it came from.
#
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh                 # connected device
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --firmware DIR  # extracted ROM dump
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --json          # for the desktop app
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --write         # put the winners in config.env
#   bash stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh --power-profile # print res/xml/power_profile.xml
#
# --power-profile prints the compiled XML tree of the power profile (the
# desktop app turns it back into a file); everything else about the run goes to
# stderr.
#
# What answers, and how far to trust it:
#
#   runtime   dumpsys display / dumpsys window — what the panel driver and the
#             running framework report. Survives a GSI for anything the display
#             hardware tells Android (corners, refresh rates), but says nothing
#             about the OEM ROM once the OEM system partition is gone.
#   resource  cmd overlay lookup android:... — the value the framework is
#             serving right now. On a GSI that can be the GSI's own default, so
#             it is evidence of "what Android uses", not of "what the OEM chose".
#   firmware  aapt2 over framework-res.apk and the overlay APKs of an unpacked
#             ROM. The only source that still has the OEM's cutout path when a
#             GSI has replaced the system partition.
#
# Nothing here is root-only.
# =============================================================================

set -uo pipefail

# adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
# are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1

winpath() {
    if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then cygpath -w "$1"; else printf '%s' "$1"; fi
}

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"

mode="device"
serial=""
want_json=0
want_write=0
power_mode=0
check_profile=0
adb="${ADB:-}"
aapt2="${AAPT2:-}"
fwdir=""

usage() {
    sed -n '3,39p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
}

die() { printf 'device-probe: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }

# Multi-device selection lives next to this script and is shared with the UDFPS
# probe, so both ask the same question and accept the same --device value.
ADB_DEVICE_LIB="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/adb-device.sh"
[ -f "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB" ] || die "stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh is missing — the checkout is incomplete"
. "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB"

note() { notes+=("$1"); }
warn() { warnings+=("$1"); }

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --device)
            mode="device"
            shift
            if [ $# -gt 0 ] && [ "${1#--}" = "$1" ]; then serial="$1"; shift; fi
            ;;
```

```
      // handleConfigApply saves the rows the form changed. Edits are addressed by

      func (a *App) handleConfigApply(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        var body struct {
          Edits []ConfigEdit `json:"edits"`
        }
        if !decode(w, r, &body) {
          return

          return

        }

        if err != nil {
          writeError(w, http.StatusConflict, err.Error())
          return
        }
        if next != string(text) {
          if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(next), 0o644); err != nil {
            writeError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, err.Error())
            return
          }

        doc, _ := parseConfig(next)
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"config": doc, "text": next})
      }
      
      // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

      // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      // An addon is a tweak the module owns: either a Settings value it writes on the
      // phone (the volume panel side, the screen timeout) or, for the overlay addons,
      // a resource the build bakes into the APK. Either way the choice lives in
      // src/module/addons.conf instead of config.env, which is why the tab is

      //
      // The catalog and the rules are in src/webui/addons.sh — the same file the

      // a form over that script rather than a second list to keep in sync. The script

      // build.sh packs into the module.
      const addonsScript = "src/webui/addons.sh"
      
      // The script validates both; these only keep a request from being turned into

      var (
        addonID     = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z0-9_]+$`)
        addonChoice = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z0-9]+$`)
      )
      
      // addonsEnv points the helper at the clone instead of an installed module.
      // Paths are POSIX: Git Bash on Windows reads a backslash as an escape.
      func (a *App) addonsEnv() []string {
        root := filepath.ToSlash(a.Root())
        return []string{
          "ADDONS_DIR=" + root,
          "ADDONS_CONF=" + root + "/src/module/addons.conf",
        }
      }
      
      func (a *App) runAddons(args ...string) ([]byte, error) {
        root := a.Root()
        if !isClone(root) {
          return nil, errors.New("no clone selected")
        }
        bash := a.Bash()
        if !fileExists(bash) {
          return nil, errors.New("bash was not found — pick it with the Path chip")
        }
        // Short on purpose: six `settings` calls on a phone, and no work at all in
        // the clone.
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, bash, append([]string{addonsScript}, args...)...)
        // Hide the console Windows would otherwise flash for this child. The tab
        // runs the helper on open and on every save, so an un-hidden window is a
        // black rectangle blinking at the user each time.
        setProcAttr(cmd)
        cmd.Dir = root
        // A stale ADDONS_* in the app's own environment would otherwise win over
        // the paths below (Windows keeps the first duplicate in the block).
        env := make([]string, 0, len(os.Environ())+2)
        for _, kv := range os.Environ() {
          if strings.HasPrefix(kv, "ADDONS_") {
            continue
          }
          env = append(env, kv)
        }
        cmd.Env = append(env, a.addonsEnv()...)
        var stderr strings.Builder
        cmd.Stderr = &stderr
        out, err := cmd.Output()
        if err != nil {
          msg := strings.TrimSpace(stderr.String())
          if msg == "" {
            msg = err.Error()
          }
          return nil, errors.New(msg)
        }
        return out, nil
      }
      
      // addonsDoc is the helper's own JSON, passed through: the page renders exactly
      // what the module will enforce.
      func (a *App) addonsDoc() (map[string]any, error) {
        out, err := a.runAddons("list")
        if err != nil {
          return nil, err
        }
        var doc map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(out, &doc); err != nil {
          return nil, fmt.Errorf("the addons helper did not return JSON: %v", err)
        }
        return doc, nil
      }
      
      func (a *App) handleAddons(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        doc, err := a.addonsDoc()
        if err != nil {
          writeError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err.Error())
          return
        }
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, doc)
      }

      func (a *App) handleAddonsSave(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        var body struct {
```

```
              fi
              printf '{"id":"%s","kind":"%s","label":"%s","summary":"%s","choices":[%s],"default":"%s","value":"%s","saved":%s,"live":"%s"}' \
                  "$id" "$kind" \
                  "$(printf '%s' "$label" | sed 's/\\/\\\\/g; s/"/\\"/g')" \
                  "$(printf '%s' "$summary" | sed 's/\\/\\\\/g; s/"/\\"/g')" \
                  "$(printf '%s' "$choices" | awk -F, '{ for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) printf "%s\"%s\"", (i > 1 ? "," : ""), $i }')" \
                  "$def" "$value" "$is_saved" "$(live_value "$id")"
          done
          printf ']}\n'
      }
      
      cmd_set() { # ID=VALUE ... — save, then make it true now
          rc=0
          for pair in "$@"; do
              id=${pair%%=*}
              if [ "$id" = "$pair" ]; then
                  say "x '$pair' is not ID=VALUE"
                  rc=1
                  continue
              fi
              v=${pair#*=}
              if [ -z "$(default_of "$id")" ]; then
                  say "x $id: no such addon"
                  rc=1
                  continue
              fi
              if ! valid_value "$id" "$v"; then
                  bad_value "$id" "$v"
                  rc=1
                  continue
              fi
              # Only deviations are kept: setting an addon back to its default hands
              # that setting back to the ROM instead of pinning it on every boot.
              if [ "$v" = "$(default_of "$id")" ]; then
                  del_conf "$id"
              else
                  put_conf "$id" "$v" || rc=1
              fi
              say "+ $id=$v"
              # An overlay addon only exists inside the APK. Saving it is the shell's
              # whole job: the page writes the entry with Apply, and build.sh emits it
              # (or stops emitting it, when the choice is the default).
              if [ "$(kind_of "$id")" = overlay ]; then
                  if [ "$v" = "$(default_of "$id")" ]; then
                      say "  overlay addon: saved as the default — nothing to enforce"
                  else
                      say "  overlay addon: saved — Apply on the phone, or the next build, writes it"
                  fi
                  continue
              fi
              # On a desktop with no phone there is nothing to apply to, and the file
              # is the whole job; the script still exits 0 so the choice is saved.
              if have_settings; then
                  # A failed put stays saved on purpose: the next boot tries again,
                  # and `list` reports the row as saved but not live.
                  apply_one "$id" "$v" || rc=1
              fi
          done
          mirror_conf
          # The choice is saved even when the device rejected a put (the next boot
          # tries again), but the exit code says so: the phone's page turns it into a
          # warning, and the desktop app has no `settings` to fail with.
          return $rc
      }
      
      cmd_apply() { # [ID ...] — apply what is saved; no output when nothing is
          rc=0
          if [ $# -gt 0 ]; then list="$*"; else list=$(ids); fi
          for id in $list; do
              v=$(conf_value "$id")
              [ -n "$v" ] || continue
              # A line left by an older catalog is not an error at boot; it is just
              # ignored. `reset` is what deletes it.
              [ -n "$(default_of "$id")" ] || continue
              # Overlay addons are already inside the APK; there is nothing to set.
              if [ "$(kind_of "$id")" = overlay ]; then
                  continue
              fi
              apply_one "$id" "$v" || { rc=1; continue; }
              # Read it back: a put that the system rejected (a restricted namespace,
              # for instance) prints nothing but leaves the old value in place.
              now=$(live_value "$id")
              if [ "$now" != "$v" ]; then
                  say "x $id: the device still reports '${now:-unset}'"
                  rc=1
              else
                  say "+ $id=$v"
              fi
          done
          return $rc
      }
      
      cmd_reset() {
          rc=0
          kept_overlay=no
          for id in $(ids); do
              v=$(conf_value "$id")
              [ -n "$v" ] || continue
              if [ "$(kind_of "$id")" = overlay ]; then
                  # The flashed APK cannot be un-built from here. On the phone the
                  # line stays because it describes what is installed; on the
                  # desktop (no phone, no `settings`) it is just a build choice and
                  # Clear all must remove it.
                  if have_settings; then
                      kept_overlay=yes
                  else
                      del_conf "$id"
                  fi
                  continue
              fi
              # Same guard as `set`: with no phone there is nothing to restore, and
              # clearing the file is the whole job.
              if have_settings; then
                  apply_one "$id" "$(default_of "$id")" || rc=1
              fi
              del_conf "$id"
          done
          # Drop lines for addons that no longer exist (an older catalog shipped the
          # battery percentage and the clock seconds, which a GSI exposes itself).
          if [ -f "$CONF" ]; then
              for id in $(grep '^[A-Za-z]' "$CONF" 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f1); do
                  [ -n "$(default_of "$id")" ] || del_conf "$id"
              done
          fi
          mirror_conf
          say "+ live addons are back to their defaults; nothing is applied on boot"
          [ "$kept_overlay" = yes ] && say "  overlay addons stay as they are — the installed APK still has them"
          return $rc
      }
      
      cmd_status() { # key=value, the way apply.sh status reports
          for id in $(ids); do
              printf '%s=%s\n' "$id" "$(live_value "$id")"
          done
      }
      
      usage() {
          say "usage: addons.sh list | set ID=VALUE ... | apply [ID ...] | reset | status"
          say "       addons.sh restore-conf"
      }
      
      cmd=${1:-list}
      [ $# -gt 0 ] && shift
      
      case "$cmd" in
          list)         cmd_list ;;
          set)          cmd_set "$@" ;;
          apply)        cmd_apply "$@" ;;
          reset)        cmd_reset ;;
          status)       cmd_status ;;
          restore-conf) restore_conf ;;
          catalog)      catalog ;;
          help|-h|--help) usage ;;
          *)
              say "x unknown command: $cmd"
              usage
              exit 2 ;;
      esac
      exit $?
```

```
# =============================================================================
# Treble Overlay — Device Configuration
# =============================================================================
# Edit this file to match YOUR device, then run: ./build.sh/cmd
#   Preview what these values produce (no tools, no build): ./build.sh/cmd --dry-run
#   Check them only:                                        ./build.sh/cmd check
#
#   Lines starting with # are OFF. Remove the # to turn one on.
#
#   Manufacturer  adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer
#   Model         adb shell getprop ro.product.model
#   Codename      adb shell getprop ro.product.device
#                 (on a GSI this often shows the ROM's name — see below)
#
# Reference values: config.env.example (Samsung Galaxy A90 5G)
# =============================================================================

# ── Device identity ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Drives the module/overlay names. Codename also names the match property below.
DEVICE_MANUFACTURER="Xiaomi"
DEVICE_MODEL="Redmi Note 17"
DEVICE_CODENAME="Zephyr"
# Battery/power profile: src/framework/res/xml/power_profile.xml (docs/device-extraction.md)

# ── Module metadata ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# What Magisk/KernelSU/APatch show on the Modules page, and the version of both
# APKs. Bump OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE on every release — it must be a whole number.
OVERLAY_VERSION="2.0"
OVERLAY_VERSION_CODE=2
# Author of the module. Left empty, module.prop falls back to DEVICE_MANUFACTURER.
MODULE_AUTHOR="uzbforce"

# ── Overlay activation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The overlay applies only while DEVICE_PROP_NAME == DEVICE_PROP_VALUE.
# Keep persist.sys.overlay.<codename> = true: it is readable from every domain
# and build.sh sets it at boot before zygote. DEVICE_PROP_NAME="" drops the
# check entirely (module only ever lands on this one device).
#   Why not ro.product.device? On a GSI that is the ROM's name (mivendor,
#   phh_treble, …) and zygote cannot read the prop holding the real codename.
#   Details + per-device prop table: docs/configuration.md#choosing-the-match-property
# Is it really applied? (an [x] in `cmd overlay list` does not prove it)
#   adb shell cmd overlay lookup <package> android:dimen/status_bar_height_default
#
#  If you want to use a different property, set it here and also in
#  docs/configuration.md#choosing-the-match-property
DEVICE_PROP_NAME="persist.sys.overlay.zephyr"
DEVICE_PROP_VALUE="true"

# ── Overlay Priority ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OVERLAY_PRIORITY=628
OVERLAY_PRIORITY_SYSTEMUI=9999

# ── Display ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Screen corner radius. Also the reference for the padding below.
ROUNDED_CORNER_RADIUS=135
# Status bar height in px, portrait and landscape. The effective height is
# max(this value, display-cutout inset).
STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT=113
STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT_LANDSCAPE=70

# ── Status bar content padding ────────────────────────────────────────────
#   >>> OFF BY DEFAULT — uncomment the three STATUS_BAR_* lines to turn it on.
#
# Moves the clock and the status icons away from the left/right edges, so they
# do not sit under the rounded corners. Left commented, the bar keeps the
# ROM/GSI layout.
#
#   STATUS_BAR_PADDING_START / _END   SystemUI status_bar_padding_*  <- GSI obeys this
#   STATUS_BAR_CONTENT_PADDING        framework rounded_corner_content_padding
#
# Set all three to the SAME number. Rule of thumb: ROUNDED_CORNER_RADIUS / 3
# (15-20 should fit a 120-150px corner). The two paths never stack.
#   Measured on this device: framework value alone did nothing on the GSI,
#   the SystemUI pair moved the clock 1:1.
# More: docs/configuration.md#status-bar-content-padding-start--end
#STATUS_BAR_CONTENT_PADDING=15
#STATUS_BAR_PADDING_START=15
#STATUS_BAR_PADDING_END=15

# Rarely needed fine-tuning of the same block (all optional):
#STATUS_BAR_PADDING_TOP=0
#STATUS_BAR_ICONS_PADDING_START=3dp
#STATUS_BAR_ICONS_PADDING_END=4dp
#STATUS_BAR_DOT_MIN_PADDING=20dp
# Turns the camera/mic privacy dot off (also frees its 20dp end-side reserve).
#HAS_PRIVACY_DOT=false
# Notch / Display Cutout (SVG Path)
# Leave commented out if your device has no notch.
# Reference (Samsung Infinity-U):
DISPLAY_CUTOUT="M 0,0 H -29 V 118 H 29 V 0 H 0 Z"

# ── Waterfall panel (optional) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# A waterfall screen curves down the sides, so the framework reserves a strip
# there and every app keeps its content out of it — that is the gutter buttons
# and lists show on the left and right. These are the four insets of that strip
# (px, or dp). Commented out, the ROM's own values stay. Only the edges your
# panel actually curves need a value.
# More: docs/configuration.md#waterfall-cutout-band
#WATERFALL_EDGE_LEFT=40
#WATERFALL_EDGE_RIGHT=40
#WATERFALL_EDGE_TOP=0
#WATERFALL_EDGE_BOTTOM=0

# ── Fingerprint (UDFPS) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# HAS_UDFPS also registers config_biometric_sensors (0:2:15 by default).
# The coordinates are optional: when all three are set they are written to
# config_udfps_sensor_props. When they are not set, the GSI/HAL reports the
# sensor location itself and the array is left untouched.
HAS_UDFPS=true
UDFPS_X=540
UDFPS_Y=2198
UDFPS_RADIUS=89
# Override the biometric sensor list (id:modality:strength; separate with ;)
#CONFIG_BIOMETRIC_SENSORS="0:2:15"
HAS_SAMSUNG_FINGERPRINT=false

# ── Samsung Vendor Service Control ────────────────────────────────────────
HAS_SAMSUNG_FOD=false
HAS_SAMSUNG_VIBRATOR=false
```

```
          const enabled = isBool ? true : on.checked;
```

> _Reasoning_
> The config parse needs line-based editing to preserve comments: parse section titles from `# ── Title ───` lines, entries KEY=VALUE with `enabled` (commented `#KEY=`), and a comment block for each key.
> 
> I'll implement a bash config parser:
> - `cfg_sections()` prints `line|title` for section headers matching `^# ── `.
> - entries: lines matching `^([[:space:]]*#)?([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)=(.*)$` → line, key, value (strip quotes), enabled.
> - Set value at line: rewrite the line preserving enabled state and quote style: use `KEY="value"` if original quoted, else `KEY=value`; keep the leading `#` for disabled, or drop it to enable.
> - The value may contain special chars; use a safe quoting function (escape `\`, `"`, `$`, backtick in double quotes). Actually config.env values include things like `M 0,0 H -29 ...` and `true`, `3dp`. Use double-quoted and escape `\ " $ \``.
> 
> Multi-line comment lookup for "what does this setting do": gather contiguous comment lines immediately above the entry (skipping blank). Good enough.

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# udfps-probe.sh — find a device's in-display fingerprint (UDFPS) geometry
# =============================================================================
# UDFPS_X / UDFPS_Y / UDFPS_RADIUS in config.env are the sensor's centre and
# radius in px, written to android:array/config_udfps_sensor_props. Guessing
# them puts the lock-screen icon next to the sensor instead of on it, so this
# asks the phone (or a firmware dump) the same question several ways and says
# where each answer came from.
#
#   bash stuff/scripts/udfps-probe.sh                 # connected device
#   bash stuff/scripts/udfps-probe.sh --firmware DIR  # extracted ROM dump
#   bash stuff/scripts/udfps-probe.sh --json          # for the desktop app
#   bash stuff/scripts/udfps-probe.sh --write         # put the winner in config.env
#
# Three situations, in the order the guide describes them:
#
#   1. OEM ROM on the phone. The vendor FOD properties and the preinstalled
#      device overlay are both present, so this is the strongest evidence.
#   2. GSI on the phone. The system partition is the GSI's, but /vendor and
#      /persist keep the OEM's properties, and the phh/device overlay that was
#      flashed with the GSI usually still carries the resource. Both are read
#      here; a value that came from an overlay this tool itself modified is
#      marked as such instead of being counted as independent.
#   3. Firmware files. Only useful once the images are unpacked: super.img
#      needs lpunpack before any APK or build.prop inside it can be read, so a
#      bare fastboot ROM reports what it is missing instead of guessing.
#
# Nothing here is root-only. The overlay APKs and properties it reads are
# world-readable on a normal boot.
# =============================================================================

set -uo pipefail

# adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
# are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
# The local half of a pull is converted back with winpath() instead, because the
# same binary cannot open an MSYS /tmp path.
export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1

winpath() {
    if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then cygpath -w "$1"; else printf '%s' "$1"; fi
}

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"

mode="device"
serial=""
want_json=0
want_write=0
adb="${ADB:-}"
aapt2="${AAPT2:-}"
fwdir=""
scan_all_apks=0

usage() {
    sed -n '3,30p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
}

die() { printf 'udfps-probe: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }
```

```
3:# adb-device.sh — which connected phone a probe talks to
4:# =============================================================================
5:# Sourced by device-probe.sh and udfps-probe.sh. Both used to carry the same
6:# rule ("exactly one device, or stop"), which stops being useful the moment a
7:# second phone is on the desk.
9:#   adb_pick_device ADB SERIAL PROGRAM
11:# ADB is the adb binary to run, SERIAL is what --device said ("" for automatic),
12:# PROGRAM names the script in the messages. On success DEVICE_SERIAL holds the
13:# serial to pass to `adb -s`; on failure the reason has already been printed.
15:# The state matters. adb can see a phone it cannot talk to (unauthorized,
16:# offline, no permissions), and each of those has its own fix — telling the user
17:# to plug the phone in is wrong advice for all three.
19:# Detection is the fragile part, so it is hardened against what adb actually
20:# does rather than what its manual says:
22:#   * `adb devices` is a stream, not a table. A daemon start, a version
23:#     mismatch, or a "no permissions" line shares it with the devices, so only
24:#     lines whose second column is a real state are read as devices.
25:#   * the listing can lie. It is a snapshot, so the chosen serial is confirmed
26:#     with `get-state` before anything is run against it.
27:#   * a wedged server hangs instead of failing. Every adb call here is bounded,
28:#     and a timeout says "adb kill-server" instead of hanging the probe.
29:#   * the first call after the server restarts can come back with no header at
30:#     all. That is retried; a genuinely empty list is not.
31:#   * a phone that is still "connecting" (wireless adb, or just plugged in)
32:#     becomes ready in a second or two, so it is waited for briefly.
33:#   * a serial can be listed twice, and wireless transports look like
34:#     `192.168.1.5:5555`; duplicates are dropped and the transport is labelled.
35:# =============================================================================
37:# The states adb puts in the second column of `devices`, space-padded so a
38:# value can be tested with `index(states, " " $2 " ")`.
41:# The model and product from one `adb devices -l` line, for a menu a human can
42:# read. Both are optional in adb's output, so this never assumes either. A
43:# TCP/mDNS serial is called out: with USB and wireless adb on, the same phone
44:# can be listed twice and the two entries are otherwise identical.
```
