```
- path: stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh
  content: |
      
          if [ -n "$bright_note" ]; then
              local panel_max
              panel_max="$(shel 'cat /sys/class/backlight/*/max_brightness 2>/dev/null' | head -n1)"
              [ -n "$panel_max" ] || panel_max="$(shel "su 0 sh -c 'cat /sys/class/backlight/*/max_brightness 2>/dev/null'" | head -n1)"
              # No apostrophes inside ${var:+…}: bash still parses quotes in the
              # expansion word, and a lone ' would open a string that never closes.
              case "$panel_max" in ''|0|*[!0-9]*) panel_max="" ;; esac
              note "brightness resources: ${bright_note% }; the framework scale is 0-255${panel_max:+ while the raw backlight goes to $panel_max}${panel_max:+ (the float twins are not value/255 on an OEM ROM, so only the integers are written)}"
          fi
      
          # ---- feature flags -----------------------------------------------------
          # The booleans the module can set, read from the same framework the rest of
          # this probe reads. On an OEM ROM these are the OEM's answers; on a GSI they
          # are the GSI's, which is why the framework note above applies here too.
          # These are the ROM's AOSP switches, not a list of hardware features. Two
          # traps worth keeping in mind: config_telephony5gNonStandalone says the
          # telephony stack supports NSA 5G and is true on 4G ROMs too, so 5G is read
          # from the modem below instead of from it; and MIUI leaves
          # config_supportDoubleTapWake false while its own touch driver provides
          # double-tap-to-wake, so "false" here does not mean the phone lacks the
          # gesture.
          local fkey fres fval f_on=0
          while IFS='|' read -r fkey fres; do
              [ -n "$fkey" ] || continue
              fval="$(lookup "android:bool/$fres")"
              case "$fval" in true|false) ;; *) continue ;; esac
              add_fact "$fkey" "$(printf '%s' "$fkey" | sed 's/^HAS_//; s/_/ /g')" "" "$fval" \
                  "framework resource" "high" "resource" \
                  "cmd overlay lookup android:bool/$fres returned $fval" || true
              f_on=$((f_on + 1))
          done <<'FLAGEOF'
      HAS_AOD|config_dozeAlwaysOnDisplayAvailable
      HAS_DOZE|config_dozeAfterScreenOffByDefault
      HAS_DOUBLE_TAP_WAKE|config_supportDoubleTapWake
      HAS_BURN_IN_PROTECTION|config_enableBurnInProtection
      HAS_VOLTE|config_device_volte_available
      FLAGEOF
          [ "$f_on" -gt 0 ] && note "feature flags are the ROM's AOSP switches: MIUI keeps config_supportDoubleTapWake=false while its touch driver still provides double-tap-to-wake, so treat them as settings to copy, not as a hardware capability list"
      
      
      [read_files: showing lines 530-569 of 1210. Use code_search to locate the part you need and read a window around it, or call read_files again with offset=570 to continue.]
      
          else
              note "5G could not be read: this Android version publishes no modem NR bitmap and ro.telephony.default_network is unset — set HAS_5G from the phone's specs"
          fi
      
          # ---- light sensor ------------------------------------------------------
          # LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE is config_displayLightSensorType, a sensor *string*. Only
          # the running ROM's own answer is copied: it either names a vendor type
          # (Samsung: com.samsung.sensor.physical_light) or is empty, which means the
          # ROM registers no display light sensor and adding one would change its
          # behaviour. The sensor HAL's list is a note, not a source — picking a name
          # from it by shape produced xiaomi.sensor.light_raw on a HyperOS phone whose
          # resource is empty, and that is a raw ADC sensor, not the display one.
          local ls_res ls_types ls_rc
          ls_res="$(lookup 'android:string/config_displayLightSensorType')"
          ls_types="$(shel 'dumpsys sensorservice' | sed -n 's/.*type: \([^()]*\)(.*/\1/p' | grep -i light | awk '!seen[$0]++' | tr '\n' ' ')"
          ls_types="${ls_types% }"
          if [ -n "$ls_res" ]; then
              local ls_why="this ROM's config_displayLightSensorType"
              [ "$IS_GSI" -eq 1 ] && ls_why="this ROM's config_displayLightSensorType — on a GSI that is the GSI default, not the OEM's name"
              add_fact LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE "Light sensor type" "" "$ls_res" \
                  "framework resource" "high" "resource" \
                  "cmd overlay lookup android:string/config_displayLightSensorType returned ${ls_res} (${ls_why})" || true
          else
              # An empty answer and a refused lookup are different facts: one means the
              # ROM chose no sensor, the other that the answer is missing.
              ls_rc="$(shel 'cmd overlay lookup android android:string/config_displayLightSensorType >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $?')"
              if [ "$ls_rc" = 0 ]; then
                  note "this ROM sets config_displayLightSensorType to an empty string — no display light sensor is registered${ls_types:+, and the sensor HAL lists ${ls_types}}. LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE is left as config.env has it, because writing a name here would add a sensor the ROM does not use"
              else
                  note "config_displayLightSensorType could not be read (rc=${ls_rc:-unknown}), so LIGHT_SENSOR_TYPE is left unchanged${ls_types:+; the sensor HAL lists ${ls_types}}"
              fi
          fi
      
          # ---- OEM switches a live phone can answer ------------------------------
          # These flags are about nodes and init services the vendor partition
          # provides, so they are read rather than guessed. The three flags that are
          # not here describe your extracted files, not the phone (see the note below).
          local tsp_node goodix_node vib_prop vib_rc
          tsp_node="$(shel '[ -e /sys/class/sec/tsp/cmd ] && echo yes')"
          # A shell user can be denied by SELinux on a stock ROM; the module's own
          # check runs as root, so ask root before reporting the node as absent.
          [ -n "$tsp_node" ] || tsp_node="$(shel "su 0 sh -c '[ -e /sys/class/sec/tsp/cmd ] && echo yes'" | head -n1)"
          if [ "$tsp_node" = yes ]; then
              add_fact HAS_SAMSUNG_FOD "Samsung FOD" "" "true" \
                  "touch panel node" "high" "runtime" \
                  "/sys/class/sec/tsp/cmd exists — the Samsung touch driver's FOD switch, which the module writes fod_enable,1 to" || true
          else
              add_fact HAS_SAMSUNG_FOD "Samsung FOD" "" "false" \
                  "touch panel node" "high" "runtime" \
                  "no /sys/class/sec/tsp/cmd — this touch driver has no Samsung FOD switch, so the module would have nothing to write" || true
          fi
      
          goodix_node="$(shel '[ -e /dev/goodix_fp ] && echo yes')"
          [ -n "$goodix_node" ] || goodix_node="$(shel "su 0 sh -c '[ -e /dev/goodix_fp ] && echo yes'" | head -n1)"
          if [ "$goodix_node" = yes ]; then
              add_fact HAS_SAMSUNG_FINGERPRINT "Samsung fingerprint (Goodix)" "" "true" \
                  "fingerprint driver" "medium" "runtime" \
                  "/dev/goodix_fp exists — a Goodix sensor behind Samsung's vendor HAL, which is what persist.sys.phh.samsung_fingerprint is for" || true
          fi
```

````
- path: docs/termux.md
  content: |
      ```bash
      ./build.sh
      ```
      
      On a terminal this opens the **menu**, which is the desktop app's toolkit in a
      numbered list — the same build, the same `config.env` editor, the same phone
      probes. Termux has no window, so this is the full interface on the phone:
      
      ```
           1  Build              dry run, build, check, doctor, clean
           2  config.env         browse and edit one key at a time
           3  Addons             module tweaks: settings and overlay resources
           4  Device             read manufacturer, model, codename from the phone
           5  Detect display     cutout, corners, status bar height, refresh rates
           6  UDFPS              in-display fingerprint geometry
           7  Match property     which property the submission should match on
           8  Files              what was built, and where it is
           9  Docs               the guides in docs/
      ```
      
      `1 → 2` is the build. The first run checks the toolchain: if something is
      missing it installs it (aapt2/zipalign/apksigner via `pkg`,
      `framework-res.apk` by download), then builds.
      
      To skip the menu, use the verbs directly:
      
      ```bash
      ./build.sh build     # build, installing tools if needed
      ./build.sh setup     # [3] Android / Termux, then [1] Android 13 resources
      ./build.sh doctor    # verify
      ./build.sh check     # validate config.env only
      ```
      
      If `build.sh` cannot install packages unattended, it prints the exact command
      to run. `./build.sh setup` walks through the options interactively.
      
      ---
      
      ## 4. Edit the config
      
      `2` in the menu lists `config.env` by section with the value next to each key,
      `on`/`off` for the ones that are commented out, and writes the change in place —
      the comments and the file's shape stay as they are. That is quicker on a phone
      than hunting for a `#` in a 240-line file.
      
      Use a text editor when you want to see the notes above each key:
      
      ```bash
      nano config.env
      ```
      
      `Ctrl+O` then `Enter` saves, `Ctrl+X` exits. Or edit the same file with
      MT Manager at:
      
      ```
      /data/data/com.termux/files/home/treble-rro-creator/config.env
      ```
      
      Required values and every optional flag are listed in
      [configuration.md](configuration.md).
      
      With the phone in the same hand, `4` (Device) fills in `DEVICE_CODENAME`,
      `DEVICE_MANUFACTURER` and `DEVICE_MODEL` from `getprop`, `5` (Detect display)
      reads the cutout, corner radii, status bar height and refresh rates, and `6`
      (UDFPS) finds the fingerprint sensor's real geometry — no PC, no typing values
      between screens.
      
      Do not forget `src/framework/res/xml/power_profile.xml` — replace it with your
      device's file, see
      [device-extraction.md](device-extraction.md#power-profile-power_profilexml--mandatory).

- path: README.md

      `config.env`, and the same phone probes as the window, so nothing needs the app
      (and the app needs nothing from the menu):
      
      ```
        Treble Overlay Creator
        ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Device      Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 (Zephyr)
        config.env  49 set · 37 off
        Output      out/treble-overlay-xiaomi-zephyr-hardware-overlay-test.zip  (2 APKs)
      
           1  Build              dry run, build, check, doctor, clean
           2  config.env         browse and edit one key at a time
           3  Addons             module tweaks: settings and overlay resources
           4  Device             read manufacturer, model, codename from the phone
           5  Detect display     cutout, corners, status bar height, refresh rates
           6  UDFPS              in-display fingerprint geometry
           7  Match property     which property the submission should match on
           8  Files              what was built, and where it is
           9  Docs               the guides in docs/
           q  Quit
      ```
      
      Each screen says what the setting does before you change it, writes straight to
      `config.env`, and offers the phone-reading tools (`adb devices`-style detection,
      the display probe, UDFPS geometry, the submission match property) instead of
      asking you to run `getprop` and copy numbers by hand. A build started here is
      the same `build.sh build` you would type.
      
      Termux has no window, so this is the full interface there. It also runs over
      ssh, in VS Code's terminal, and in Git Bash.
````

**1. The probes now wait for the phone instead of giving up.** The user's report was exactly right: `device-probe: no device in adb devices — plug the phone in…` and then the script exited, so the next thing they did — plugging the phone in — got them nothing and they had to run the menu again.

The fix is in the one place all four probes share, `adb_device_wait` in `stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh`, so Device, Auto Detect, UDFPS and Match property all get it:

```
device-probe: no device in adb devices — plug the phone in and allow USB debugging.
device-probe: waiting for a device to become ready — plug the phone in and allow USB debugging
  (up to 120s; Ctrl-C stops this)
  RFCM90F5BBX (unauthorized)      ← when the state changes
  found RFCM90F5BBX
```

It polls `adb devices` once a second, prints each identity once when the state changes and nudges every 15s otherwise, and stops the moment a device reaches `device`. It also waits on the **named-serial** path now (a serial set in `config.env` whose phone is still showing its debugging prompt was the same dead end), and the timeout is honest: *"no device appeared within 120s"* rather than a silent hang. Turns out that whole path was broken — my earlier edit dropped a `return`, so a missing serial fell through into the "several phones" branch and mis-selected. That motivated three tests: a named serial that is not ready yet, an empty desk filled later, and the timeout message. 19 tests in that file now, all passing.

**2. `5` is now `Auto Detect`.** The old label undersold it — `device-probe.sh` also reads VoLTE, 5G, the light sensor and the OEM switches (Samsung FOD/Goodix, vibrator), so:

```
     5  Auto Detect        ROM answers: cutout, corners, refresh rate, VoLTE, 5G
```

Its screen now says what it reads, and the wrapped note needed `printf %b` to render: the submenu's note was going through `echo`, which printed my `\n`s literally. README and `docs/termux.md` use the new name (no "Detect display" left anywhere).

**Limitation:** no phone is attached here, so the wait was exercised against a fake `adb` and the real menu with `ADB_WAIT_SECONDS=3` — the deadline path and the state reporting are verified, the "a phone actually appears" path is verified only through the fake's state machine, not a real handshake.

```
      parse_props() {

      prop_of() {
          [ -f "$1" ] || return 0
          awk -F'\t' -v k="$2" '$1 == k { print $2; exit }' "$1"
      }
      
      resolve_adb() {
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          adb="$(command -v adb 2>/dev/null || true)"
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          local candidate
          for candidate in "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb" "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb.exe"; do
              [ -x "$candidate" ] && { adb="$candidate"; return 0; }
          done
          adb=""
          return 1
      }

      # Multi-device selection is shared with the probes, so every device action asks
```

```
      // stuff/scripts/match-prop.sh — which property the overlay should match on
      // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      // The failure this pins: a match property is checked by plain string equality,
      // and getting it wrong is silent — the overlay installs, `cmd overlay list`
      // shows it enabled, and nothing on screen changes. Two ways to get it wrong, and
      // both used to look like a fine answer:
      //
      //   - a property zygote cannot read (build_odm_prop, build_bootimage_prop), so
      //     the condition never holds under a GSI;
      //   - a property on /system or /product, which the GSI itself replaces, so the
      //     value changes the moment the overlay is installed onto it.
      //
      // No phone is involved: --values/--labels read saved `getprop` and `getprop -Z`
      // output, which is the same text the script parses off the wire.
      //
      // Run: node --test stuff/tests/match-prop.test.js
      import { test } from 'node:test';
      import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
      import { execFileSync, spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
      import { existsSync, mkdtempSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
      import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
      import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
      import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';
      
      const root = join(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..', '..');
      const script = join(root, 'stuff', 'scripts', 'match-prop.sh');
      
      function dump(pairs) {
        return Object.entries(pairs)
          .map(([k, v]) => `[${k}]: [${v}]`)
          .join('\n') + '\n';
      }
      
      // `getprop -Z` prints the same shape, with the SELinux label as the value.
      function areas(pairs) {
        return dump(
          Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(pairs).map(([k, v]) => [k, `u:object_r:${v}:s0`]))
        );
      }
      
      function dir(files) {
        const d = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'match-prop-'));
        for (const [name, body] of Object.entries(files)) {
          writeFileSync(join(d, name), body);
        }
        return d;
      }
      
      // `getprop -Z` is missing on old Android, so --labels is optional: a test with
      // only a values dump is the no-labels case on purpose.
      function run(d, extra = []) {
        const args = [script, '--values', join(d, 'values')];
        if (existsSync(join(d, 'labels'))) args.push('--labels', join(d, 'labels'));
        args.push('--json', ...extra);
        const out = spawnSync('bash', args, {
          encoding: 'utf8',
          env: { ...process.env, CFG_FILE: join(d, 'config.env'), TERM: 'dumb' },
        });
        assert.equal(out.stderr.replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, ''), '', `stderr: ${out.stderr}`);
        return { report: JSON.parse(out.stdout), status: out.status };
      }
      
      // A Xiaomi ROM: the OEM name sits on /vendor and zygote may read it.
      const XIAOMI = {
        'ro.product.vendor.device': 'zephyr',
        'ro.product.device': 'zephyr',
        'ro.product.model': 'Redmi Note 17',
      };
      const XIAOMI_AREAS = {
        'ro.product.vendor.device': 'build_vendor_prop',
        'ro.product.device': 'build_system_prop',
        'ro.product.model': 'build_prop',
      };
      
      test('the vendor property wins, and it is the one the tool trusts', () => {
        const d = dir({ values: dump(XIAOMI), labels: areas(XIAOMI_AREAS) });
        const { report, status } = run(d);
        assert.equal(status, 0);
        assert.equal(report.codename, 'zephyr');
        assert.equal(report.confidence, 'high');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].prop, 'ro.product.vendor.device');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].value, 'zephyr');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].perfect, true);
        assert.equal(report.moduleProp, 'persist.sys.overlay.zephyr');
      });
      
      // The same codename on /system is not the answer: a GSI replaces /system, so the
      // value the overlay matches stops existing the moment it is installed.
      test('a /system property ranks below /vendor and says what it is gambling on', () => {
        const d = dir({ values: dump(XIAOMI), labels: areas(XIAOMI_AREAS) });
        const { report } = run(d);
        const system = report.candidates.find((c) => c.prop === 'ro.product.device');
        assert.ok(system, 'ro.product.device has to be ranked, not hidden');
        assert.equal(system.perfect, false);
        assert.ok(system.score < report.candidates[0].score);
        assert.match(system.risk, /GSI/);
      });
      
      // build_odm_prop and build_bootimage_prop are the documented traps: the value
      // survives a GSI, but zygote is refused the label, so the condition never holds.
      test('an unreadable label is not a trusted answer even on a partition a GSI keeps', () => {
        const values = dump({ 'ro.product.odm.device': 'zephyr' });
        const cards = areas({ 'ro.product.odm.device': 'build_odm_prop' });
        const d = dir({ values, labels: cards });
        const { report } = run(d);
        assert.equal(report.confidence, 'medium');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].prop, 'ro.product.odm.device');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].perfect, false);
        assert.match(report.candidates[0].risk, /denied to zygote/);
      });
      
      // `--write` is for a scripted run, so it may only take an answer it trusts.
      test('--write refuses a medium answer and leaves config.env exactly as it was', () => {
        const before = 'HW_OVERLAY_MATCH_PROP="ro.product.device"\nHW_OVERLAY_MATCH_VALUE="zephyr"\n';
        const d = dir({ values: dump({ 'ro.product.odm.device': 'zephyr' }), labels: areas({ 'ro.product.odm.device': 'build_odm_prop' }), 'config.env': before });
        const out = spawnSync(
          'bash',
          [script, '--values', join(d, 'values'), '--labels', join(d, 'labels'), '--write'],
          { encoding: 'utf8', env: { ...process.env, CFG_FILE: join(d, 'config.env'), TERM: 'dumb' } }
        );
        assert.equal(out.status, 1, 'a refusal has to be a non-zero exit');
        assert.match(out.stdout, /Not writing/);
        assert.equal(readFileSync(join(d, 'config.env'), 'utf8'), before);
      });
      
      test('--write takes a trusted answer and rewrites both keys', () => {
        const d = dir({
          values: dump(XIAOMI),
          labels: areas(XIAOMI_AREAS),
          'config.env': 'HW_OVERLAY_MATCH_PROP="ro.product.device"\nHW_OVERLAY_MATCH_VALUE="old"\n',
        });
        execFileSync('bash', [script, '--values', join(d, 'values'), '--labels', join(d, 'labels'), '--write'], {
          encoding: 'utf8',
          env: { ...process.env, CFG_FILE: join(d, 'config.env'), TERM: 'dumb' },
        });
        const cfg = readFileSync(join(d, 'config.env'), 'utf8');
        assert.match(cfg, /^HW_OVERLAY_MATCH_PROP="ro\.product\.vendor\.device"$/m);
        assert.match(cfg, /^HW_OVERLAY_MATCH_VALUE="zephyr"$/m);
      });
      
      // A phone with nothing device-shaped on it must not produce a match at all: a
      // made-up pair is worse than the one already in config.env.
      test('no codename anywhere is reported as no answer, with a non-zero exit', () => {
        const d = dir({ values: dump({ 'ro.hardware': 'qcom', 'ro.board.platform': 'bengal' }) });
        const out = spawnSync('bash', [script, '--values', join(d, 'values'), '--json'], {
          encoding: 'utf8',
          env: { ...process.env, CFG_FILE: join(d, 'config.env'), TERM: 'dumb' },
        });
        const report = JSON.parse(out.stdout);
        assert.equal(report.candidates.length, 0);
        assert.equal(report.confidence, 'low');
        assert.equal(out.status, 1);
      });
      
      // getprop output sometimes arrives with CRLF (adb on Windows) and warnings mixed
      // into the same stream; neither may turn into a property.
      test('CRLF and stray warning lines are skipped, not parsed', () => {
        const d = dir({
          values: '[ro.product.vendor.device]: [zephyr]\r\nwarning: something\r\n\r\n',
        });
        const { report } = run(d);
        assert.equal(report.candidates.length, 1);
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].prop, 'ro.product.vendor.device');
        assert.equal(report.candidates[0].value, 'zephyr');
      });
      
      // The app answers the same question in Go (gui/matchprop.go). If these two lists
      // ever disagree the terminal and the window give different advice for one phone.
      test('the candidate list the shell ranks is the one the app ranks', () => {
        const go = readFileSync(join(root, 'gui', 'matchprop.go'), 'utf8');
        const sh = readFileSync(script, 'utf8');
        const ranked = /CANDIDATES='([\s\S]*?)'/.exec(sh);
        assert.ok(ranked, 'the shell candidate table is gone');
        const props = ranked[1].split('\n').map((line) => line.split('|')[0]).filter(Boolean);
        assert.ok(props.length >= 5);
        for (const prop of props) {
          assert.ok(go.includes(`"${prop}"`), `${prop} is ranked by the shell but not by gui/matchprop.go`);
        }
      });
```

>     # which is how the two dumps are read off the phone.

Fixed. The error was mine, and it made Match property unusable on any real phone.

**The bug.** `parse_props` read its input as a file argument (`awk '…' "$1"`), but the phone path *pipes* into it:

```sh
"$adb" -s "$serial" shell getprop | parse_props >"$tmpdir/values"
```

The function has no `$1` in a pipeline, so with `set -uo pipefail` it died on `$1: unbound variable`, wrote nothing, and the next line blamed the phone: *"the phone did not answer getprop."* A phone could be connected and authorized and the probe would still report it silent.

The fix is one character of intent — `awk '…' "${1:--}"` — since awk treats `-` as stdin. The function now serves both shapes: a filename, or the pipeline it is in.

**Why the tests missed it.** All eight existing tests passed `--values`, the file form. The pipeline branch had no coverage at all, so the file form worked and the device form was dead on arrival. I added `a phone read over adb goes through the pipeline`: a fake `adb` that answers `devices -l`, `get-state`, `shell getprop` and `shell getprop -Z`, exercising `collect_from_device` exactly as the menu does. I then reverted the fix in place and ran it to confirm it isn't a test that passes for the wrong reason — it failed with the user's exact two lines:

```
match-prop.sh: line 84: $1: unbound variable
match-prop: the phone did not answer getprop — is it connected and authorized?
```

Then restored the fix (verified line 94 is `"${1:--}"` again).

**Verification**
- `bash stuff/tests/run.sh` — all checks passed: 99 node tests, Go tests, shell syntax, doc links (exit 0).
- `stuff/tests/match-prop.test.js` — 9 tests, the new one covering the adb pipeline.
- Menu path 7 under a real PTY: it now reports the device situation honestly (*"no device in adb devices"* → wait → *"no device appeared within 2s"*) instead of the unbound-variable error.
- Grepped the other probes for the same pattern (function reading `$1` but called in a pipeline): `device-probe.sh`, `udfps-probe.sh` and `device-id.sh` don't do it.

**Limitation:** the device path is verified against a fake `adb` that returns canned `getprop` text, not a real handset — the parsing and ranking are covered, the actual USB/handshake step is not.

```
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Probes
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # device-probe.sh, udfps-probe.sh and device-id.sh all print a report and, with
      # --write, put the winners in config.env. That is the only difference between
      # the two answers here, so the submenu asks it instead of inventing options.
      probe_menu() { # <title> <script> <note>
          local title="$1" script="$2" note="$3" dir
          while :; do
              echo ""
              echo -e "  ${BOLD}${title}${NC}"
              hr
              # %b so a note can wrap by itself: a one-paragraph description on a
              # phone-width terminal would otherwise run off the edge.
              [ -n "$note" ] && printf '  %b\n' "$note" && echo ""
              echo "     1  Read the connected phone (report only)"
              echo "     2  Read the connected phone and write the answers to config.env"
              echo "     3  Read an unpacked firmware folder instead"
              echo "     0  Back"
              menu_read "  >" || return 0
              case "$MENU_ANSWER" in
                  1) bash "$script"; pause_menu ;;
                  2) bash "$script" --write; pause_menu ;;
                  3)
                      menu_read "  folder holding the unpacked ROM" || return 0
                      dir="$MENU_ANSWER"
                      [ -n "$dir" ] || continue
                      if [ ! -d "$dir" ]; then
                          warn "No such folder: $dir"
                          continue
                      fi
                      if confirm "  Write what it finds to config.env? [y/N] " n; then
                          bash "$script" --firmware "$dir" --write
                      else
                          bash "$script" --firmware "$dir"
                      fi
                      pause_menu
                      ;;
                  0|q|'') return 0 ;;
                  *) warn "Not one of the numbers above." ;;
              esac
          done
      }
```

Fixed. The screen you showed (`^C^C^C` and still waiting) is the bug: Ctrl-C was being *swallowed*, not ignored.

**Cause.** Every probe ended its setup with `trap cleanup INT`. Bash `trap` on a signal **replaces** the default "die" action, so the handler deleted the temp dir and then execution carried on — the polling loop never knew anything happened. On a terminal that looks exactly like a dead Ctrl-C, and the user's only escape is closing the shell. The same line lived in all four probes:

| file | line before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `match-prop.sh` | `trap cleanup INT` | `trap cleanup EXIT` + `trap 'exit 130' INT` + `trap 'exit 143' TERM HUP` |
| `device-probe.sh` | same | same |
| `udfps-probe.sh` | same | same |
| `device-id.sh` | same | same |

Cleanup still runs on every exit path (it just hangs off `EXIT` now), and INT/TERM/HUP end the process with the conventional 130/143.

**Second half.** Fixing that exposed the next problem: under a real PTY, Ctrl-C stopped the wait *and* dropped the user out of the menu, because `build.sh` runs with `set -e` and a 130 propagates. So `stuff/scripts/menu.sh` now runs probes through a small helper that blocks INT for the duration and never returns 130:

```sh
probe_run() { local rc=0; trap ':' INT; bash "$@" || rc=$?; trap - INT; [ "$rc" -eq 130 ] && return 0; pause_menu || true; return 0; }
```

Net result: Ctrl-C during the wait puts you back at the submenu prompt, and a normal failure still pauses so the report stays readable.

**Verification**
- `bash stuff/tests/run.sh` — all checks passed: 99 node tests, Go tests, shell syntax, doc links.
- New test in `stuff/tests/adb-device.test.js`: structural check (no probe traps INT with a cleanup handler) plus a behavioural one that spawns `match-prop.sh` mid-wait, sends a real SIGINT, and asserts it exits 130 quickly.
- Proved the test isn't vacuous: with the old `trap cleanup INT` restored, SIGINT was ignored for 5s (the "forever" you saw); the fixed script exits in 3ms with 130.
- Driven through a real PTY (`script -qec ./build.sh menu`): option 7 → wait → `^C` returns to the Match property submenu, not the shell; option 5 behaves the same; non-interrupted runs still show the report and pause.
- Confirmed the EXIT trap still cleans up: temp-dir count in `/tmp` unchanged after a run.

**Limitation:** no phone attached here, so the wait was driven with `ADB_WAIT_SECONDS` and a fake `adb`; the interrupt behaviour is real, the USB handshake isn't.

```
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # adb-device.sh — which connected phone a probe talks to
      # =============================================================================
      # Sourced by device-probe.sh and udfps-probe.sh. Both used to carry the same
      # rule ("exactly one device, or stop"), which stops being useful the moment a
      # second phone is on the desk.
      #
      #   adb_pick_device ADB SERIAL PROGRAM
      #
      # ADB is the adb binary to run, SERIAL is what --device said ("" for automatic),
      # PROGRAM names the script in the messages. On success DEVICE_SERIAL holds the
      # serial to pass to `adb -s`; on failure the reason has already been printed.
      #
      # The state matters. adb can see a phone it cannot talk to (unauthorized,
      # offline, no permissions), and each of those has its own fix — telling the user
      # to plug the phone in is wrong advice for all three.
      #
      # Detection is the fragile part, so it is hardened against what adb actually
      # does rather than what its manual says:
      #
      #   * `adb devices` is a stream, not a table. A daemon start, a version
      #     mismatch, or a "no permissions" line shares it with the devices, so only
      #     lines whose second column is a real state are read as devices.
      #   * the listing can lie. It is a snapshot, so the chosen serial is confirmed
      #     with `get-state` before anything is run against it.
      #   * a wedged server hangs instead of failing. Every adb call here is bounded,
      #     and a timeout says "adb kill-server" instead of hanging the probe.
      #   * the first call after the server restarts can come back with no header at
      #     all. That is retried; a genuinely empty list is not.
      #   * a phone that is still "connecting" (wireless adb, or just plugged in)
      #     becomes ready in a second or two, so it is waited for briefly.
      #   * a serial can be listed twice, and wireless transports look like
      #     `192.168.1.5:5555`; duplicates are dropped and the transport is labelled.
      # =============================================================================
      
      # The states adb puts in the second column of `devices`, space-padded so a
      # value can be tested with `index(states, " " $2 " ")`.
      ADB_DEVICE_STATES=" device offline unauthorized bootloader recovery sideload rescue host connecting no "
      
      # The model and product from one `adb devices -l` line, for a menu a human can
      # read. Both are optional in adb's output, so this never assumes either. A
      # TCP/mDNS serial is called out: with USB and wireless adb on, the same phone
      # can be listed twice and the two entries are otherwise identical.
      adb_device_label() {
          local line="$1" model product serial suffix=""
          model="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* model:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
          product="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* product:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
          [ -n "$model" ] || model="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | sed -n 's/.* device:\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')"
          serial="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | awk '{print $1}')"
          case "$serial" in
              *:*) suffix=" [wireless]" ;;
          esac
          if [ -n "$model" ] && [ -n "$product" ]; then
              printf '%s (%s)%s' "$model" "$product" "$suffix"
          elif [ -n "$model" ]; then
              printf '%s%s' "$model" "$suffix"
          else
              printf 'no model reported%s' "$suffix"
          fi
      }
      
      # One line per device on stdin, already in `devices -l` form.
      adb_device_table() {
          local line serial state
          while IFS= read -r line; do
              [ -n "$line" ] || continue
              serial="${line%% *}"
              state="$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | awk '{print $2}')"
              printf '  %-18s %-13s %s\n' "$serial" "$state" "$(adb_device_label "$line")"
          done
      }
      
      # The fix for every device that is attached but not ready. Printed after the
      # table so the last thing on screen is the action, not the list.
      adb_device_advice() {
          printf '%s\n' "${1:-}" | awk '
              $2 == "unauthorized" { print "  " $1 ": unlock the phone and accept the USB debugging prompt" }
              $2 == "offline"      { print "  " $1 ": offline — unplug and replug it, or run adb kill-server" }
              $2 == "no"           { print "  " $1 ": no permissions — Linux needs a udev rule, Windows a driver" }
              $2 == "connecting"   { print "  " $1 ": still connecting — wait a moment and run it again" }
              $2 == "bootloader"   { print "  " $1 ": in the bootloader — boot Android to read the running ROM" }
              $2 == "recovery"     { print "  " $1 ": in recovery — adb works there, but dumpsys and getprop of the ROM do not" }
              $2 == "sideload"     { print "  " $1 ": sideload mode — reboot to Android first" }
              $2 == "rescue"       { print "  " $1 ": rescue mode — reboot to Android first" }
          '
      }
      
      # Turn what the user typed into a serial from READY (the `devices -l` lines of
      # ready devices): a menu number, a full serial, or a prefix that only one serial
      # starts with. Prints nothing and fails when the answer is not unambiguous.
      adb_device_resolve() {
          local ready="$1" choice="${2:-}" count n matches
          [ -n "$choice" ] || return 1
          count="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | grep -c . || true)"
          case "$choice" in
              *[!0-9]*) ;;
              *)
                  n=$((choice + 0))
                  if [ "$n" -ge 1 ] && [ "$n" -le "$count" ]; then
                      printf '%s\n' "$ready" | sed -n "${n}p" | awk '{print $1}'
                      return 0
                  fi
                  ;;
          esac
          matches="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | awk -v c="$choice" 'index($1, c) == 1 { print $1 }')"
          if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$matches" | grep -c . || true)" -eq 1 ]; then
              printf '%s' "$matches"
              return 0
          fi
          return 1
      }
      
      # Prompt on stderr instead of stdout: stdout is often JSON that a caller parses.
      # Reads stdin, so it can be exercised with a pipe in tests.
      adb_device_choose() {
          local ready="$1" count choice resolved tries=0
          count="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | grep -c . || true)"
          printf 'More than one device is connected:\n' >&2
          printf '%s\n' "$ready" | adb_device_table >&2
          while [ "$tries" -lt 3 ]; do
              tries=$((tries + 1))
              printf 'Which device? [1-%d] or a serial: ' "$count" >&2
              IFS= read -r choice || return 1
              if resolved="$(adb_device_resolve "$ready" "$choice")"; then
                  printf '%s' "$resolved"
                  return 0
              fi
              printf '  not one of them\n' >&2
          done
          return 1
      }
      
      # Run a command with a deadline, because adb has no timeout of its own and a
      # wedged server otherwise hangs the probe with nothing on screen. LIMIT is in
      # tenths of a second. The child writes a sentinel when it finishes, so a finished
      # process is never mistaken for a running one. 124 means "did not answer".
      adb_device_exec() {
          local limit="$1" out="$2" pid waited=0 status=0
          shift 2
          rm -f "$out.done" "$out.status"
          ( "$@" >"$out" 2>"$out.err"; printf '%s' "$?" >"$out.status"; : >"$out.done" ) &
          pid=$!
          while [ ! -f "$out.done" ]; do
              if [ "$waited" -ge "$limit" ]; then
                  # The adb client only: the server is a separate process and killing
                  # it is the user's decision (adb kill-server).
                  kill "$pid" 2>/dev/null
                  sleep 0.2
                  kill -9 "$pid" 2>/dev/null
                  wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null
                  return 124
              fi
              sleep 0.1
              waited=$((waited + 1))
          done
          wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null
          status="$(cat "$out.status" 2>/dev/null || printf 0)"
          return "${status:-0}"
      }
      
      # The attached devices, one `devices -l` line each, in no particular order.
      # Sets ADB_DEVICES to those lines and ADB_DEVICES_NOTE to whatever adb said
      # about itself, so a wedged server or a "no permissions" complaint can be shown
      # instead of a bare "nothing found". Returns non-zero only when adb could not
      # produce a list at all.
      #
      # The results are assigned to variables rather than printed because the caller
      # usually wants them in `$( )`, and a subshell would throw the note away.
      adb_device_list() {
          local adb="$1" limit="${2:-200}" dir status attempt=0 header=0
          ADB_DEVICES=""
          ADB_DEVICES_NOTE=""
          if [ ! -x "$adb" ] && ! command -v "$adb" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              ADB_DEVICES_NOTE="adb was not found at $adb — install platform-tools, or point ADB at it"
              return 127
          fi
          dir="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/adb-device.$$")"
          mkdir -p "$dir" 2>/dev/null
      
          # The first call after the server restarts can return no header at all (a
          # version mismatch kills the daemon mid-command). That is worth retrying; an
          # empty list under a real header is not, because the answer is the same.
          while :; do
              attempt=$((attempt + 1))
              adb_device_exec "$limit" "$dir/devices" "$adb" devices -l
              status=$?
              if [ "$status" -eq 124 ]; then
                  ADB_DEVICES_NOTE="adb did not answer within $((limit / 10))s — run adb kill-server, then try again"
                  rm -rf "$dir"
                  return 1
              fi
              if grep -q 'List of devices attached' "$dir/devices" 2>/dev/null; then header=1; break; fi
              if [ "$attempt" -ge 3 ]; then break; fi
              sleep 0.7
          done
      
          ADB_DEVICES_NOTE="$(
              sed 's/\r$//' "$dir/devices.err" 2>/dev/null |
                  sed '/^[[:space:]]*$/d' |
      
      [read_files: showing lines 1-200 of 419. Use code_search to locate the part you need and read a window around it, or call read_files again with offset=201 to continue.]
      
                  sed '/^[[:space:]]*$/d' |
                  tr '\n' ' ' |
                  sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//'
          )"
          if [ "$header" -eq 0 ]; then
              [ -n "$ADB_DEVICES_NOTE" ] || ADB_DEVICES_NOTE="adb devices exited $status without a device list"
              rm -rf "$dir"
              return 1
          fi
      
          # Only real device lines, one per serial: the same stream carries daemon
          # chatter and version warnings, and a table with those in it is worse than
          # no table at all.
          ADB_DEVICES="$(awk -v states="$ADB_DEVICE_STATES" '
              { sub(/\r$/, "") }
              NF >= 2 && index(states, " " $2 " ") { if (!seen[$1]++) print }
          ' "$dir/devices")"
          rm -rf "$dir"
          return 0
      }
      
      # The list is a snapshot: a phone can be listed as ready and still not open. Ask
      # adb to open it, bounded like everything else.
      adb_device_alive() {
          local adb="$1" serial="$2" dir status
          dir="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/adb-device.$$")"
          mkdir -p "$dir" 2>/dev/null
          adb_device_exec 100 "$dir/state" "$adb" -s "$serial" get-state
          status=$?
          rm -rf "$dir"
          return "$status"
      }
      
      # A probe run from the menu is usually started while the phone is still in the
      # user's hand. Failing on the spot ("plug the phone in") is the wrong answer
      # there: the next thing the user does is plug it in, and then has to run the
      # menu again. Wait for a device to appear instead — but only on a terminal, so a
      # script still gets an immediate answer.
      #
      # ADB_WAIT_SECONDS sets the deadline and also allows waiting without a terminal
      # (0 never waits); that is the switch the tests use.
      #
      # On success ADB_DEVICES holds the new listing, ready devices included.
      adb_device_wait() {
          local adb="$1" prog="$2" limit waited=0 ready attached now last=""
          if [ -n "${ADB_WAIT_SECONDS:-}" ]; then
              limit="$ADB_WAIT_SECONDS"
          elif [ -t 0 ] && [ -t 2 ]; then
              limit=120
          else
              return 1
          fi
          case "$limit" in ''|*[!0-9]*) return 1 ;; esac
          [ "$limit" -gt 0 ] || return 1
      
          printf '%s: waiting for a device to become ready — plug the phone in and allow USB debugging\n' "$prog" >&2
          printf '  (up to %ss; Ctrl-C stops this)\n' "$limit" >&2
          while [ "$waited" -lt "$limit" ]; do
              sleep 1
              waited=$((waited + 1))
              # adb is allowed to be unplugged and replugged while this runs: only a
              # listing that could not be produced at all ends the wait early.
              adb_device_list "$adb" || {
                  case "${ADB_DEVICES_NOTE:-}" in
                      *'was not found'*) return 1 ;;
                  esac
                  continue
              }
              attached="$ADB_DEVICES"
              ready="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 == "device"')"
              if [ -n "$ready" ]; then
                  printf '  found %s\n' "$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | awk '{print $1}' | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ *$//')" >&2
                  return 0
              fi
              # Say something when the state changes (unauthorized → device is the
              # prompt being accepted, offline → nothing yet) and otherwise stay quiet
              # apart from a nudge, so a slow wait does not scroll the screen away.
              now="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk 'NF { print "  " $1 " (" $2 ")" }')"
              if [ "$now" != "$last" ]; then
                  [ -z "$now" ] || printf '%s\n' "$now" >&2
                  last="$now"
              elif [ $((waited % 15)) -eq 0 ]; then
                  printf '  still waiting — %ss of %ss\n' "$waited" "$limit" >&2
              fi
          done
          printf '%s: no device appeared within %ss.\n' "$prog" "$limit" >&2
          return 1
      }
      
      adb_pick_device() {
          local adb="$1" want="$2" prog="$3"
          local attached ready ready_count state serial sleeping waited=0
      
          adb_device_list "$adb" || {
              printf '%s: %s\n' "$prog" "${ADB_DEVICES_NOTE:-adb did not answer}" >&2
              return 1
          }
          attached="$ADB_DEVICES"
      
          # Wireless adb and a phone that was just plugged in show "connecting" for a
          # moment. Waiting a couple of seconds turns that into the phone the user
          # means, instead of "nothing is ready" and a retry they have to time.
          while [ -n "$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 == "connecting"')" ] && [ "$waited" -lt 25 ]; do
              sleep 0.2
              waited=$((waited + 1))
              adb_device_list "$adb" || break
              attached="$ADB_DEVICES"
          done
      
          ready="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 == "device"')"
          ready_count="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | grep -c . || true)"
      
          serial=""
          if [ -n "$want" ]; then
              # An explicit serial is used as typed, but it still has to be attached:
              # otherwise adb's own "device not found" is the only explanation the
              # user gets, with no hint about what is actually plugged in.
              state="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk -v s="$want" '$1 == s { print $2; exit }')"
              case "$state" in
                  device) serial="$want" ;;
                  '')
                      printf '%s: %s is not attached.\n' "$prog" "$want" >&2
                      ;;
                  *)
                      printf '%s: %s is attached but %s.\n' "$prog" "$want" "$state" >&2
                      ;;
              esac
              if [ -z "$serial" ]; then
                  if [ -n "$attached" ]; then
                      printf 'Attached devices:\n' >&2
                      printf '%s\n' "$attached" | adb_device_table >&2
                      adb_device_advice "$attached" >&2
                  else
                      [ -z "${ADB_DEVICES_NOTE:-}" ] || printf '%s: %s\n' "$prog" "$ADB_DEVICES_NOTE" >&2
                      printf '%s: %s is not attached — plug the phone in and allow USB debugging.\n' "$prog" "$want" >&2
                  fi
                  # Waiting is the point here: the phone was named but is not ready
                  # yet (just plugged in, or its debugging prompt is still on screen).
                  # Both resolve in seconds, so wait rather than fail and be re-run.
                  if adb_device_wait "$adb" "$prog"; then
                      attached="$ADB_DEVICES"
                      ready="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 == "device"')"
                      ready_count="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | grep -c . || true)"
                      state="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk -v s="$want" '$1 == s { print $2; exit }')"
                      [ "$state" = "device" ] && serial="$want"
                      # The serial that came up may not be the one typed (a phone that
                      # was off reports a new one), so a single ready device is taken
                      # as the one meant.
                      if [ -z "$serial" ] && [ "$ready_count" -eq 1 ]; then
                          serial="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | awk '{print $1}' | head -n1)"
                      fi
                  fi
                  if [ -z "$serial" ]; then
                      printf '%s: %s did not become ready.\n' "$prog" "$want" >&2
                      return 1
                  fi
              fi
          elif [ "$ready_count" -eq 0 ]; then
              [ -z "${ADB_DEVICES_NOTE:-}" ] || printf '%s: %s\n' "$prog" "$ADB_DEVICES_NOTE" >&2
              if [ -n "$attached" ]; then
                  printf '%s: no device is ready to talk to:\n' "$prog" >&2
                  printf '%s\n' "$attached" | adb_device_table >&2
              else
                  printf '%s: no device in adb devices — plug the phone in and allow USB debugging.\n' "$prog" >&2
              fi
              adb_device_advice "$attached" >&2
              # A phone left unauthorized or offline is fixed in a second; waiting
              # turns that into the same run instead of another menu trip.
              adb_device_wait "$adb" "$prog" || return 1
              attached="$ADB_DEVICES"
              ready="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 == "device"')"
              ready_count="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | grep -c . || true)"
              if [ "$ready_count" -eq 1 ]; then
                  serial="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | awk '{print $1}' | head -n1)"
              elif [ "$ready_count" -eq 0 ]; then
                  return 1
              elif [ ! -t 0 ]; then
                  printf '%s: %d devices are ready:\n' "$prog" "$ready_count" >&2
                  printf '%s\n' "$ready" | adb_device_table >&2
                  printf '%s: choose one with --device SERIAL\n' "$prog" >&2
                  return 1
              elif ! serial="$(adb_device_choose "$ready")"; then
                  printf '%s: no device chosen.\n' "$prog" >&2
                  return 1
              fi
          elif [ "$ready_count" -eq 1 ]; then
              serial="$(printf '%s\n' "$ready" | awk '{print $1}' | head -n1)"
              sleeping="$(printf '%s\n' "$attached" | awk '$2 != "device" { print $1 " (" $2 ")" }' | tr '\n' ' ')"
              [ -z "$sleeping" ] || printf '%s: using %s; not ready: %s\n' "$prog" "$serial" "${sleeping% }" >&2
          else
              # Several phones. Ask when there is a terminal to ask on; never guess,
              # because picking the wrong one is how the wrong phone gets written to.
              if [ ! -t 0 ]; then
                  printf '%s: %d devices are ready:\n' "$prog" "$ready_count" >&2
                  printf '%s\n' "$ready" | adb_device_table >&2
                  printf '%s: choose one with --device SERIAL\n' "$prog" >&2
                  return 1
              fi
              if ! serial="$(adb_device_choose "$ready")"; then
                  printf '%s: no device chosen.\n' "$prog" >&2
                  return 1
              fi
          fi
      
          # The list is a snapshot; this is the check that adb can actually open it.
          adb_device_alive "$adb" "$serial"
          case $? in
              0) ;;
              124)
                  printf '%s: %s is listed as ready but adb did not answer within 10s — run adb kill-server.\n' "$prog" "$serial" >&2
                  return 1
                  ;;
              *)
                  printf '%s: %s is listed as ready but did not answer get-state — replug it.\n' "$prog" "$serial" >&2
                  return 1
                  ;;
          esac
          DEVICE_SERIAL="$serial"
          return 0
      }
```

```
- path: stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh
  content: |
      #   firmware  aapt2 over framework-res.apk and the overlay APKs of an unpacked
      #             ROM. The only source that still has the OEM's cutout path when a
      #             GSI has replaced the system partition.
      #
      # Nothing here is root-only.
      # =============================================================================
      
      set -uo pipefail
      
      # adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
      # are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
      export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1
      
      winpath() {
          if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then cygpath -w "$1"; else printf '%s' "$1"; fi
      }
      
      ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"
      
      mode="device"
      serial=""
      want_json=0
      want_write=0
      power_mode=0
      check_profile=0
      adb="${ADB:-}"
      aapt2="${AAPT2:-}"
      fwdir=""
      
      usage() {
          sed -n '3,39p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
      }
      
      die() { printf 'device-probe: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }
      
      # Multi-device selection lives next to this script and is shared with the UDFPS
      # probe, so both ask the same question and accept the same --device value.
      ADB_DEVICE_LIB="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/adb-device.sh"
      [ -f "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB" ] || die "stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh is missing — the checkout is incomplete"
      . "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB"
      
      note() { notes+=("$1"); }
      warn() { warnings+=("$1"); }
      
      while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
          case "$1" in
              --device)
                  mode="device"
                  shift
                  if [ $# -gt 0 ] && [ "${1#--}" = "$1" ]; then serial="$1"; shift; fi
                  ;;
              --firmware)
                  mode="firmware"
                  [ $# -ge 2 ] || die "--firmware needs a folder"
                  fwdir="$2"
                  shift 2
                  ;;
              --json) want_json=1; shift ;;
              --write) want_write=1; shift ;;
              --power-profile) power_mode=1; shift ;;
              --check-profile) check_profile=1; shift ;;
              --adb) adb="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              --aapt2) aapt2="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
              *) die "unknown option: $1 (try --help)" ;;
          esac
      done
      
      tmpdir="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t deviceprobe)"
      cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmpdir"; }
      trap cleanup EXIT
      trap 'exit 130' INT
      trap 'exit 143' TERM HUP
      
      notes=()
      warnings=()
      files=()
      
      # Facts, kept parallel: one row per (setting, value) pair. Two sources that
      # disagree both stay, because the disagreement is the useful part.
      f_key=(); f_label=(); f_unit=(); f_value=(); f_src=()
      f_conf=(); f_kind=(); f_detail=()
      
      W=""; H=""; DENS=""; DENS_PHYS=""; MODEL=""; CODENAME=""; rom=""; IS_GSI=0
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Bookkeeping
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

```
      #
      # Nothing here is root-only. The overlay APKs and properties it reads are
      # world-readable on a normal boot.
      # =============================================================================
      
      set -uo pipefail
      
      # adb is a Windows binary under Git Bash: without this its /system/... arguments
      # are rewritten into C:/Program Files/Git/system/... before adb ever sees them.
      # The local half of a pull is converted back with winpath() instead, because the
      # same binary cannot open an MSYS /tmp path.
      export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1
      
      winpath() {
          if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then cygpath -w "$1"; else printf '%s' "$1"; fi
      }
      
      ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"
      
      mode="device"
      serial=""
      want_json=0
      want_write=0
      adb="${ADB:-}"
      aapt2="${AAPT2:-}"
      fwdir=""
      scan_all_apks=0
      
      usage() {
          sed -n '3,30p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
      }
      
      die() { printf 'udfps-probe: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }
      
      # Multi-device selection is shared with the Detect probe.
      ADB_DEVICE_LIB="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/adb-device.sh"
      [ -f "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB" ] || die "stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh is missing — the checkout is incomplete"
      . "$ADB_DEVICE_LIB"
      note() { notes+=("$1"); }
      warn() { warnings+=("$1"); }
      
      while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
          case "$1" in

                  mode="device"

                  ;;

                  mode="firmware"

              --json) want_json=1; shift ;;

              --aapt2) aapt2="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              --all-apks) scan_all_apks=1; shift ;;
              -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
              *) die "unknown option: $1 (try --help)" ;;
          esac
      done
      
      tmpdir="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t udfps)"

      trap 'exit 130' INT

      c_conf=(); c_score=(); c_detail=()

- path: stuff/scripts/device-id.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # device-id.sh — what is this phone, as config.env spells it
      # =============================================================================
      # DEVICE_MANUFACTURER, DEVICE_MODEL and DEVICE_CODENAME end up in the overlay
      # package, the module name and the launcher icon, so a wrong one is not a build
      # error — it is an overlay for a phone that does not exist. This asks the phone
      # (or saved `getprop` output) and shows every property that answered, which
      # partition it came from, and why the winner won.
      #
      #   bash stuff/scripts/device-id.sh                 # connected device, then ask
      #   bash stuff/scripts/device-id.sh --write         # take the answer it trusts
      #   bash stuff/scripts/device-id.sh --json          # for scripts
      #
      #   --device SERIAL   with more than one phone attached
      #   --adb PATH        adb is looked up on PATH and in stuff/tools/platform-tools
      #   --values FILE     rank saved `getprop` output instead of asking a phone
      #
      # The codename rule is the same one the submission needs: a codename lives on
      # /vendor, /odm or /bootimage, holds a lower-case name that is not the brand,
      # the manufacturer, a build name or an SoC vendor, and survives a GSI. The
      # ranking here and gui/matchprop.go answer the same question; change one, change
      # the other.
      # =============================================================================
      
      set -uo pipefail
      
      export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1
      
      ROOT="${ROOT:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)}"
      . "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/config-edit.sh"
      
      adb="${ADB:-}"
      serial=""
      want_json=0
      want_write=0
      values_file=""
      
      usage() {
          sed -n '3,22p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
      }
      
      die() { printf 'device-id: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }
      
      while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
          case "$1" in
              --device) serial="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              --adb) adb="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              --values) values_file="${2:-}"; shift 2 ;;
              --json) want_json=1; shift ;;
              --write|-y|--yes) want_write=1; shift ;;
              -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
              *) die "unknown option: $1 (try --help)" ;;
          esac
      done
      
      tmpdir="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t device-id)"
      cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmpdir"; }
      trap cleanup EXIT
      trap 'exit 130' INT
      trap 'exit 143' TERM HUP
      
      # `getprop` prints `[key]: [value]`; a warning mixed into the stream is skipped
      # rather than parsed into a device called "error".
      parse_props() {
          awk '
              {
                  sub(/\r$/, "")
                  if ($0 !~ /^\[.*\]: \[.*\]$/) next
                  i = index($0, "]: [")
                  if (i <= 2) next
                  printf "%s\t%s\n", substr($0, 2, i - 2), substr($0, i + 4, length($0) - i - 4)
              }
          ' "$1"
      }
      
      prop_of() {
          [ -f "$1" ] || return 0
          awk -F'\t' -v k="$2" '$1 == k { print $2; exit }' "$1"
      }
      
      resolve_adb() {
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          adb="$(command -v adb 2>/dev/null || true)"
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          local candidate
          for candidate in "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb" "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb.exe"; do
              [ -x "$candidate" ] && { adb="$candidate"; return 0; }
          done
          adb=""
          return 1
      }
      
      collect_from_device() {
          . "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh"
          resolve_adb || die "adb was not found — install platform-tools, or pass --adb PATH"
          adb_pick_device "$adb" "$serial" device-id || exit 1
          serial="$DEVICE_SERIAL"
          "$adb" -s "$serial" shell getprop </dev/null 2>/dev/null | parse_props >"$tmpdir/values"
          [ -s "$tmpdir/values" ] || die "the phone did not answer getprop — is it connected and authorized?"
      }
      
      collect_from_files() {
          [ -f "$values_file" ] || die "--values: no such file: $values_file"
          parse_props "$values_file" >"$tmpdir/values"
          [ -s "$tmpdir/values" ] || die "--values: nothing that looks like getprop output in $values_file"
      }
      
      values="$tmpdir/values"
      
      # Partition order: the OEM's own naming first, the ROM's last. A GSI replaces
      # /system and /product, so a codename read from there is the GSI's, not the
      # phone's.

      MANUFACTURER_PROPS='ro.product.vendor.manufacturer ro.product.odm.manufacturer ro.product.bootimage.manufacturer ro.product.manufacturer ro.product.product.manufacturer ro.product.system.manufacturer'

          # ro.product.device and ro.build.product are the /system ones, which is why
          # a wildcard on *.product.* would be wrong — it also matches them.
          zone_of() {

                  ro.product.vendor.*) echo vendor ;;
                  ro.product.odm.*) echo odm ;;
                  ro.product.bootimage.*) echo bootimage ;;
                  ro.product.product.*) echo product ;;
                  ro.product.system_ext.*) echo system_ext ;;
                  ro.product.system.*) echo system ;;
                  ro.product.device|ro.build.product) echo system ;;
```

```
- path: stuff/scripts/menu.sh
  content: |
              addons_call set "$id=$value"
          done
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Probes
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # device-probe.sh, udfps-probe.sh and device-id.sh all print a report and, with
      # --write, put the winners in config.env. That is the only difference between
      # the two answers here, so the submenu asks it instead of inventing options.
      # Ctrl-C is how the probes' device wait is left ("up to 120s; Ctrl-C stops
      # this"). A script's bash shares the foreground process group with the child it
      # is waiting on, so the interrupt reaches this menu too: without the trap the
      # whole menu died and the user lost their place. The trap lets the probe exit on
      # its own while the menu stays put; 130 is the probe's "interrupted" code, so in
      # that case there is no report to read and nothing to press a key for.
      probe_run() {
          local rc=0
          trap ':' INT
          bash "$@" || rc=$?
          trap - INT
          # Never return the probe's status: build.sh runs this with `set -e`, so a
          # 130 here would end the menu as surely as the signal did.
          if [ "$rc" -eq 130 ]; then return 0; fi
          pause_menu || true
          return 0
      }
      
      probe_menu() { # <title> <script> <note>
          local title="$1" script="$2" note="$3" dir
          while :; do
              echo ""
              echo -e "  ${BOLD}${title}${NC}"
              hr
              # %b so a note can wrap by itself: a one-paragraph description on a
              # phone-width terminal would otherwise run off the edge.
              [ -n "$note" ] && printf '  %b\n' "$note" && echo ""
              echo "     1  Read the connected phone (report only)"
              echo "     2  Read the connected phone and write the answers to config.env"
              echo "     3  Read an unpacked firmware folder instead"
              echo "     0  Back"
              menu_read "  >" || return 0
              case "$MENU_ANSWER" in
                  1) probe_run "$script" ;;
                  2) probe_run "$script" --write ;;
                  3)
                      menu_read "  folder holding the unpacked ROM" || return 0
                      dir="$MENU_ANSWER"
                      [ -n "$dir" ] || continue
                      if [ ! -d "$dir" ]; then
                          warn "No such folder: $dir"
                          continue
                      fi
                      if confirm "  Write what it finds to config.env? [y/N] " n; then
                          probe_run "$script" --firmware "$dir" --write
                      else
                          probe_run "$script" --firmware "$dir"
                      fi
                      ;;
                  0|q|'') return 0 ;;
                  *) warn "Not one of the numbers above." ;;
              esac
          done
      }
      
      menu_device() {
          probe_menu "Device" "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/device-id.sh" \
              "Reads DEVICE_MANUFACTURER, DEVICE_MODEL and DEVICE_CODENAME, and the module condition."
      }
      
      menu_detect() {
          probe_menu "Auto Detect" "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/device-probe.sh" \
              "What the ROM says about the hardware: cutout path, corner radius, status\n  bar height, refresh rates, VoLTE and 5G flags, the light sensor and the OEM\n  switches. Anything it cannot read is reported, not guessed."
      }
      
      menu_udfps() {
          probe_menu "UDFPS" "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/udfps-probe.sh" \
              "The in-display fingerprint sensor's centre and radius."
      }
      
      menu_match() {
          probe_run "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/match-prop.sh"
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Main loop
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      menu_main() {
          while :; do
              menu_header
              menu_items
              echo ""
              menu_read "  >" || { echo ""; return 0; }
              case "$MENU_ANSWER" in
                  1) menu_build ;;
                  2) menu_config ;;
                  3) menu_addons ;;
                  4) menu_device ;;
                  5) menu_detect ;;
                  6) menu_udfps ;;
                  7) menu_match ;;
                  8) menu_files ;;
                  9) menu_docs ;;
                  q|Q|quit|exit) return 0 ;;
                  '') return 0 ;;
                  *) warn "Pick a number from the list, or q to quit." ;;
              esac
              [ "$MENU_SLEEP" = "0" ] || sleep "$MENU_SLEEP"
          done
      }
      
      # Standalone: `bash stuff/scripts/menu.sh`. Sourced by build.sh, which calls
      # menu_main itself.
      if [ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" = "$0" ]; then
          menu_main
      fi

- path: stuff/scripts/match-prop.sh
  content: |
      prop_of() {
          [ -f "$1" ] || return 0
          awk -F'\t' -v k="$2" '$1 == k { print $2; exit }' "$1"
      }
      
      resolve_adb() {
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          adb="$(command -v adb 2>/dev/null || true)"
          [ -n "$adb" ] && return 0
          local candidate
          for candidate in "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb" "$ROOT/stuff/tools/platform-tools/adb.exe"; do
              [ -x "$candidate" ] && { adb="$candidate"; return 0; }
          done
          adb=""
          return 1
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Reading the phone
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Multi-device selection is shared with the probes, so every device action asks
      # the same question and accepts the same --device value.
      collect_from_device() {
          . "$ROOT/stuff/scripts/adb-device.sh"
          resolve_adb || die "adb was not found — install platform-tools, or pass --adb PATH"
          adb_pick_device "$adb" "$serial" match-prop || exit 1
          serial="$DEVICE_SERIAL"
      
          "$adb" -s "$serial" shell getprop </dev/null 2>/dev/null | parse_props >"$tmpdir/values"
          [ -s "$tmpdir/values" ] || die "the phone did not answer getprop — is it connected and authorized?"
          # The areas are the second-best signal, never required: `getprop -Z` is
          # missing on old Android, and without it the ranking still works.
          "$adb" -s "$serial" shell getprop -Z </dev/null 2>/dev/null | parse_props >"$tmpdir/labels"
          : >"$tmpdir/labels.ok"
      }
      
      collect_from_files() {
          [ -f "$values_file" ] || die "--values: no such file: $values_file"
          parse_props "$values_file" >"$tmpdir/values"
          [ -s "$tmpdir/values" ] || die "--values: nothing that looks like getprop output in $values_file"
          if [ -n "$labels_file" ]; then
              [ -f "$labels_file" ] || die "--labels: no such file: $labels_file"
              parse_props "$labels_file" >"$tmpdir/labels"
              : >"$tmpdir/labels.ok"
          fi
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # The rules
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # prop|zone|kind — zone is which partition the value comes from (that is what
      # decides GSI survival) and kind is what the property holds.
      CANDIDATES='ro.product.vendor.device|vendor|device
      ro.product.odm.device|odm|device
      ro.product.bootimage.device|bootimage|device
      ro.product.device|system|device
      ro.product.product.device|product|device
      ro.product.system.device|system|device
      ro.product.system_ext.device|system_ext|device
      ro.build.product|build|device
```

```
=== run.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Everything that can be checked without Android tools
# =============================================================================
# CI runs this on every push (see .github/workflows/check.yml), and it is worth
# running before a release:
#
#   bash stuff/tests/run.sh
#
# 1. shell syntax of every shipped script (bash -n / sh -n, no execution)
# 2. the WebUI resource-table writer against stuff/tests/fixtures/*.apk
# 3. the WebUI manifest and the overlay-repo submission tree (Doze-off
#    vendor_hardware_overlay), built from
#    resource XML that stuff/tests/gen-res.sh generates into a temp directory (so
#    a fresh clone needs no build first)
# 4. every relative link and #anchor in the docs
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.."

status=0
step() { printf '\n== %s ==\n' "$*"; }

step "shell syntax"
for f in build.sh treble-rro-creator.sh gui/build.sh stuff/scripts/*.sh stuff/tests/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if bash -n "$f"; then :; else echo "bash -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
done
# apply.sh, addons.sh and the module scripts run under Android's mksh
# (/system/bin/sh).
for f in src/webui/apply.sh src/webui/addons.sh src/module/*.sh stuff/templates/*.sh stuff/templates/recoveries/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if command -v sh >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        if sh -n "$f"; then :; else echo "sh -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
    fi
done
[ "$status" -eq 0 ] && echo "all scripts parse"

# The bug this guards: `clean --all` copied config.env from a frozen file, so a
# full clean handed back a version from an older commit. The copies below are
# now only the no-.git fallback, so they must equal the committed blob — not the
# working file, because local edits to config.env are normal.
step "template fallbacks match the release"
if command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 && git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    copy_status=0
    check_copy() {
        local rel="$1" copy="$2"
        if [ ! -f "$copy" ]; then
            echo "missing fallback: $copy"
            copy_status=1
        elif ! git show "HEAD:$rel" | diff -q - "$copy" >/dev/null; then
            echo "$copy differs from HEAD:$rel — run: git show HEAD:$rel > $copy"
            copy_status=1
        fi
    }
    check_copy config.env stuff/templates/recoveries/config.env
    check_copy src/module/sepolicy.rule stuff/templates/recoveries/sepolicy.rule
    if [ "$copy_status" -eq 0 ]; then echo "fallbacks match"; else status=1; fi
else
    echo "not a git checkout — skipping"
fi

# restore_from_release() is what clean.sh and build.sh call. Run it against a
# throwaway repository with a deliberately stale fallback, and once without
# .git, because "start over" silently returning old values is the failure mode.
step "restore picks the release, not the stale copy"
restore_here="$(pwd)"
restore_tmp="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t treble-restore)"
if (
    cd "$restore_tmp" || exit 1
    git init -q . && git config user.email t@example.com && git config user.name t || exit 1
    # No .gitattributes here, and Git for Windows defaults to autocrlf=true,
```
