ui_mark() {
    local kind="$1" text="$2" indent="${3:-2}" glyph color line first=1 pad
    case "$kind" in
        ok)   glyph="$UI_TICK";  color="$UI_GREEN" ;;
        warn) glyph="$UI_WARN";  color="$UI_YELLOW" ;;
        bad)  glyph="$UI_CROSS"; color="$UI_RED" ;;
        *)    glyph="$UI_DOT";   color="$UI_DIM" ;;
    esac
    printf -v pad '%*s' $((indent + 2)) ''
    ui_wrap "$text" $((indent + 2)) | while IFS= read -r line; do
        if [ "$first" = 1 ]; then
            printf '%*s%s%s%s %s\n' "$indent" '' "$color" "$glyph" "$UI_OFF" "${line#"$pad"}"
            first=0
        else
            printf '%s\n' "$line"
        fi
    done
}
---
ui_item() {
    local num="$1" label="$2" detail="${3:-}" lw="${4:-${#2}}" cols head line
    cols=$(ui_cols)
    # A label wider than the column (a long section title) widens the column
    # rather than being cut or pushing the description out of line.
    [ "$lw" -ge "${#label}" ] || lw=${#label}
    head="  $(printf '%3s' "$num")  "
    # A label longer than the window is a section header somewhere in config.env
    # — `Overlay repo submission (Doze-off, submission only)` — and it runs off a
    # phone. It wraps under the number, and the description follows it there.
    # The head is 2 spaces, three for the number and two after it: seven.
    if [ $(( 7 + ${#label} )) -ge "$cols" ]; then
        printf '  %s%3s%s\n' "$UI_BLUE" "$num" "$UI_OFF"
        ui_wrap "$label" 7 $((cols - 8)) | while IFS= read -r line; do
            printf '%s%s%s\n' "$UI_BOLD" "$line" "$UI_OFF"
        done
        [ -n "$detail" ] || return 0
        ui_wrap "$detail" 9 $((cols - 10)) | while IFS= read -r line; do
            printf '%s%s%s\n' "$UI_DIM" "$line" "$UI_OFF"
        done
        return 0
    fi
    printf '%s%s%s%s%s' "$UI_BLUE" "$head" "$UI_OFF" "$UI_BOLD" "$label"
    if [ -z "$detail" ]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$UI_OFF"
        return 0
    fi
    # 7 for the number column and its gaps, 2 between label and description.
    if [ $(( 7 + lw + 2 + ${#detail} )) -le "$cols" ]; then
        printf '%s%*s  %s%s%s\n' "$UI_OFF" $((lw - ${#label})) '' \
            "$UI_DIM" "$detail" "$UI_OFF"
        return 0
    fi
    printf '%s\n' "$UI_OFF"
    ui_wrap "$detail" 7 $((cols - 8)) | while IFS= read -r line; do
        printf '%s%s%s\n' "$UI_DIM" "$line" "$UI_OFF"
    done
}

- path: stuff/scripts/toolchain.sh
  content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # =============================================================================
      # Treble Overlay — toolchain installer and verifier
      # =============================================================================
      # Sourced by build.sh. Nothing here runs on its own.
      #
      #   ./build.sh            installs whatever is missing (sensible defaults)
      #   ./build.sh setup      interactive installer (pick distro / resource version)
      #   ./build.sh doctor     read-only check, exits 0 when a build would work
      # =============================================================================
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Windows: Google build-tools zip
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Git for Windows ships bash and coreutils, but no aapt2/zipalign/apksigner.
      # Google's Windows build-tools zip contains all three, so one download covers
      # the whole toolchain.
      install_windows_tools() {
          mkdir -p "$TOOLS_DIR"
      
          if ! command -v unzip >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              err "unzip not found — reinstall Git for Windows (it bundles unzip)"
              return 1
          fi
          if ! command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              err "curl not found — reinstall Git for Windows (it bundles curl)"
              return 1
          fi
          if ! command -v java >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              err "Java not found — apksigner needs a JDK (17 or newer)."
              echo "      Install one: https://adoptium.net/"
              echo "      or:          winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.17.JDK"
              echo "      Then re-run: build.cmd"
              return 1
          fi
      
          local tmp_zip="${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win.zip"
          local api="" url=""
      
          info "Downloading Android build-tools for Windows..."
          for api in 36 35 34; do
              url="https://dl.google.com/android/repository/build-tools_r${api}_windows.zip"
              info "  Trying build-tools r${api}..."
              if curl --fail -L --retry 2 "$url" -o "$tmp_zip" 2>/dev/null; then
                  break
              fi
              api=""
          done
      
          if [ -z "$api" ]; then
              err "Could not download the Windows build-tools."
              info "Install Android SDK build-tools and add its folder to PATH, or copy"
              info "aapt2.exe and zipalign.exe into stuff/tools/ and re-run build.cmd."
              rm -f "$tmp_zip"
              return 1
          fi
      
          rm -rf "${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win"
          mkdir -p "${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win"
          if ! unzip -q -o "$tmp_zip" -d "${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win"; then
              err "Failed to extract the build-tools archive"
              rm -f "$tmp_zip"
              return 1
          fi
          rm -f "$tmp_zip"
      
          local bt_dir
          bt_dir=$(ls -d "${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win/"* 2>/dev/null | head -1)
          if [ -z "$bt_dir" ]; then
              err "Unexpected build-tools archive layout"
              return 1
          fi
          ok "build-tools r${api} downloaded"
      
          local installed=false exe
          for exe in aapt2.exe zipalign.exe; do
              if [ -f "${bt_dir}/${exe}" ]; then
                  cp "${bt_dir}/${exe}" "${TOOLS_DIR}/${exe}"
                  ok "Installed ${exe}"
                  installed=true
              else
                  warn "${exe} not found in the build-tools package"
              fi
          done
      
          # A Linux aapt2/zipalign left in stuff/tools/ by a WSL/Kali run of this project
          # would shadow the .exe installed above and break the build with
          # "cannot execute binary file".
          local stale
          for stale in "${TOOLS_DIR}/aapt2" "${TOOLS_DIR}/zipalign"; do
              if [ -f "$stale" ] && [ "$(classify_binary "$stale")" = "linux-elf" ]; then
                  rm -f "$stale"
                  warn "Removed stale Linux binary ${stale#"${TOOLS_DIR}"/} (it shadowed the Windows one)"
              fi
          done
      
          # apksigner: bash does not resolve .bat files, so wrap the jar in a small
          # shell script — `apksigner ...` then behaves exactly like on Linux.
          if [ -f "${bt_dir}/lib/apksigner.jar" ]; then
              cp "${bt_dir}/lib/apksigner.jar" "${TOOLS_DIR}/apksigner.jar"

- path: stuff/scripts/toolchain.sh
  content: |
              cp "${bt_dir}/lib/apksigner.jar" "${TOOLS_DIR}/apksigner.jar"
              cat > "${TOOLS_DIR}/apksigner" << 'APKSIGNER_EOF'
      #!/bin/sh
      # Generated by build.sh — runs the build-tools apksigner jar.
      here=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
      case "$(uname -s 2>/dev/null)" in
          MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) here=$(cygpath -w "$here") ;;
      esac
      exec java -jar "$here/apksigner.jar" "$@"
      APKSIGNER_EOF
              chmod +x "${TOOLS_DIR}/apksigner"
              ok "Installed apksigner (java -jar stuff/tools/apksigner.jar)"
              installed=true
          else
              warn "apksigner.jar not found in the build-tools package"
          fi
      
          # Everything needed is copied into stuff/tools/; drop the ~120 MB extraction.
          rm -rf "${TOOLS_DIR}/build-tools-win"
      
          $installed
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Resource dictionary (framework-res.apk)
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # aapt2 needs the platform resource table to resolve android:* IDs. Android 13
      # is the most reliable version and links overlays for 13 through 16.
      download_platform_resources() {
          local sdk_ver="$1"
          mkdir -p "$TOOLS_DIR"
      
          local tmp_zip="${TOOLS_DIR}/platform_tmp.zip"
          local rev url success=false
      
          info "Downloading Android ${sdk_ver} resources from Google..."
          # r02 is the known-good revision for API 33; try it first, then the rest.
          for rev in r02 r01 r03 r04 r05 r06 r07 r08 ""; do
              url="https://dl.google.com/android/repository/platform-${sdk_ver}_${rev}.zip"
              url="${url%_}" # strip trailing underscore when rev is empty
              if curl --fail -L "$url" -o "$tmp_zip" 2>/dev/null; then
                  success=true
                  break
              fi
          done
      
          if [ "$success" != "true" ]; then
              err "Download failed for all revisions — Google may have moved the files."
              rm -f "$tmp_zip"
              return 1
          fi
      
          info "Extracting android.jar (resource table)..."
          if ! unzip -j -o "$tmp_zip" "*/android.jar" -d "$TOOLS_DIR/" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              err "Could not extract android.jar from the platform archive"
              rm -f "$tmp_zip"
              return 1
          fi
          if [ ! -f "$TOOLS_DIR/android.jar" ]; then
              err "The archive did not contain android.jar"
              rm -f "$tmp_zip"
              return 1
          fi
      
          mv "$TOOLS_DIR/android.jar" "$TOOLS_DIR/framework-res.apk"
          rm -f "$tmp_zip"
          ok "Android ${sdk_ver} resources installed (stuff/tools/framework-res.apk, $(du -sh "$TOOLS_DIR/framework-res.apk" | cut -f1))"
      }
      
      # acquire_framework_res <auto|ask> [force]
      # `force` asks/downloads even when a resource dictionary already exists.
      acquire_framework_res() {
          local mode="${1:-ask}" force="${2:-}"
      
          if [ -z "$force" ] && framework_res_path >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              return 0
          fi
      
          if [ "$mode" = "auto" ]; then
              download_platform_resources 33
              return $?
          fi
      
          echo ""
          info "One more piece: framework-res.apk (the resource dictionary)."
          echo "  aapt2 uses it to translate android:* resource IDs. Using the wrong"
          echo "  version causes 'resource not found' errors during the build."
          echo ""
          echo -e "  ${BOLD}Where should it come from?${NC}"
          echo -e "    ${BOLD}[1]${NC} Download Android 13 resources  (${GREEN}recommended${NC} — works for 13-16)"

              chmod +x "$TOOLS_DIR/aapt2" 2>/dev/null || true

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Treble Overlay — shared helpers
# =============================================================================
# Sourced by build.sh and by the modules in stuff/scripts/. Never run directly.
#
# The entry point sets ROOT (the project directory) and then sources this file,
# so every helper below can assume it exists and that the current directory is
# the project root.
# =============================================================================

: "${ROOT:?stuff/scripts/common.sh must be sourced by build.sh (ROOT is not set)}"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Paths
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Absolute paths are used for file tests and for zip destinations. Arguments
# handed to native tools (aapt2/zipalign) must stay RELATIVE: MSYS on Windows
# does not reliably convert a /c/... path for a native .exe.
# Everything that is not the thing you build lives under stuff/, so the root
# only holds the two entry points, config.env and the folders you open.
STUFF_DIR="$ROOT/stuff"

- path: stuff/scripts/menu.sh
  content: |
          done
      }
      
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Files
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      # Where a copy lands on the phone. /sdcard is the same folder whether it is this
      # phone (Termux, where ~/storage/shared points at it) or a cabled one (adb), so
      # the path in the message is one a reader can go and look in either way.
      FILES_PHONE_DIR="/sdcard/treble-rro-creator"
      
      # The build's own outputs, one path per line: the flashable zips and the APKs
      # sitting inside them.
      built_files() {
          find "$OUT_DIR" -maxdepth 2 -type f \( -name '*.zip' -o -name '*.apk' \) 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C sort
      }
      
      # files_copy_to_phone — put the build on the phone's shared storage.
      #
      # On the phone itself (Termux) that is a plain cp, once Termux has been given
      # access to /sdcard. From a computer it is `adb push`, because the build tree is
      # on the wrong side of the cable; the destination is the same folder, so the
      # instructions afterwards do not depend on which machine ran the build.
      files_copy_to_phone() {
          local -a files=()
          local f base="" dest copied=0 failed=0 src
          while IFS= read -r f; do files+=("$f"); done < <(built_files)
          if [ "${#files[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
              info "Nothing to copy yet — 1 → 2 builds the module."
              return 0
          fi
      
          if device_is_termux; then
              # ~/storage/shared only exists after termux-setup-storage; /sdcard is
              # still worth trying because some builds of Termux ship it ready.
              if [ -d "$HOME/storage/shared" ]; then
                  base="$HOME/storage/shared"
              elif [ -d /sdcard ]; then
                  base="/sdcard"
              fi
              if [ -z "$base" ]; then
                  err "Termux cannot see this phone's storage."
                  echo "     Run: termux-setup-storage"
                  echo "     Then: 8 → 1 again"
                  return 1
              fi
              dest="$base/treble-rro-creator"
              if ! mkdir -p "$dest" 2>/dev/null; then
                  err "Cannot create $FILES_PHONE_DIR."
                  echo "     Run: termux-setup-storage   (it asks for the storage permission)"
                  return 1
              fi
              info "Copying ${#files[@]} file(s) to $FILES_PHONE_DIR..."
              for f in "${files[@]}"; do
                  if cp -f "$f" "$dest/" 2>/dev/null; then
                      ui_mark ok "$(basename "$f")  $(du -h "$f" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)"
                      copied=$((copied + 1))
                  else
                      ui_mark bad "$(basename "$f") — could not be written"
                      failed=$((failed + 1))
                  fi
              done
          else
              # A computer: the phone is only reachable through adb, and a build for a
              # phone that is not plugged in goes nowhere.
              if ! resolve_adb; then
                  err "adb was not found — install platform-tools and try again."
                  return 1
              fi
              adb_pick_device "$adb" "" "files" || return 1
              if ! "$adb" ${DEVICE_SERIAL:+-s "$DEVICE_SERIAL"} shell "mkdir -p $FILES_PHONE_DIR" \
                      >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                  err "Could not create $FILES_PHONE_DIR on the phone."
                  echo "     Check that the phone is unlocked and the storage is not full."
                  return 1
              fi
              info "Pushing ${#files[@]} file(s) to $FILES_PHONE_DIR..."
              for f in "${files[@]}"; do
                  # A Windows adb cannot open an MSYS path, so the local half is
                  # converted when cygpath exists (Git Bash) and passed as it is
                  # everywhere else.
                  src="$f"
                  command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1 && src="$(cygpath -w "$f")"
                  if "$adb" ${DEVICE_SERIAL:+-s "$DEVICE_SERIAL"} push "$src" "$FILES_PHONE_DIR/" \
                          >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                      ui_mark ok "$(basename "$f")  $(du -h "$f" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)"
                      copied=$((copied + 1))
                  else
                      ui_mark bad "$(basename "$f") — adb push failed"
                      failed=$((failed + 1))
                  fi
              done
          fi
      
          echo ""
          if [ "$failed" -gt 0 ]; then
              warn "$copied copied, $failed failed."
              return 1
          fi
          ui_mark ok "$copied file(s) in $FILES_PHONE_DIR"
          ui_mark note "Open Files on the phone, or flash the module from there."
          return 0
      }
      
      menu_files() {
          local -a table=() f
          while :; do
              ui_heading 'Files'
              ui_panel 'Where things are' \
                  "Project|$ROOT" \
                  "config.env|$ROOT/config.env" \
                  "Build tree|${BUILD_DIR#$ROOT/}"
              echo ""
              table=()
              if [ -d "$OUT_DIR" ] && [ -n "$(ls -A "$OUT_DIR" 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
                  while IFS= read -r f; do
                      table+=("$(du -h "$f" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)|${f#$ROOT/}")
                  done < <(built_files)
              fi
              if [ "${#table[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
                  info "Nothing built yet — 1 → 2 builds the module."
                  pause_menu
                  return 0
              fi
              ui_table 'Size|Built file' "${table[@]}"
              echo ""
              ui_item 1 'Copy' "to $FILES_PHONE_DIR on the phone" 11
              ui_item 0 'Back' '' 11
              menu_read "  >" || return 0
              case "$MENU_ANSWER" in
                  1) echo ""; files_copy_to_phone; pause_menu ;;
                  0|q|'') return 0 ;;
                  *) warn "Not one of the numbers above." ;;
              esac
          done
      }

      - **The device wait.** On a PC a probe waits up to 120s for a cable to be
        plugged in. That wait cannot end on Termux, so when this machine is the phone
        the local source is chosen before the wait starts. `Ctrl-C` leaves a wait in
        any case and puts you back in the submenu.
      - **Speed.** Each read is one root call, about the same count of round trips a
        PC makes over adb — a few seconds, not instant.
      
      ---
      
      ## 6. Install the module
      
      ```bash
      cp out/*-ksu.zip /sdcard/
      ```
      
      Then either:
      
      - open your root manager (KernelSU / KSU Next / Magisk) → Modules → install the
        zip, or use MT Manager to pick it from `/sdcard/`, or
      - from a PC over ADB:
      
      ```bash
      adb shell su -c 'ksud module install /sdcard/treble-overlay-<device>-ksu.zip'
      ```
      
      Reboot when done.
      
      > **KernelSU / KSU Next:** install **Magic Mount** (or Hybrid Mount configured
      > for magic mount) before flashing overlay modules.

      ---
      
      ## 1. Prepare Termux
      
      ```bash
      termux-setup-storage
      
      apt update
      apt upgrade -y
      
      apt install -y git aapt aapt2 apksigner android-tools openjdk-17 \
                     unzip zip curl tsu
      ```
      
      If `pkg install` fails with signature or mirror errors, run
      `termux-change-repo`, pick a mirror close to you, then repeat `apt update`.
      
      > **`zipalign` comes from the `aapt` package, not from `aapt2`.** Installing
      > `aapt2`, `apksigner` and `android-tools` leaves `zipalign` missing; adding
      > `aapt` provides it. If it is still absent, `build.sh` continues and copies
      > the APK instead of aligning it (valid, just not mmap-aligned) and tells you
      > to run `pkg install aapt`.
      
      ---
      
      ## 2. Clone into the home directory
      
      ```bash
      cd ~

- path: stuff/scripts/toolchain.sh
  content: |
          return 1
      }
      
      install_linux_packages() {
          if $IS_TERMUX; then
              info "Termux detected — running: pkg install ..."
              # 'aapt' carries zipalign (the aapt2 package does not).
              if pkg install -y aapt aapt2 apksigner android-tools openjdk-17 unzip zip curl tsu; then
                  ok "Packages installed"
                  return 0
              fi
              warn "Package installation failed (often a repository mirror problem)."
              echo "     Run: termux-change-repo   → pick a nearby mirror"
              echo "     Then: apt update && ./build.sh setup"
              return 1
          fi
      
          if ! install_as_root; then
              # One machine-readable line, because the desktop app has no terminal to
              # prompt in: it asks for the password itself and re-runs the command
              # with SUDO_ASKPASS set. The pane strips this line, so nobody sees it.
              echo "@@RRO_SUDO_REQUIRED@@" >&2
              warn "Root privileges are needed to install the build tools."
              echo "     Run: $(package_install_hint)"
              echo "     Then re-run: ./build.sh"

**Copy to `/sdcard/treble-rro-creator` (Files tab → 1 Copy)**

`menu_files` now offers a copy action that writes every built output (the flashable zip and the APKs under `out/`) to one fixed destination, `/sdcard/treble-rro-creator`:

- **Termux** — plain `cp`, resolving storage through `$HOME/storage/shared` (with `/sdcard` as a fallback). If neither is visible it tells you to run `termux-setup-storage` instead of failing silently.
- **Desktop/Linux/Windows** — picks the device via the existing adb picker (`adb devices -l`, and `-s SERIAL` when there are several), creates the folder with `adb shell mkdir -p`, then pushes each file; MSYS paths are converted with `cygpath` under Git Bash so a Windows `adb` can open them.
- Each file is reported with a ✓ and its size, followed by `N file(s) in /sdcard/treble-rro-creator`, and partial failures are counted rather than hidden. Documented under "6. Install the module" in `docs/termux.md`.

**Why auto-tool install broke on Termux**

Three separate defects, all in `download_platform_resources` / the download path in `stuff/scripts/toolchain.sh`:

1. **Your `curl` cannot start** (`CANNOT LINK EXECUTABLE "curl": cannot locate symbol SSL_set_quic_tls_early_data_enabled` — an interrupted `pkg upgrade`). `command -v curl` still succeeded, so every download failed and reported "Google may have moved the files". Downloads now go through `net_get`, which tries `curl` then `wget`, and keeps *all* attempt errors so the final message names the real fix (`pkg upgrade -y`, `termux-change-repo`, or `pkg install wget`).
2. **The revision list was fiction.** Only `r01`/`r02` exist for API 33/35/36 and API 34 is published as `platform-34-ext7_r*`, not `platform-34_r*` — so the "Download Android 14" option could never work, and the list also built an empty-revision URL.
3. **No validation of what arrived.** A download now has to start with `PK` before it is unpacked, so an error page can't masquerade as a platform archive. The same fallback covers the `aapt2` jar and command-line-tools downloads, and `wget` was added to the Termux package lists (script + docs).

- `bash -n` clean on every `stuff/scripts/*.sh`, `build.sh`, `treble-rro-creator.sh`; suite **111 tests, 111 pass**.
- Real download of `platform-33_r02.zip` → `framework-res.apk` (26 MB) installed.
- Stub `curl` emitting your exact linker error → `wget` took over and installed the resources; with both stubbed broken, the output is the Termux advice above.
- Copy tested in both modes with stubs: Termux wrote both files into the storage mirror; desktop issued `devices -l`, `-s ZY22ABC123 get-state`, `shell mkdir -p /sdcard/treble-rro-creator`, then two `push` calls.

Limitations: not exercised on a real Termux install or a physically cabled phone — the phone/DNS behaviour is inferred from the stubs and the live Google request. The API 34 `ext7` names were confirmed present (HTTP 200), but only API 33 was downloaded and extracted end to end.

      # Treble RRO Creator
      
      Build a **Magisk / KernelSU / APatch module** that adapts a GSI (Generic System Image) to
      your phone's hardware: rounded corners, display cutout, brightness curve, UDFPS,
      AOD/doze, 5G/VoLTE — and optional vendor HALs for fingerprint or vibrator.
      
      Two ways in, same tool: the **desktop app**, which puts every setting and the
      whole build in a window, or the **terminal menu**, which offers the same things
      in a numbered list. Both edit the same `config.env` and run the same build.
      
      ```bash
      treble-rro-creator.cmd    # Windows: the app (double-click it too)
      ./treble-rro-creator.sh   # Linux: the app
      ./build.sh                # the terminal menu: Linux / Termux / Git Bash
      build.cmd                 #                      Windows
      ```
      
      The first run installs the Android build tools automatically (about 33 MB on
      disk; on Linux it uses your package manager when permitted, and otherwise
      prints the exact command to run). Every later run goes straight to the menu.
      No terminal (a script, a CI job)? `./build.sh` without a terminal still builds,
      and `./build.sh build` always builds.

      ## Requirements
      
      | Platform | What you need |
      |---|---|
      | **Windows** | [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) + JDK 17 or newer (`winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.17.JDK`) |
      | **Linux** | `bash`, `curl`, `unzip`, `zip` and JDK 17+. `./build.sh` can install the rest with your package manager, or use `./build.sh setup` |
      | **Termux** | Termux from **F-Droid** (not Google Play). See [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md) |
      | **Phone** | A GSI-based ROM and a root manager (KernelSU, KSU Next, APatch or Magisk) |
      
      ---
      
      ## Quick start
      
      ### Desktop app (Windows / Linux)
      
      The window is the same tool: it finds the clone it lives in, edits `config.env`,
      and runs the same `build.sh` commands — **Build**, **Dry run**, **Check**,
      **Doctor**, **Setup**, **Clean** — with the output streaming into a pane.
      Nothing is reimplemented, so the app and the CLI can be mixed freely.
      
      It also covers what used to need a terminal: `config.env` as a form (a switch
      per setting, ⓘ for the note the file already carries, the raw file one click
      away); a **Device** tab with an adb console, the commands worth running on a
      phone, and a button that installs platform-tools if you do not have them; and a
      **Files** tab that is the `src/` workspace — drop a vendor HAL tree in, disable
      a file out of the build without deleting it, and write the SELinux rules and
      VINTF manifests a custom HAL needs, checked as you type; and a **UDFPS** tab
      that finds the sensor's real geometry on the phone or in an OEM firmware — a
      `super.img`, a Samsung `AP_*.tar.md5` or an extracted tree, all unpacked by the
      app itself — with the source of every answer, instead of asking you to guess
      three numbers.
      The header tells you
      when a newer release exists, and an update that would overwrite your own edits
      asks first and backs them up.
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator
      cd treble-rro-creator
      ./treble-rro-creator.sh   # Linux   — builds itself first (Go and missing GTK/WebKitGTK headers are installed for you)
      treble-rro-creator.cmd    # Windows — double-clickable, no console left open; Go and MinGW-w64 gcc are downloaded
      ```
      
      The first launch builds it and says what is missing if anything is. **Setup**,
      and the first build, install the Android tools with the distro's package
      manager — when sudo asks for a password, the app asks for it in a dialog and
      repeats the command, so nothing has to be typed into a terminal. Later launches
      open straight away, and a `git pull` only triggers a rebuild when the Go
      sources actually changed. Full guide, including what each button does and what
      to do when no window appears: [docs/gui.md](docs/gui.md).
      
      ### Windows (command line)
      
      1. Install **Git for Windows** and **JDK 17+**.
      2. Clone or download this project.
      3. Double-click **`build.cmd`**.
      
      From a terminal (cmd, PowerShell, VS Code) run `build.cmd` — from PowerShell use
      `.\build.cmd`. Do **not** run the `.sh` files in a WSL terminal on a Windows
      drive; see [docs/windows.md](docs/windows.md) for why and what to do instead.
      
      ### Linux
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator
      cd treble-rro-creator
      ./build.sh
      ```
      
      ### Termux
      
      ```bash

      ```
      
      Full Termux walkthrough: [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md).
      
      ### The terminal menu (Linux / Termux / Git Bash)
      
      `./build.sh` with no arguments opens a menu. It runs the same build, the same
      `config.env`, and the same phone probes as the window, so nothing needs the app

      ```
        Treble Overlay Creator
        ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Device      Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 (Zephyr)
        config.env  49 set · 37 off
        Output      out/treble-overlay-xiaomi-zephyr-hardware-overlay-test.zip  (2 APKs)
      
           1  Build              dry run, build, check, doctor, clean
           2  config.env         browse and edit one key at a time
           3  Addons             module tweaks: settings and overlay resources
           4  Device             read manufacturer, model, codename from the phone
           5  Auto Detect        ROM answers: cutout, corners, refresh rate, VoLTE, 5G
           6  UDFPS              in-display fingerprint geometry
           7  Match property     which property the submission should match on
           8  Files              what was built, and where it is
           9  Docs               the guides in docs/
           q  Quit
      ```
      
      Each screen says what the setting does before you change it, writes straight to
      `config.env`, and offers the phone-reading tools (`adb devices`-style detection,
      the display probe, UDFPS geometry, the submission match property) instead of
      asking you to run `getprop` and copy numbers by hand. A build started here is
      the same `build.sh build` you would type.
      
      Termux has no window, so this is the full interface there. It also runs over
      ssh, in VS Code's terminal, and in Git Bash.
      
      In Termux the probes read **this** phone instead of one on a cable — the menu
      offers it once per session and the same `getprop`/`dumpsys`/`/vendor` reads run
      natively. That needs root: start it with `tsu ./build.sh` (`pkg install tsu`),
      or accept the `su` prompt when the menu asks. Details in
      [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md#5-root-for-the-phone-probes).
      
      ---
      
      ## Configure your device
      
      Open `config.env`. Only a few values are required:
      
      | Setting | What it is | How to find it |
      |---|---|---|
      | `DEVICE_CODENAME` | Device codename, e.g. `r3q` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.device` |
      | `DEVICE_MANUFACTURER` | Manufacturer, e.g. `samsung` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer` |
      | `DEVICE_MODEL` | Model name, e.g. `SM-A908N` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.model` |
      | `DEVICE_PROP_NAME` | Property the overlay matches | `persist.sys.overlay.<codename>` (set by the module), or empty for no condition |
      | `DEVICE_PROP_VALUE` | Value the overlay matches | `true` for a `persist.sys.*` property |
      | `ROUNDED_CORNER_RADIUS` | Screen corner radius in px | Measure or take from your stock overlay |
      | `STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT` | Status bar height in px | Take from your stock overlay |
      
      Everything else is optional and documented in
      [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md).
      
      > **First run without `config.env`?** `build.sh` offers the example config
      > (Samsung A90 5G) or writes a placeholder and tells you what to edit.
      >
      > **`power_profile.xml` matters.** Replace
      > `src/framework/res/xml/power_profile.xml` with your device's file —
      > see [docs/device-extraction.md](docs/device-extraction.md#power-profile-power_profilexml--mandatory).
      > Until you do, the empty template is detected and **left out** of the APK
      > instead of wiping the GSI's battery and CPU data.
      
      ---
      
      ## Commands
      
      `build.sh` and `build.cmd` are the only entry points. Everything else in the
      project is called by them.
      
      | Command | What it does |
      |---|---|
      | `./treble-rro-creator.sh` / `treble-rro-creator.cmd` | **Open the desktop app** — the window for everything below. Builds it on the first run, then just launches it. |
      | `./build.sh` | **The terminal menu** (on a terminal); a plain build without a terminal. |
      | `./build.sh menu` | The menu, even when there is no terminal |
      | `./build.sh build` | Build. Installs missing tools first. |
      | `./build.sh setup` | Install or repair the toolchain (menu: distro / resource version) |
      | `./build.sh doctor` | Check the toolchain, install nothing (exit 0 = ready) |
      | `./build.sh check` | Validate `config.env`, build nothing |
      | `./build.sh --dry-run` | Print the resources `config.env` emits, build nothing |
      | `./build.sh clean` | Remove `stuff/build/` and `out/` |
      | `./build.sh clean --all` | Start over for a different device (restores templates) |
      
      Options: `-y` / `--yes` (no prompts), `--with-vendor-hals` (with `--yes`),
      `--dry-run` (resource plan only), `--allow-unknown-resources` (build even when a
      resource is missing from the dictionary — see the audit note below), `--force`
      (with `setup`: re-pick the resource dictionary), `--help`.
      
      `--dry-run` is the fast feedback loop: it generates the resource XML from
      `config.env` and prints every resource it would emit (type, name, value, which
      overlay APK), without aapt2, signing or packaging. `check` reports the same
      config warnings and stops there.
      
      To check the project itself (the WebUI's resource-table writer, the manifest it
      renders from, script syntax, documentation anchors):
      
      ```bash
      bash stuff/tests/run.sh    # what CI runs, no Android tools needed
      ```
      
      On Windows, use the same words with `build.cmd`:
      `build.cmd setup`, `build.cmd doctor`, `build.cmd clean --all`.
      
      ---
      
      ## Output
      
      Everything is written to `out/`:
      
      | File | Purpose |
      |---|---|
      | `out/apks/<name>.apk` | Framework overlay (signed) |
      | `out/apks/<name>-systemui.apk` | SystemUI overlay (signed, if used) |
      | `out/<name>-ksu.zip` | **Module zip** — install this in any supported manager |
      | `out/<name>-hardware-overlay.zip` | Sources to submit to the Doze-off overlay repo |
      | `out/<name>-hardware-overlay-test.zip` | Test build of the repo version |
      
      Install `out/<name>-ksu.zip` in KernelSU, KSU Next, APatch or Magisk and reboot.
      
      ### Getting it built into the GSI (no module)
      
      `out/<name>-hardware-overlay.zip` is the source tree the
      [Doze-off overlay repo](https://github.com/Doze-off/vendor_hardware_overlay)
      compiles into the GSI builds: submit it as a pull request (base branch `pie`)
      and the device gets the overlay with no module to install or update. The zip
      contains the exact folders, the `overlay.mk` lines and a `HOW-TO-SUBMIT.md`
      filled in for your device; read **[docs/submission.md](docs/submission.md)**
      first — the wiki's `+*brand/model*` match pattern never matches anything, and
      this project writes the exact value instead.
      The zip is a standard module: the same file works in all four managers (the
      `-ksu` suffix is historical; it is not KernelSU-only). It contains the normal
      `customize.sh` that KSU/APatch source and Magisk's `META-INF` installer, plus
      the shared `webroot/` page.
      
      > ⚠ **KernelSU / KSU Next:** use **Magic Mount** (or Hybrid Mount with magic
      > mount). **Do not use OverlayFS** — it mounts the module fine, but a single
      > mistake in your own `sepolicy.rule` or VINTF manifests then bootloops the
      > device, where magic mount ignores the bad file and boots anyway.
      > Why: [docs/how-it-works.md](docs/how-it-works.md#why-a-module-is-needed).
      >
      > ⚠ Do not copy APKs into `/system/product/overlay/` by hand. Dynamic
      > partitions do not keep them, and they miss the permissions the module sets.
      
      ### Live editing (module WebUI)
      
      The module ships a page under `webroot/`. Open the module and tap **WebUI** to
      change the corner radius, status bar height/padding and a few toggles, then
      apply them **without rebuilding or reflashing**: the page writes the value into
      `resources.arsc` of the overlay APK that is already installed (a pristine copy
      is kept for **Reset**) and restarts the framework so it is read. A value the
      build did not ship — `config.env` leaves the optional padding keys commented
      out — is added to that table first, so a commented-out key no longer blocks the
      sliders. That is the only way to set a dimension at runtime —
      `cmd overlay fabricate` rejects the dimension type outright, so it is only used
      for the doze boolean.
      
      - **KernelSU / KSU Next / APatch:** built in — the module page has a WebUI
        button.
      - **Magisk:** the official app has no WebUI. Open the same page with a WebUI
        host such as **WebUI X** (MMRL / portable), **KsuWebUI** or **MMRL**. They
        provide a root exec bridge that the page detects, so the page and helper are
        shared by every manager.
      
      Below the five sliders, **All resources** lists everything else the build
      writes — booleans, integers, strings and the remaining dimens — from
      `webui-manifest.json`, which `build.sh` generates from the same XML it compiles.
      Values that are not one value (auto-brightness arrays, landscape-only configs,
      `power_profile.xml`) are shown read-only and still need a rebuild.
      
      Two safety nets: saved values survive a module update (they re-apply onto the
      new APKs the next time the page is opened), and if a patch ever prevents a
      complete boot the next boot restores the build's APKs automatically. Details
      and limits: [docs/webui.md](docs/webui.md).
      
      ### Module addons (things `config.env` does not cover)
      
      The **Addons** tab is the module's own feature set: tweaks that are neither a
      `config.env` key nor a plain overlay resource. **Live** addons are Settings
      values the module writes itself — the volume panel side, a screen that never
      sleeps, hiding the status-bar clock, the captive-portal probe. **Overlay**
      addons are resources the build bakes in — upside-down rotation, a navigation bar
      with no padding but the pill kept, a status bar with no background, and a notch
      the display is masked away from so nothing can draw under the camera. Pick them
      in the app and they are packed into the module (`src/module/addons.conf`). From
      the module's WebUI both kinds can be changed: live ones immediately (and they are
      re-applied on every boot), overlay ones by **Apply**, which writes the resource
      into the installed APK — and **Use default** removes it again. Only the addons
      you chose are enforced, so an untouched install behaves exactly like the ROM.
      Details: [docs/addons.md](docs/addons.md).
      
      Both overlays are **static** RROs: Android enables them during boot, and
      `cmd overlay enable` cannot change them afterwards. Verify after reboot:
      
      ```bash
      adb shell cmd overlay list | grep <your-package>
      adb shell cmd overlay lookup <your-package> android:dimen/rounded_corner_radius
      adb shell cmd overlay lookup <your-package> android:dimen/status_bar_height_default
      ```
      
      Every build also writes `out/<name>-overrides.txt`, listing each resource as
      `APPLIES` or `IGNORED` against the target framework. If a generated name does
      not exist in the target, the build refuses to continue — a resource Android
      does not recognise is silently ignored, which is how an overlay can look
      correct and change nothing.
      
      The status bar uses `status_bar_height_default` (Android 12L+), not the old
      `status_bar_height`; both are generated, including a landscape variant. See
      [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#status-bar-height).
      
      ---
      
      ## Project layout
      
      ```
      .
      ├── build.sh / build.cmd        ← the command line
      ├── treble-rro-creator.sh/.cmd  ← desktop app: build if stale, then launch
      ├── config.env                  ← your device settings (created on first run)
      ├── config.env.example          ← filled-in Samsung A90 5G example
      ├── src/
      │   ├── framework/res/          framework overlay resources (+ power_profile.xml)
      │   ├── systemui/res/          SystemUI overlay resources
      │   ├── module/                 optional overrides + sepolicy.rule
      │   ├── webui/                  shared WebUI page + apply.sh (packed as webroot/)
      │   └── vendor/                 optional extracted vendor HALs (git-ignored)
      ├── docs/                       guides
      ├── out/                        APKs and flashable zips (git-ignored)
      ├── gui/                        desktop app sources (+ go.mod at the root)
      └── stuff/                      everything the build uses and you do not
          ├── scripts/                internals used by build.sh and the menu (not run directly)
          ├── templates/              reference scripts + clean templates
          ├── keys/                   platform signing key (shipped)
          ├── windows/                helpers for build.cmd
          ├── tests/                  the checks CI runs
          ├── tools/                  downloaded toolchain (git-ignored)
          ├── build/                  intermediate files (git-ignored)
          └── backups/                copies made before clean/rebuild (git-ignored)
      ```
      
      The root keeps only what you act on: the two entry points, `config.env`, `src/`
      (the resources you edit), `docs/`, `gui/` and `out/` (where the APKs and zips
      appear). Everything else moved into `stuff/` — one folder instead of nine. The
      signing key, the templates, the tests and the downloaded toolchain all keep
      their own names there, so `keys/platform.pk8` became
      `stuff/keys/platform.pk8`.
      
      ---
      
      ## Coming from an older version?
      
      The scripts were merged and the folders reorganised. Old commands and files
      still work like this:
      
      | You used to run | Run now |
      |---|---|
      | `./setup.sh` / `setup.cmd` | `./build.sh setup` / `build.cmd setup` |
      | `./setup.sh --doctor` / `setup.cmd --doctor` | `./build.sh doctor` / `build.cmd doctor` |
      | `./cleanup.sh` / `cleanup.cmd` | `./build.sh clean` / `build.cmd clean` |
      | `./build.sh` / `build.cmd` | unchanged, but with no arguments it now opens the menu on a terminal (use `build` for the old behaviour) |
      
      | Old location | New location |
      |---|---|
      | `res/` | `src/framework/res/` |
      | `systemui_overlay/res/` | `src/systemui/res/` |
      | `customize.sh`, `service.sh`, `sepolicy.rule` | `src/module/` (scripts are generated by default) |
      | `system/vendor/` | `src/vendor/` |
      | `TEMPLATE RECOVERIES (Don't touch)/` | `stuff/templates/recoveries/` (fallback for `clean --all` when there is no `.git`) |
      | `YOUR BACKUPS/` | `stuff/backups/` |
      | `keys/`, `scripts/`, `templates/`, `tests/`, `windows/`, `tools/`, `build/`, `backups/` | the same names inside `stuff/` |
      
      `build.sh` moves anything it still finds in the old places into the new layout
      on the next run: the file is copied first and the old location is removed only
      afterwards, so an existing checkout keeps working after a `git pull`. If both
      locations exist, it warns and leaves the old one alone instead of overwriting
      the new one.
      
      ---

      |---|---|
      | [docs/submission.md](docs/submission.md) | Getting the overlay built into the GSI (Doze-off repo PR) |
      | [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) | Every `config.env` option |
      | [docs/webui.md](docs/webui.md) | KernelSU WebUI: change values without rebuilding |
      | [docs/addons.md](docs/addons.md) | Module addons: live Settings (screen timeout, volume panel side) and overlay ones (180° rotation, navigation-bar padding) |
      | [docs/windows.md](docs/windows.md) | Windows, PowerShell, VS Code and WSL |
      | [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md) | Building on the phone |
      | [docs/device-extraction.md](docs/device-extraction.md) | Extracting vendor HALs and `power_profile.xml` |
      | [docs/udfps.md](docs/udfps.md) | Finding UDFPS coordinates and enabling the touch-panel FOD mode |
      | [docs/detect.md](docs/detect.md) | Reading the cutout, corner radius, status bar and refresh rate off the device or a ROM |
      | [docs/troubleshooting.md](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Doctor, bootloops, SELinux, overlay inactive |
      | [docs/how-it-works.md](docs/how-it-works.md) | RROs, module mechanics, build steps |

- path: stuff/tests/docs-links.js
  content: |
      /* Every relative link in the docs and the README has to point at a real file
         and, when it carries #anchor, at a heading that exists. The docs cross-link a
         lot (config.env points into docs/configuration.md, troubleshooting points at
         sections elsewhere), and a renamed heading otherwise only shows up as a dead
         link on GitHub.
      
         Run: node stuff/tests/docs-links.js */
      "use strict";
      
      const fs = require("fs");
      const path = require("path");
      
      const ROOT = path.join(__dirname, "..", "..");
      const errors = [];
      
      // GitHub's heading slug: lowercase, drop everything that is not a letter,
      // digit, space, hyphen or underscore, then spaces -> hyphens. Spaces are not
      // collapsed: "padding (start / end)" becomes "padding-start--end", which is
      // why the anchors in these docs have a double hyphen.
      function slug(text) {
        return text
          .trim()
          .toLowerCase()
          .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, "")
          .replace(/[`*~]/g, "")
          .replace(/[^\p{L}\p{N}\s_-]/gu, "")
          .replace(/ /g, "-");
      }
      
      function anchorsOf(file) {
        const text = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf8");
        const out = new Set();
        const seen = new Map();
        for (const line of text.split(/\r?\n/)) {
          const m = /^(#{1,6})\s+(.*)$/.exec(line);
          if (!m) continue;
          const base = slug(m[2]);
          // GitHub suffixes repeated headings: name, name-1, name-2 …
          const n = seen.get(base) || 0;
          seen.set(base, n + 1);
          out.add(n === 0 ? base : base + "-" + n);
        }
        return out;
      }
      
      function markdownFiles(dir, acc = []) {
        for (const entry of fs.readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
          // Downloaded trees are not ours: Go's own docs come with the toolchain
          // fetch in gui/build.sh, and theirs are written for golang.org.
          if (entry.name === "node_modules" || entry.name.startsWith(".") ||
              entry.name.startsWith("_") || entry.name === "build" || entry.name === "out") continue;
          const full = path.join(dir, entry.name);
          if (entry.isDirectory()) markdownFiles(full, acc);
          else if (/\.md$/i.test(entry.name)) acc.push(full);
        }
        return acc;
      }
      
      const cache = new Map();
      function anchorsFor(file) {
        if (!cache.has(file)) cache.set(file, anchorsOf(file));
        return cache.get(file);
      }
      
      for (const file of markdownFiles(ROOT)) {
        const text = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf8");
        const rel = path.relative(ROOT, file).replace(/\\/g, "/");
        // [text](target) — the target is everything up to the first ) or space.
        const linkRe = /\]\(([^)\s]+)(?:\s+"[^"]*")?\)/g;
        let m;
        while ((m = linkRe.exec(text)) !== null) {
          const raw = m[1];
          if (/^(https?:|mailto:|#)/.test(raw)) continue;      // external or same-page
          const [target, hash] = raw.split("#");
          if (!target) continue;
          const resolved = path.resolve(path.dirname(file), decodeURI(target));
          if (!fs.existsSync(resolved)) {
            errors.push(`${rel}: ${raw} -> file not found`);
            continue;
          }
          if (hash && /\.md$/i.test(resolved)) {
            const anchors = anchorsFor(resolved);
            if (!anchors.has(decodeURIComponent(hash))) {
              errors.push(`${rel}: ${raw} -> no heading with that anchor`);
            }
          }
        }
      }
      
      if (errors.length) {
        console.error("Broken documentation links:");
        for (const e of errors) console.error("  " + e);
        process.exit(1);
      }
      console.log("docs: every relative link resolves");
      
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Everything that can be checked without Android tools
# =============================================================================
# CI runs this on every push (see .github/workflows/check.yml), and it is worth
# running before a release:
#
#   bash stuff/tests/run.sh
#
# 1. shell syntax of every shipped script (bash -n / sh -n, no execution)
# 2. the WebUI resource-table writer against stuff/tests/fixtures/*.apk
# 3. the WebUI manifest and the overlay-repo submission tree (Doze-off
#    vendor_hardware_overlay), built from
#    resource XML that stuff/tests/gen-res.sh generates into a temp directory (so
#    a fresh clone needs no build first)
# 4. every relative link and #anchor in the docs
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.."

status=0
step() { printf '\n== %s ==\n' "$*"; }

step "shell syntax"
for f in build.sh treble-rro-creator.sh gui/build.sh stuff/scripts/*.sh stuff/tests/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if bash -n "$f"; then :; else echo "bash -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
done
# apply.sh, addons.sh and the module scripts run under Android's mksh
# (/system/bin/sh).
for f in src/webui/apply.sh src/webui/addons.sh src/module/*.sh stuff/templates/*.sh stuff/templates/recoveries/*.sh; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if command -v sh >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        if sh -n "$f"; then :; else echo "sh -n failed: $f"; status=1; fi
    fi
done
[ "$status" -eq 0 ] && echo "all scripts parse"

````

- path: README.md
  content: |
      # Treble RRO Creator
      
      Build a **Magisk / KernelSU / APatch module** that adapts a GSI (Generic System Image) to
      your phone's hardware: rounded corners, display cutout, brightness curve, UDFPS,
      AOD/doze, 5G/VoLTE — and optional vendor HALs for fingerprint or vibrator.
      
      Two ways in, same tool: the **desktop app**, which puts every setting and the
      whole build in a window, or the **terminal menu**, which offers the same things
      in a numbered list. Both edit the same `config.env` and run the same build.
      
      ```bash
      treble-rro-creator.cmd    # Windows: the app (double-click it too)
      ./treble-rro-creator.sh   # Linux: the app
      ./build.sh                # the terminal menu: Linux / Termux / Git Bash
      build.cmd                 #                      Windows
      ```
      
      The first run installs the Android build tools automatically (about 33 MB on
      disk; on Linux it uses your package manager when permitted, and otherwise
      prints the exact command to run). Every later run goes straight to the menu.
      No terminal (a script, a CI job)? `./build.sh` without a terminal still builds,
      and `./build.sh build` always builds.
      
      ---
      
      ## Requirements
      
      | Platform | What you need |
      |---|---|
      | **Windows** | [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) + JDK 17 or newer (`winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.17.JDK`) |
      | **Linux** | `bash`, `curl`, `unzip`, `zip` and JDK 17+. `./build.sh` can install the rest with your package manager, or use `./build.sh setup` |
      | **Termux** | Termux from **F-Droid** (not Google Play). See [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md) |
      | **Phone** | A GSI-based ROM and a root manager (KernelSU, KSU Next, APatch or Magisk) |
      
      ---
      
      ## Quick start
      
      ### Desktop app (Windows / Linux)
      
      The window is the same tool: it finds the clone it lives in, edits `config.env`,
      and runs the same `build.sh` commands — **Build**, **Dry run**, **Check**,
      **Doctor**, **Setup**, **Clean** — with the output streaming into a pane.
      Nothing is reimplemented, so the app and the CLI can be mixed freely.
      
      It also covers what used to need a terminal: `config.env` as a form (a switch
      per setting, ⓘ for the note the file already carries, the raw file one click
      away); a **Device** tab with an adb console, the commands worth running on a
      phone, and a button that installs platform-tools if you do not have them; and a
      **Files** tab that is the `src/` workspace — drop a vendor HAL tree in, disable
      a file out of the build without deleting it, and write the SELinux rules and
      VINTF manifests a custom HAL needs, checked as you type; and a **UDFPS** tab
      that finds the sensor's real geometry on the phone or in an OEM firmware — a
      `super.img`, a Samsung `AP_*.tar.md5` or an extracted tree, all unpacked by the
      app itself — with the source of every answer, instead of asking you to guess
      three numbers.
      The header tells you
      when a newer release exists, and an update that would overwrite your own edits
      asks first and backs them up.
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator
      cd treble-rro-creator
      ./treble-rro-creator.sh   # Linux   — builds itself first (Go and missing GTK/WebKitGTK headers are installed for you)
      treble-rro-creator.cmd    # Windows — double-clickable, no console left open; Go and MinGW-w64 gcc are downloaded
      ```
      
      The first launch builds it and says what is missing if anything is. **Setup**,
      and the first build, install the Android tools with the distro's package
      manager — when sudo asks for a password, the app asks for it in a dialog and
      repeats the command, so nothing has to be typed into a terminal. Later launches
      open straight away, and a `git pull` only triggers a rebuild when the Go
      sources actually changed. Full guide, including what each button does and what
      to do when no window appears: [docs/gui.md](docs/gui.md).
      
      ### Windows (command line)
      
      1. Install **Git for Windows** and **JDK 17+**.
      2. Clone or download this project.
      3. Double-click **`build.cmd`**.
      
      From a terminal (cmd, PowerShell, VS Code) run `build.cmd` — from PowerShell use
      `.\build.cmd`. Do **not** run the `.sh` files in a WSL terminal on a Windows
      drive; see [docs/windows.md](docs/windows.md) for why and what to do instead.
      
      ### Linux
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator
      cd treble-rro-creator
      ./build.sh
      ```
      
      ### Termux
      
      ```bash
      pkg install -y git
      cd ~ && git clone https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator
      cd treble-rro-creator
      ./build.sh
      ```
      
      Full Termux walkthrough: [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md).
      
      ### The terminal menu (Linux / Termux / Git Bash)
      
      `./build.sh` with no arguments opens a menu. It runs the same build, the same
      `config.env`, and the same phone probes as the window, so nothing needs the app
      (and the app needs nothing from the menu):
      
      ```
        Treble Overlay Creator
        ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Device      Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 (Zephyr)
        config.env  49 set · 37 off
        Output      out/treble-overlay-xiaomi-zephyr-hardware-overlay-test.zip  (2 APKs)
      
           1  Build              dry run, build, check, doctor, clean
           2  config.env         browse and edit one key at a time
           3  Addons             module tweaks: settings and overlay resources
           4  Device             read manufacturer, model, codename from the phone
           5  Auto Detect        ROM answers: cutout, corners, refresh rate, VoLTE, 5G
           6  UDFPS              in-display fingerprint geometry
           7  Match property     which property the submission should match on
           8  Files              what was built, and where it is
           9  Docs               the guides in docs/
           q  Quit
      ```
      
      Each screen says what the setting does before you change it, writes straight to
      `config.env`, and offers the phone-reading tools (`adb devices`-style detection,
      the display probe, UDFPS geometry, the submission match property) instead of
      asking you to run `getprop` and copy numbers by hand. A build started here is
      the same `build.sh build` you would type.
      
      Termux has no window, so this is the full interface there. It also runs over
      ssh, in VS Code's terminal, and in Git Bash.
      
      In Termux the probes read **this** phone instead of one on a cable — the menu
      offers it once per session and the same `getprop`/`dumpsys`/`/vendor` reads run
      natively. That needs root: start it with `tsu ./build.sh` (`pkg install tsu`),
      or accept the `su` prompt when the menu asks. Details in
      [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md#5-root-for-the-phone-probes).
      
      ---
      
      ## Configure your device
      
      Open `config.env`. Only a few values are required:
      
      | Setting | What it is | How to find it |
      |---|---|---|
      | `DEVICE_CODENAME` | Device codename, e.g. `r3q` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.device` |
      | `DEVICE_MANUFACTURER` | Manufacturer, e.g. `samsung` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer` |
      | `DEVICE_MODEL` | Model name, e.g. `SM-A908N` | `adb shell getprop ro.product.model` |
      | `DEVICE_PROP_NAME` | Property the overlay matches | `persist.sys.overlay.<codename>` (set by the module), or empty for no condition |
      | `DEVICE_PROP_VALUE` | Value the overlay matches | `true` for a `persist.sys.*` property |
      | `ROUNDED_CORNER_RADIUS` | Screen corner radius in px | Measure or take from your stock overlay |
      | `STATUS_BAR_HEIGHT` | Status bar height in px | Take from your stock overlay |
      
      Everything else is optional and documented in
      [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md).
      
      > **First run without `config.env`?** `build.sh` offers the example config
      > (Samsung A90 5G) or writes a placeholder and tells you what to edit.
      >
      > **`power_profile.xml` matters.** Replace
      > `src/framework/res/xml/power_profile.xml` with your device's file —
      > see [docs/device-extraction.md](docs/device-extraction.md#power-profile-power_profilexml--mandatory).
      > Until you do, the empty template is detected and **left out** of the APK
      > instead of wiping the GSI's battery and CPU data.
      
      ---
      
      ## Commands
      
      `build.sh` and `build.cmd` are the only entry points. Everything else in the
      project is called by them.
      
      | Command | What it does |
      |---|---|
      | `./treble-rro-creator.sh` / `treble-rro-creator.cmd` | **Open the desktop app** — the window for everything below. Builds it on the first run, then just launches it. |
      | `./build.sh` | **The terminal menu** (on a terminal); a plain build without a terminal. |
      | `./build.sh menu` | The menu, even when there is no terminal |
      | `./build.sh build` | Build. Installs missing tools first. |
      | `./build.sh setup` | Install or repair the toolchain (menu: distro / resource version) |
      | `./build.sh doctor` | Check the toolchain, install nothing (exit 0 = ready) |
      | `./build.sh check` | Validate `config.env`, build nothing |
      | `./build.sh --dry-run` | Print the resources `config.env` emits, build nothing |
      | `./build.sh clean` | Remove `stuff/build/` and `out/` |
      | `./build.sh clean --all` | Start over for a different device (restores templates) |
      
      Options: `-y` / `--yes` (no prompts), `--with-vendor-hals` (with `--yes`),
      `--dry-run` (resource plan only), `--allow-unknown-resources` (build even when a
      resource is missing from the dictionary — see the audit note below), `--force`
      (with `setup`: re-pick the resource dictionary), `--help`.
      
      `--dry-run` is the fast feedback loop: it generates the resource XML from
      `config.env` and prints every resource it would emit (type, name, value, which
      overlay APK), without aapt2, signing or packaging. `check` reports the same
      config warnings and stops there.
      
      To check the project itself (the WebUI's resource-table writer, the manifest it
      renders from, script syntax, documentation anchors):
      
      ```bash
      bash stuff/tests/run.sh    # what CI runs, no Android tools needed
      ```
      
      On Windows, use the same words with `build.cmd`:
      `build.cmd setup`, `build.cmd doctor`, `build.cmd clean --all`.
      
      ---
      
      ## Output
      
      Everything is written to `out/`:
      
      | File | Purpose |
      |---|---|
      | `out/apks/<name>.apk` | Framework overlay (signed) |
      | `out/apks/<name>-systemui.apk` | SystemUI overlay (signed, if used) |
      | `out/<name>-ksu.zip` | **Module zip** — install this in any supported manager |
      | `out/<name>-hardware-overlay.zip` | Sources to submit to the Doze-off overlay repo |
      | `out/<name>-hardware-overlay-test.zip` | Test build of the repo version |
      
      Install `out/<name>-ksu.zip` in KernelSU, KSU Next, APatch or Magisk and reboot.
      
      ### Getting it built into the GSI (no module)
      
      `out/<name>-hardware-overlay.zip` is the source tree the
      [Doze-off overlay repo](https://github.com/Doze-off/vendor_hardware_overlay)
      compiles into the GSI builds: submit it as a pull request (base branch `pie`)
      and the device gets the overlay with no module to install or update. The zip
      contains the exact folders, the `overlay.mk` lines and a `HOW-TO-SUBMIT.md`
      filled in for your device; read **[docs/submission.md](docs/submission.md)**
      first — the wiki's `+*brand/model*` match pattern never matches anything, and
      this project writes the exact value instead.
      The zip is a standard module: the same file works in all four managers (the
      `-ksu` suffix is historical; it is not KernelSU-only). It contains the normal
      `customize.sh` that KSU/APatch source and Magisk's `META-INF` installer, plus
      the shared `webroot/` page.
      
      > ⚠ **KernelSU / KSU Next:** use **Magic Mount** (or Hybrid Mount with magic
      > mount). **Do not use OverlayFS** — it mounts the module fine, but a single
      > mistake in your own `sepolicy.rule` or VINTF manifests then bootloops the
      > device, where magic mount ignores the bad file and boots anyway.
      > Why: [docs/how-it-works.md](docs/how-it-works.md#why-a-module-is-needed).
      >
      > ⚠ Do not copy APKs into `/system/product/overlay/` by hand. Dynamic
      > partitions do not keep them, and they miss the permissions the module sets.
      
      ### Live editing (module WebUI)
      
      The module ships a page under `webroot/`. Open the module and tap **WebUI** to
      change the corner radius, status bar height/padding and a few toggles, then
      apply them **without rebuilding or reflashing**: the page writes the value into
      `resources.arsc` of the overlay APK that is already installed (a pristine copy
      is kept for **Reset**) and restarts the framework so it is read. A value the
      build did not ship — `config.env` leaves the optional padding keys commented
      out — is added to that table first, so a commented-out key no longer blocks the
      sliders. That is the only way to set a dimension at runtime —
      `cmd overlay fabricate` rejects the dimension type outright, so it is only used
      for the doze boolean.
      
      - **KernelSU / KSU Next / APatch:** built in — the module page has a WebUI
        button.
      - **Magisk:** the official app has no WebUI. Open the same page with a WebUI
        host such as **WebUI X** (MMRL / portable), **KsuWebUI** or **MMRL**. They
        provide a root exec bridge that the page detects, so the page and helper are
        shared by every manager.
      
      Below the five sliders, **All resources** lists everything else the build
      writes — booleans, integers, strings and the remaining dimens — from
      `webui-manifest.json`, which `build.sh` generates from the same XML it compiles.
      Values that are not one value (auto-brightness arrays, landscape-only configs,
      `power_profile.xml`) are shown read-only and still need a rebuild.
      
      Two safety nets: saved values survive a module update (they re-apply onto the
      new APKs the next time the page is opened), and if a patch ever prevents a
      complete boot the next boot restores the build's APKs automatically. Details
      and limits: [docs/webui.md](docs/webui.md).
      
      ### Module addons (things `config.env` does not cover)
      
      The **Addons** tab is the module's own feature set: tweaks that are neither a
      `config.env` key nor a plain overlay resource. **Live** addons are Settings
      values the module writes itself — the volume panel side, a screen that never
      sleeps, hiding the status-bar clock, the captive-portal probe. **Overlay**
      addons are resources the build bakes in — upside-down rotation, a navigation bar
      with no padding but the pill kept, a status bar with no background, and a notch
      the display is masked away from so nothing can draw under the camera. Pick them
      in the app and they are packed into the module (`src/module/addons.conf`). From
      the module's WebUI both kinds can be changed: live ones immediately (and they are
      re-applied on every boot), overlay ones by **Apply**, which writes the resource
      into the installed APK — and **Use default** removes it again. Only the addons
      you chose are enforced, so an untouched install behaves exactly like the ROM.
      Details: [docs/addons.md](docs/addons.md).
      
      Both overlays are **static** RROs: Android enables them during boot, and
      `cmd overlay enable` cannot change them afterwards. Verify after reboot:
      
      ```bash
      adb shell cmd overlay list | grep <your-package>
      adb shell cmd overlay lookup <your-package> android:dimen/rounded_corner_radius
      adb shell cmd overlay lookup <your-package> android:dimen/status_bar_height_default
      ```
      
      Every build also writes `out/<name>-overrides.txt`, listing each resource as
      `APPLIES` or `IGNORED` against the target framework. If a generated name does
      not exist in the target, the build refuses to continue — a resource Android
      does not recognise is silently ignored, which is how an overlay can look
      correct and change nothing.
      
      The status bar uses `status_bar_height_default` (Android 12L+), not the old
      `status_bar_height`; both are generated, including a landscape variant. See
      [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#status-bar-height).
      
      ---
      
      ## Project layout
      
      ```
      .
      ├── build.sh / build.cmd        ← the command line
      ├── treble-rro-creator.sh/.cmd  ← desktop app: build if stale, then launch
      ├── config.env                  ← your device settings (created on first run)
      ├── config.env.example          ← filled-in Samsung A90 5G example
      ├── src/
      │   ├── framework/res/          framework overlay resources (+ power_profile.xml)
      │   ├── systemui/res/          SystemUI overlay resources
      │   ├── module/                 optional overrides + sepolicy.rule
      │   ├── webui/                  shared WebUI page + apply.sh (packed as webroot/)
      │   └── vendor/                 optional extracted vendor HALs (git-ignored)
      ├── docs/                       guides
      ├── out/                        APKs and flashable zips (git-ignored)
      ├── gui/                        desktop app sources (+ go.mod at the root)
      └── stuff/                      everything the build uses and you do not
          ├── scripts/                internals used by build.sh and the menu (not run directly)
          ├── templates/              reference scripts + clean templates
          ├── keys/                   platform signing key (shipped)
          ├── windows/                helpers for build.cmd
          ├── tests/                  the checks CI runs
          ├── tools/                  downloaded toolchain (git-ignored)
          ├── build/                  intermediate files (git-ignored)
          └── backups/                copies made before clean/rebuild (git-ignored)
      ```
      
      The root keeps only what you act on: the two entry points, `config.env`, `src/`
      (the resources you edit), `docs/`, `gui/` and `out/` (where the APKs and zips
      appear). Everything else moved into `stuff/` — one folder instead of nine. The
      signing key, the templates, the tests and the downloaded toolchain all keep
      their own names there, so `keys/platform.pk8` became
      `stuff/keys/platform.pk8`.
      
      ---
      
      ## Coming from an older version?
      
      The scripts were merged and the folders reorganised. Old commands and files
      still work like this:
      
      | You used to run | Run now |
      |---|---|
      | `./setup.sh` / `setup.cmd` | `./build.sh setup` / `build.cmd setup` |
      | `./setup.sh --doctor` / `setup.cmd --doctor` | `./build.sh doctor` / `build.cmd doctor` |
      | `./cleanup.sh` / `cleanup.cmd` | `./build.sh clean` / `build.cmd clean` |
      | `./build.sh` / `build.cmd` | unchanged, but with no arguments it now opens the menu on a terminal (use `build` for the old behaviour) |
      
      | Old location | New location |
      |---|---|
      | `res/` | `src/framework/res/` |
      | `systemui_overlay/res/` | `src/systemui/res/` |
      | `customize.sh`, `service.sh`, `sepolicy.rule` | `src/module/` (scripts are generated by default) |
      | `system/vendor/` | `src/vendor/` |
      | `TEMPLATE RECOVERIES (Don't touch)/` | `stuff/templates/recoveries/` (fallback for `clean --all` when there is no `.git`) |
      | `YOUR BACKUPS/` | `stuff/backups/` |
      | `keys/`, `scripts/`, `templates/`, `tests/`, `windows/`, `tools/`, `build/`, `backups/` | the same names inside `stuff/` |
      
      `build.sh` moves anything it still finds in the old places into the new layout
      on the next run: the file is copied first and the old location is removed only
      afterwards, so an existing checkout keeps working after a `git pull`. If both
      locations exist, it warns and leaves the old one alone instead of overwriting
      the new one.
      
      ---
      
      ## Documentation
      
      | Guide | Contents |
      |---|---|
      | [docs/submission.md](docs/submission.md) | Getting the overlay built into the GSI (Doze-off repo PR) |
      | [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) | Every `config.env` option |
      | [docs/webui.md](docs/webui.md) | KernelSU WebUI: change values without rebuilding |
      | [docs/addons.md](docs/addons.md) | Module addons: live Settings (screen timeout, volume panel side) and overlay ones (180° rotation, navigation-bar padding) |
      | [docs/windows.md](docs/windows.md) | Windows, PowerShell, VS Code and WSL |
      | [docs/termux.md](docs/termux.md) | Building on the phone |
      | [docs/device-extraction.md](docs/device-extraction.md) | Extracting vendor HALs and `power_profile.xml` |
      | [docs/udfps.md](docs/udfps.md) | Finding UDFPS coordinates and enabling the touch-panel FOD mode |
      | [docs/detect.md](docs/detect.md) | Reading the cutout, corner radius, status bar and refresh rate off the device or a ROM |
      | [docs/troubleshooting.md](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Doctor, bootloops, SELinux, overlay inactive |
      | [docs/how-it-works.md](docs/how-it-works.md) | RROs, module mechanics, build steps |
      
      ---
      
      *Built for the GSI community. Reference device: Samsung Galaxy A90 5G (SM-A908N / r3q).*
      
      MIT licensed — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

builds itself first |\n| `config.env` | Your device values |\n| `src/framework/res/`, `src/systemui/res/` | Overlay resources you edit |\n| `src/module/` | Module overrides, `sepolicy.rule`, `addons.conf` |\n| `src/webui/` | WebUI page and `apply.sh`, packed as `webroot/` |\n| `src/vendor/` | Extracted vendor HALs, optional and git-ignored |\n| `out/` | APKs, zips, override report (git-ignored) |\n| `gui/` | Desktop app sources (GTK + WebKit, Go) |\n| `docs/` | Guides |\n| `stuff/` | Scripts, templates, signing key, tests, downloaded tools, build scratch |\n\n## Docs\n\n| Guide | Covers |\n|---|---|\n| [configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) | Every `config.env` key |\n| [detect.md](docs/detect.md) | Reading cutout, corners, status bar, refresh rate |\n| [udfps.md](docs/udfps.md) | Fingerprint coordinates and touch-panel FOD mode |\n| [addons.md](docs/addons.md) | Module tweaks |\n| [webui.md](docs/webui.md) | Editing values after install |\n| [submission.md](docs/submission.md) | Getting the overlay into the GSI |\n| [device-extraction.md](docs/device-extraction.md) | Vendor HALs and `power_profile.xml` |\n| [gui.md](docs/gui.md) | Desktop app |\n| [windows.md](docs/windows.md) | Windows, PowerShell, WSL |\n| [termux.md](docs/termux.md) | Building on the phone |\n| [troubleshooting.md](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Build failures, bootloops, inactive overlays |\n| [how-it-works.md](docs/how-it-works.md) | RRO mechanics and build steps |\n\n## Upgrading from an older layout\n\n`build.sh` moves anything it finds in the old paths (`res/`, `systemui_overlay/res/`, `YOUR BACKUPS/`, root-level `scripts/` and friends) into the current ones on the next run, copying first and deleting afterwards.       <p align="center">
        <a href="https://github.com/uzbforce/treble-rro-creator"><img alt="Platform" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows%20%7C%20Linux%20%7C%20Termux-B93D0E?style=flat-square"></a>
